Lectures on YouTube by Achim Krause and Thomas Nikolaus

_________________________________________________________________ WHAT’S A PUBLISHER?

 

Abstract

These are notes taken live while watching the YouTube lectures about topological cyclic homology by Thomas Nikolaus and Achim Krause. Note that we use homological grading throughout because the lecturers are homotopy theorists.

__________________________________________________________________________________

Motivation: trace methods

One motivation to study topological cyclic homology is its relation to crystalline cohomology and syntomic cohomology in arithmetic geometry. However, this is very involved, so we will not discuss it in depth. We will instead discuss the original motivation, which are trace methods in algebraic K-theory.

Let R be a ring. There is an invariant, called algebraic K-theory, which produces groups K∗(R) for all ∗≥0. These are very important, but are almost impossible to compute or to understand structurally. For example, even K∗(ℤ) is not very well-understood. They are known in all odd degrees, conjectured to vanish in degrees divisible by 4 (this is equivalent to the Kummer-Vandiver conjecture in number theory).

If you are a topologist, then one motivation is to study whether a retract X of a finite CW complex is itself a finite CW complex. The obstruction to this lies in

K∗(ℤ[π1(X)]).

Another motivation is that by work of Whitehead and others (the s-cobordism theorem), the obstruction for a cobordism to be trivial lies in an algebraic K-theory group. There is now a higher version of this theorem which relates diffeomorphism groups to algebraic K-theory. A third motivation comes from the Baum-Connes conjecture, which has other applications in geometric topology.

For other applications, the group K0 was first invented by Grothendieck to give a statement of the Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch theorem, and algebraic K-theory is also related to special values of L-functions.

Definition. For a ring R, the group K0(R) is the Grothendieck group of isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective R-modules under the operation of direct sum.

Higher K-groups are defined as homotopy groups of the space obtained by group completing the category of finitely-generated projective R-modules. This can be made precise using higher algebra and actually produces a spectrum, and then we can take its homotopy groups. We can see why this is so complicated.

Example. It is easy to see that K0(field)=ℤ, but of course the higher K-groups are very complicated. Quillen computed them for finite fields, but if we leave this case this becomes extremely difficult.

Approximation of algebraic K-theory

We will attempt to approximate algebraic K-theory using more algebraic invariants. There is a Dennis trace map to Hochschild homology. There are refinements of this which fit into a diagram

Slogan. The cyclotomic trace is often close to an isomorphism.

There are also relative K-groups K∗(R,I) for any ideal I⊆R, which is simply the homotopy fiber of K(R)→K(R/I). There are also relative TC groups, which are defined in the same way. We can also define groups with coefficients like K∗(R,ℤp) and TC∗(R,ℤp).

Theorem (Dundas-Goodwillie-McCarthy, Clausen-Matthew-Morrow).

1.
If I⊆R is a nilpotent ideal, then
cyctr:K∗(R,I)→TC∗(R,I)

is an isomorphism.

2.
If R is commutative and I-complete, the same conclusion holds with p-adic coefficients. In other words, we have
K∗(R,I,ℤp)≅TC∗(R,I,ℤp).
3.
If R is p-complete, then
TC∗(R,ℤp)≅K∗e´t(R,ℤp).

Why the trace map is a trace

Let k be a field, R be a k-algebra, and P be a finitely generated projective right R-module. Then we have

HomR⁡(P,P)≅P⊗RHomR⁡(P,R).

We would attempt to go to R by an evaluation map

P⊗RHomR⁡(P,R)→evR,

but this doesn’t actually land in R. Instead, we see that

x⊗rφ↦r⋅φ(x)xr⊗φ↦φ(xr)=φ(x)⋅r.

The best we can do is to consider the quotient

R/[R,R]

as an abelian group, so in conclusion we have

tr:HomR⁡(P,P)→R/[R,R].

Note that an R-R-bimodule is equivalently an R⊗kRop-module. Then, we in fact have

R/[R,R]≅R⊗R⊗kRopR.

Deriving this expression, we will see later that

HH(R,k)≅R⊗R⊗kRop𝕃R.

The Dennis trace will refine this trace in the sense that on K0, it will send a projective module P to the trace of the identity endomorphism.

1 ∞-categories and higher algebra

In this chapter, we give a user’s guide to ∞-categories and the homotopy-enriched algebra of spectra following the higher algebra playlist.

1.1 ∞-categories

Infinity-categories are a simultaneous generalization of both ordinary categories and of the homotopy theory of spaces which form a natural home for derived phenomena. We will not aim to cover the entire theory but instead to give an idea of how to work with and think about ∞-categories.

Convention 1.1.0.1. We will resolve size issues by assuming the existence of a Grothendieck universe 𝒰. Elements of 𝒰 will be called small sets. We will take categories to have large object sets and large morphism sets. Therefore, for us we will take Set to mean the category of small sets.

1.1.1 ∞-categories

Definition 1.1.1.1. An ∞-category is is a (large) simplicial set 𝒞 with the property that any diagram admits a filling for all 0<i<n. Here, Λin is the i-th horn given by taking the boundary of Δn and removing the facet opposite to the i-th vertex.

A functor 𝒞→𝒟 is a map of simplicial sets.

It is not clear why this definition should be related to categories at all, but we will construct an example of an ∞-category from an ordinary category.

Example 1.1.1.2. Let 𝒞 be an ordinary category. Define the nerve of C to be the simplicial set given by

(N𝒞)n=Fun([n],𝒞),

where [n] is the poset given by 0≤1≤⋯≤n.

Exercise 1.1.1.3.

1.
Show that N𝒞 is an ∞-category;
2.
Show that functors N𝒞→N𝒟 are in bijection with functors 𝒞→𝒟.

Now let 𝒞 be an ∞-category. We will call 𝒞0 the set of objects and 𝒞1 the set of morphisms. Note that it is not clear what the composition of two morphisms should be. For any f∈𝒞1, we will view f as a morphism

f:a→b,a=∂1f,b=∂0f.

Definition 1.1.1.4. Two morphisms f,g:a→b are equivalent if there exists a 2-simplex σ∈𝒞2 of the form In this case, we write f≃g.

This notion is extremely boring for the nerve of a 1-category. It is more interesting in the next example.

Example 1.1.1.5. Let 𝒞 be a Kan complex. This means that all horns can be filled in, so in particular 𝒞 is an ∞-category. For example, if X is a topological space, then the singular simplicial set Sing(X) is a Kan complex. Here, objects are points of X, morphisms are paths in X, and equivalence is simply homotopy of paths relative to the endpoints. If we pass to equivalence classes, we obtain the fundamental groupoid of X, so we can think of Sing(X) as being an ∞-categorical version of the fundamental groupoid. Note here that composition of paths is only associative up to homotopy.

Definition 1.1.1.6. Let f:a→b and g:b→c be morphisms. A composition of f and g is a 2-simplex σ of the form In this case, we will write h≃g∘f.

Exercise 1.1.1.7. Check that two different choices of compositions, h≃g∘f and h′≃g∘f, are equivalent.

The non-existence of uniqueness may seem like a defect, but if we consider coproducts in ordinary categories, being unique up to unique isomorphism is enough because it allows us to not have to think about a coproduct functor being associative (or maybe only in a weak sense).

Definition 1.1.1.8. Let f:a→b be a morphism. It is an equivalence if there exists a morphism g:b→a such that ida≃g∘f and idb≃f∘g.

Recall that the functors between ordinary categories form a category. We will upgrade this to ∞-categories.

Definition 1.1.1.9. Let 𝒞 and 𝒟 be simplicial sets. Then we define the simplicial set Fun(𝒞,𝒟) by the formula

Fun(𝒞,𝒟)n={𝒞×Δn→𝒟}.

Proposition 1.1.1.10. Let 𝒞 be an arbitrary simplicial set and 𝒟 be an ∞-category. Then Fun(𝒞,𝒟) is an ∞-category.

Note that a morphism η:f→g is a functor 𝒞×Δ1→𝒟 which restricts to f and g on the boundaries. We will call these natural transformations. A natural transformation η is an equivalence in Fun(𝒞,𝒟) if and only if it is objectwise an equivalence in 𝒟.

Definition 1.1.1.11. A functor f:𝒞→𝒟 is an equivalence if there exists a functor g:𝒟→𝒞 and natural equivalences f∘g≃id𝒟 and g∘f≃id𝒞. In this case, we will write 𝒞≃𝒟.

We would now like to discuss something that is like the fact that equivalences of ordinary categories are fully faithful and essentially surjective. Unfortunately, we don’t really have the machinery to do this yet.

Definition 1.1.1.12. Let a,b∈𝒞 be two objects in an ∞-category. We define the mapping space to be the simplicial set (in fact a Kan complex) which is the pullback in the diagram Note that the 0-simplices in this mapping space are simply morphisms f:a→b and that 1-simplices are equivalences. Thus π0Map𝒞(a,b) is the set of equivalence classes of morphisms a→b.

Exercise 1.1.1.13.

1.
Check that in N𝒞 for a 1-category 𝒞, mapping spaces are discrete and agree with morphism sets, and that the composition map recovers ordinary composition.
2.
Check that in Sing(X), the mapping space
MapSing(X)(a,b)

is homotopy equivalent to the space of paths from a to b in X and that the composition map comes from path composition.

Definition 1.1.1.14. A functor f:𝒞→𝒟 between ∞-categories is fully faithful if for any pair of objects a,b∈𝒞, the map

Map𝒞(a,b)→Map𝒟(f(a),f(b))

is a homotopy equivalence.

Definition 1.1.1.15. A functor f:𝒞→𝒟 between ∞-categories is essentially surjective if for all d∈𝒟, there exists some c∈𝒞 and an equivalence d≃f(c).

Proposition 1.1.1.16. A functor f:𝒞→𝒟 between ∞-categories is an equivalence if and only if f is fully faithful and essentially surjective.

Recall the notion of a full subcategory. We will define an ∞-categorical version of this.

Definition 1.1.1.17. Let S⊂𝒞0. We define the full subcategory 𝒞S⊆𝒞 to consist of all simplices with vertices in S.

Note that if we first saturate S under equivalence of objects to form S⊆S¯, we obtain an equivalence

𝒞S→CS¯.

We will now discuss a way to upgrade compositions to mapping spaces. Consider the pullback which is a triple mapping space.

Lemma 1.1.1.18. The triple mapping space Map𝒞(a,b,c) is a Kan complex and fits in a diagram induced by the horn-filling

Λ12→Δ2←Δ1.

A choice of a homotopy inverse S gives us a composition map

Map𝒞(b,c)×Map𝒞(a,b)→SMap𝒞(a,b,c)→∂1Map𝒞(a,b).

This seems to depend on the choice of S, but it is unique up to unique homotopy. In fact, the space of all possible homotopy inverses is contractible.

Similarly, we can define Map𝒞(a,b,c,d), which parameterizes the associativity of composition. We can compare this to Segal categories, where data like this is an axiom and gives us categories weakly enriched in spaces. In our approach, we get this for free.

Until now, we have seen two kinds of ∞-categories: (nerves of) ordinary categories and Kan complexes (where all morphisms are invertible, sometimes called ∞-groupoids). We will now discuss another example, the ∞-category of spaces, which is the prototypical example of an ∞-category.

Recall that the category of Kan complexes is enriched in simplicial sets. This enrichment actually lands in Kan complexes, so we would like to form an ∞-category.

Construction 1.1.1.19. For a finite, nonempty, totally ordered set J, define a simplicially enriched category

ℭ[ΔJ]

where objects are elements of J and for any i,j∈J, the mapping simplicial set is given by

Hom⁡(i,j)=N{K⊆J∣minK=i,maxk=j}.

Here, composition is induced by union of subsets of J.

Definition 1.1.1.20. Define a simplicial set 𝒮 by the formula

𝒮n=Fun(ℭ[Δn],Kan).

The simplicies look like the follows:

  • 0-simplices are Kan complexes;
  • 1-simplices are simply morphisms of Kan complexes;
  • 2-simplices correspond to diagrams

Theorem 1.1.1.21. This simplicial set 𝒮 is an ∞-category, and for all X,Y, there is a homotopy equivalence

Map𝒮(X,Y)≃HomKan⁡(X,Y).

Definition 1.1.1.22. For an arbitrary simplicially enriched category 𝒞, we can define the homotopy-coherent nerve NΔ(𝒞) by the formula

NΔ(𝒞)n=Fun(ℭ[Δn],𝒞).

Proposition 1.1.1.23. If 𝒞 is enriched in complexes, then NΔ(𝒞) is an ∞-category and we have equivalences

MapNΔ(𝒞)≃Hom𝒞⁡(a,b).

1.1.2 Limits

We will again neglect to develop the full theory in favor of giving an idea of how to work with limits.

Notation 1.1.2.1. From now on, we will denote the ∞-category of functors from a simplicial set I to an ∞-category 𝒞 by 𝒞I≔Fun(I,𝒞).

In this subsection, we will let I be a small simplicial set, 𝒞 be an ∞-category, and F:I→𝒞 be a functor.

Definition 1.1.2.2. A cone over F is a pair consisting of an object y∈𝒞, together with a natural transformation

η:cy→F,

where

cy:I→Δ0→y𝒞

is the constant functor on y.

Construction 1.1.2.3. Let (y,η) be a cone over F and x∈𝒞. We will construct a map

Map𝒞(x,y)→Map𝒞I(cx,F)

as the composite

Map𝒞(x,y)→cMap𝒞I(cx,cy)→η∗Map𝒞I(cx,F).

This is well-defined up to a contractible choice.

Definition 1.1.2.4. A cone (y,η) over F is a limit cone (or just limit) in 𝒞 if for all x∈𝒞, the map

Map𝒞(x,y)→Map𝒞I(cx,F)

is a homotopy equivalence. We will denote this by

y=limIF=limi∈IF(i).

Exercise 1.1.2.5. If I→𝒞 is a functor of ordinary categories, check that limits of NI→N𝒞 correspond exactly to ordinary limits of I→𝒞.

Example 1.1.2.6. Let I=∅. Then Fun(I,𝒞)≃pt. Therefore, every y∈𝒞 is a cone, and it is a limit if

Map𝒞(x,y)≃pt

for all x∈𝒞. In other words, y must be a terminal object and we will denote it by ∗ or pt.

Example 1.1.2.7. If I is a discrete set, then

Fun(I,𝒞)≅∏I𝒞.

Therefore, a functor I→𝒞 is simply a sequence {yi}i∈I, and a cone is an object y∈𝒞 with maps {πi:y→yi}i∈I. This is a limit cone if for all objects x∈𝒞, we have an equivalence

Map𝒞(x,y)→(πi)∗∏i∈IMap𝒞(x,yi).

For example, in 𝒮, the products are given by products of Kan complexes.

Lemma 1.1.2.8. Any two limits y,y′ of F are canonically equivalent.

Proof. The space of maps y→y′ is simply

{y→y′}≃{cy→F}.

We define a map f:y→y′ by simply pulling back η. By construction, we have η′∘f≃η. Doing this in the other direction, we have g:y′→y such that η∘g≃η′. We see that

η∘g∘f≃η′∘f≃η,

which implies that g∘f≃id. Applying this argument to f∘g yields the desired result. □

Remark 1.1.2.9. We can strengthen the previous lemma to the statement that the ∞-category of limit cones over F:I→𝒞 is either empty or trivial.

Remark 1.1.2.10. We have allowed I to be an arbitrary simplicial set, which may lack the lifting properties in the definition of an ∞-category. However, we can form a larger simplicial set I⊂I′ by gluing in fillers for horns which do not have fillers, and then we actually have an equivalence

𝒞I′≃𝒞I

which is even a Kan fibration.

We will now turn to some examples which have some coherence issues. The first are fiber products. Here, let Then a functor F:I→C is simply a diagram in 𝒞.

Lemma 1.1.2.11. A natural transformation ca→F for some object a∈𝒞 is, up to equivalence, given by the data of maps i:a→b and j:a→c together with an equivalence

h∘i≃k∘j:a→d

in 𝒞.

Proof. Because I=Δ1⊔Δ0Δ1 is a pushout, the functor category

𝒞I≃𝒞Δ1×𝒞𝒞Δ1

is a fiber product. Therefore a functor ca→F is given by diagrams Gluing the two edges involving f together, we are done. □

To actually work with limits, we need results about the functoriality and compatibility of mapping spaces.

Lemma 1.1.2.12 (Workhorse lemma). Let 𝒞 be a Kan-enriched category, F:I→NΔ(𝒞) be a functor, z∈𝒮 be a Kan complex, and x∈𝒞 be an object. Then the internal hom

Hom(z,Map𝒞I(cx,F))≃Map𝒮I(cz,Hom(x,F(−))).

Furthermore, if 𝒞=𝒮, then this space is also equivalent to

Map𝒮I(cz×x,F).

Proposition 1.1.2.13. A cone (y,η) over F in 𝒮 is a limit if and only if for all x∈𝒮, the map

[x,y]𝒮≔π0(Map𝒮(x,y))→π0(MapSI(cx,F))≕[cx,F]SI

is an isomorphism.

Proof. We have an equivalence for all z using the workhorse lemma. □

If we have a square in 𝒮, it is a pullback if maps x→a are up to homotopy the same as maps x→b and x→c together with a homotopy between x→c→d and x→b→d.

Exercise 1.1.2.14. Check that a pullback of a diagram

b→d←c

in 𝒮 can be computed as the ordinary limit of the diagram of simplicial sets.

Proposition 1.1.2.15. For any functor F:I→𝒮, the space

Map𝒮I(cpt,F)

is the limit of F. In particular, 𝒮 has all (small) limits.

Proof. We need to check that

Map𝒮(x,Map𝒮I(cpt,F))≃Map𝒮I(cx,F).

This is true by using the exponential law to put cx×pt=cx on the RHS. To construct the cone, we simply put the identity map on the LHS. □

Example 1.1.2.16. Let X be any simplicial set and let F=cx be the constant functor on a space x∈𝒮. Then

limIF=ℳ𝒶𝓅𝒮I(cpt,cx)=Hom(I,Map[S](pt,x))=Hom(I,x).

This tells us a lot more than a 1-categorical limit. For example, it sees all of the higher homotopy groups of x by inputting spheres.

Example 1.1.2.17. Let I′=N(ℕ,≤)op. This is an ∞-category. We will consider the simplicial set

I=Δ1⊔Δ0Δ1⊔Δ0Δ1⊔Δ0⋯=0←1←2←3←⋯

Therefore, functors I→𝒮 are simply sequences

a←b←c←d←⋯

Then the limit of this diagram in 𝒮 is simply the mapping telescope.

We will now consider an arbitrary Kan-enriched category 𝒞, a functor F:I→NΔ(𝒞), and an object x∈𝒞. We will consider the internal Hom functor

Hom(x,−):𝒞→sSet,

which induces a mapping space

Map(x,−):NΔ(𝒞)→𝒮.

Theorem 1.1.2.18. A cone (y,η) over F is a limit cone if and only if the induced cone

(Hom𝒞(x,y),NΔHom𝒞⁡(x,η))

is a limit cone in 𝒮 for all x∈𝒞. In fact, there is an equivalence

Map𝒞(x,limIF)≃limi∈IMap𝒮(x,F(i)).

Remark 1.1.2.19. We could try to take this as a definition, but it has two disadvantages:

1.
We would have to define limits in spaces;
2.
We would have issues with the functoriality of mapping spaces.

Proof. Being a limit cone in 𝒞 is the same thing as an equivalence

ℳ𝒶𝓅𝒞(x,y)≃Map𝒞I(cx,F).

This is now equivalent to having an equivalence

Hom𝒮(z,Map𝒞(x,y))≃Hom𝒮(z,Map𝒞I(cx,F))

for any space z. But now this is equivalent to checking that

Map𝒮(z,Hom𝒞⁡(x,y))≃Map𝒮I(cz,Hom(x,F(−))),

which is the condition about the induced cones. □

Remark 1.1.2.20. In our definition, a cone over F is a functor

I×Δ1I×{0}→𝒞.

There is in fact a “smaller” model for this quotient called I◃=Δ0∗I. Then Map𝒞I(cx,F) is the pullback This model is the one that is used by Lurie and Joyal.

1.1.3 Colimits

Colimits are formally dual to limits. If 𝒞 is an ∞-category, there is an opposite ∞-category 𝒞op defined by

Δop→(−)opΔop→𝒞Set.

Then we can define the colimit F:I→𝒞 as the limit of the functor

Fop:Iop→𝒞op.

Explicitly, we first define a cone under F to be an object y∈𝒞 together with a natural transformation η:F→cy. This is a colimit cone if for any z∈𝒞, the map

Map𝒞(y,z)→η∗Map𝒞I(F,cz)

is an equivalence.

Proposition 1.1.3.1. Extending an object y∈𝒮 to a colimit cone over a fixed F:I→𝒮 is equivalent to providing a natural isomorphism

[y,z]𝒞≃[F,cz]𝒞I,

where naturality is in z.

Example 1.1.3.2. If I=∅, then a colimit over I is an initial object, which will be denoted by ∅. It is given by the property that

Map𝒞(∅,z)≃∗.

In 𝒮, this is actually given by the empty set.

Example 1.1.3.3. If I is discrete, then a functor is F={yi}i∈I, and the colimit is called a coproduct and denoted by

colimI⁡F≕⨆i∈Iyi.

It is characterized by the property that

Map𝒞(⨆i∈Iyi,z)≃∏i∈IMap𝒞(yi,z).

In 𝒮, it is given by the disjoint union.

Example 1.1.3.4. Suppose that Then a functor is simply a diagram The colimit, called a pushout and denoted b⊔ac, is characterized by the universal property that for all z∈𝒞, we have

Map𝒞(b⊔ac,z)≃Map𝒞(b,z)×Map𝒞(a,z)Map𝒞(c,z),

where we are taking the homotopy fiber product in 𝒮.

We will now consider pushouts in the category of spaces. Given a diagram of spaces, we form the simplicial set

b⊔a×{0}a×Δ1⊔a×{1}c,

which is usually called the double mapping cylinder. It corresponds to the diagram Then we will replace this by a Kan complex d, and the resulting diagram is a pushout.

Exercise 1.1.3.5. Check that this is actually true.

We have seen that the category of spaces has all coproducts and pushouts, and we now want to show that it has all (small) colimits. One way is to write this is to consider

[I→𝒮,(I×𝒮𝒮∗)K],

which is a formula for the colimit. Instead, we will show that any ∞-category with all coproducts and pushouts has all colimits.

Example 1.1.3.6. A coequalizer is a colimit over

I=(0⇉1)=Δ1⊔Δ1∼.

a coequalizer is simply a universal c which fits into a diagram

a⇉b→c,

and is in fact the pushout

Exercise 1.1.3.7. Prove this.

Example 1.1.3.8. A pushout is actually a coequalizer

a⇉b⊔c→d.

We will now discuss sequential colimits. Here, we consider

I=Δ1⊔Δ0Δ1⊔Δ0Δ1⊔Δ0⋯

Functors I→𝒞 and colimits are simply sequences

(y0→y1→⋯)→y∞=lim→⁡yi.

This is actually a coequalizer

Definition 1.1.3.9. A simplicial set I is called finite if it has only finitely many non-degenerate simplices. Colimits over finite simplicial sets will be called finite colimits.

Theorem 1.1.3.10. For an ∞-category 𝒞, the following are equivalent:

1.
𝒞 admits an initial object and all pushouts;
2.
𝒞 admits all finite coproducts and all coequalizers;
3.
𝒞 admits all finite colimits.

Proof, but not really. First, we note that coproducts a⊔b are pushouts In the other direction, the initial object is the empty coproduct.

Now, we need to write arbitrary finite colimits using the basic colimits (coproducts, coequalizers, and pushouts). If I is a finite simplicial set, we write

I0⊆I1⊆⋯⊆In=I

and consider the attaching construction of I, which is For any F:I→𝒞, we have an equivalence

colimI⁡F≃colimIn−1⁡F⊔colim⨆J∂Δn⁡F|∂Δncolim⨆JΔn⁡F|Δn.

Here, we use the fact that

colim⨆JΔn⁡G≃⨆JcolimΔn⁡G|Δn≃⨆J(G|Δn)(n).

This allows us to prove the existence of finite coproducts by inducting on the dimension of I, where the base case is simply the case of coproducts. □

Exercise 1.1.3.11. Let I be a poset with a terminal object. Show that colimits over F:I→𝒞 are simply given by evaluating F at the terminal object.

We know already that the category of spaces has all finite colimits since we already wrote down finite coproducts and pushouts. However, we want all colimits.

Theorem 1.1.3.12. Suppose 𝒞 admits all coproducts. Then the following are equivalent:

1.
𝒞 admits all colimits;
2.
𝒞 admits all pushouts;
3.
𝒞 admits all coequalizers;
4.
𝒞 admits all geometric realizations, or in other words colimits indexed over NΔop.

Proof. We already know that pushouts and coequalizers are equivalent. We now need to write arbitrary colimits using pushouts and coequalizers. We now write

I=⋃(I0⊆I1⊆⋯).

Then we write

colimI⁡(F)≃colimn∈ℕ⁡(limInF|In),

and sequential colimits are simply coequalizers.

We now want to construct pushouts from Δop. Here, we realize the pushout as a colimit of the simplicial diagram This proves the result. □

Corollary 1.1.3.13. The ∞-category 𝒮 of spaces has all colimits.

We will discuss limits and colimits freely in some other ∞-categories.

Definition 1.1.3.14. The ∞-category 𝒮∗ of pointed spaces is the homotopy-coherent nerve

NΔ(Kan∗),

where Kan∗ is the simplicially enriched category of pointed Kan complexes.

Definition 1.1.3.15. The ∞-category Cat∞ of ∞-categories is given by the homotopy-coherent nerve

NΔ(Cat∞Δ),

where Cat∞Δ is the simplicially enriched category where objects are ∞-categories and morphisms

HomCat∞Δ(x,y)⊆Fun(x,y)

are given by the maximal Kan complexes.

Theorem 1.1.3.16. The ∞-categories Cat∞ and 𝒮∗ have all limits and colimits.

1.1.4 Derived catgories

We will construct an ∞-categorical refinement of the derived category 𝒟(𝒜) of an abelian category 𝒜, which encode Ext groups in the mapping spaces. We will first describe an ∞-category where equivalence classes of morphisms are chain homotopy classes, and then we will use Dwyer-Kan localizations to localize at quasi-isomorphisms. The resulting category, 𝒟(𝒜), will be characterized by the following:

  • Objects will be (unbounded) chain complexes in 𝒜;
  • Equivalence classes of morphisms will be given by the usual derived Hom.

Definition 1.1.4.1. For an abelian category 𝒜, denote the 1-category of chain complexes by Ch(𝒜). It is enriched over Ch(ℤ) and is therefore a dg category.

Construction 1.1.4.2 (Dold-Kan). There is a lax monoidal functor

Γ:Ch(ℤ)≥0→≃Fun(Δop,Ab).

Then we form the composite

K:Ch(ℤ)→τ≥0Ch(ℤ)≥0→ΓFun(Δop,Ab)→Fun(Δop,Set).

Each functor in this composition is lax monoidal, so we can turn every dg category into a simplicially enriched category by applying K.

The functor K has two nice properties. First, it produces Kan complexes, not just simplicial sets. The homotopy groups are given by the non-negative homology groups of the complex, or in other words

πnK(C)=Hn(C)

for all n≥0.

Definition 1.1.4.3. For a dg category 𝒞, define the dg-nerve of 𝒞 to be

Ndg(𝒞)≔NΔ(𝒞Δ),

where 𝒞Δ, where 𝒞Δ is obtained from 𝒞 by applying K to all Hom complexes.

Note that this produces an ∞-category.

Definition 1.1.4.4. For an abelian category 𝒜, define

𝒦(𝒜)≔Ndg(Ch(𝒜)).

This actually has some very nice properties with respect to limits and colimits regardless of the abelian category 𝒜.

Proposition 1.1.4.5. The ∞-category 𝒦(𝒜) has all finite limits and colimits.

Proof. First, note that 0∈𝒦(𝒜) is the initial and terminal object. In particular, we see that

Map𝒦(𝒜)(0,E)≃K(Hom⁡(0,E))=Δ0

and that

Map𝒦(𝒜)(E,0)≃Δ0

for any E∈𝒦(𝒜).

Next, let C,D∈𝒦(𝒜). The coproduct will be C⊕D. Here, we need to check that

Map𝒦(𝒜)(C⊕D,E)≃Map𝒦(𝒜)(C,E)×Map𝒦(𝒜)(D,E).

Similarly, C⊕D is also the product.

Pushouts are trickier. Let f:C→D and g:C→D′ be morphisms. Then we will construct the mapping cone C(f,g) by setting the n-th element of the complex to be

C(f,g)n≔Dn⊕Dn′⊕Cn−1

with the differential

∂(d,d′,c)≔(∂d+f(c),∂d′−g(c),∂c).

This gives us a pushout square We will omit checking that this is actually a pushout. There is a similar description for fiber products. □

Note that 𝒦(𝒜) is not the actual derived category of 𝒜. For example, there is a morphism

(⋯ℤ→2ℤ⋯)→(⋯0→ℤ/2⋯)

but not a morphism in the other direction. We want to localize at such quasi-isomorphisms, and the localization we will take is called Dwyer-Kan localization.

Definition 1.1.4.6. Let 𝒞 be an ∞-category and W⊆𝒞1 be any subset of morphisms. A functor

f:𝒞→𝒞′

is a Dwyer-Kan localization at W if

  • f takes W to equivalences in 𝒞′;

  • For any 𝒟, the functor

    Fun(𝒞′,𝒟)→Fun(𝒞,𝒟)

    is fully faithful with essential the full subcategory

    FunW(𝒞,𝒟)⊆Fun(𝒞,𝒟)

    on those functors 𝒞→𝒟 which take W to equivalences. We will denote such a 𝒞′ by 𝒞[W−1].

Example 1.1.4.7. Let 𝒞=Δ1 and let W consist of the nontrivial morphism 0→1. Then

𝒞[W−1]≃Δ0

because if we invert the morphism, the two objects become equivalent. We will check the universal property now. Clearly, the functor Δ1→Δ0 takes the unique element of W to an equivalence. We now need to check that

Fun(Δ0,𝒟)→FunW(Δ1,𝒟)

is an equivalence. To prove that it is essentially surjective, we need to check that isomorphisms d≃d′ are equivalent to d→idd, which is left as an exercise. To prove that it is fully faithful, we need to check that

Map(a→fa′,b→gb′)

is a fiber product of the diagram This proof will also be omitted.

Exercise 1.1.4.8. Show that every object

(d→≃d′)∈FunW(Δ1,𝒟)

is equivalent to (d→idd).

Having defined Dwyer-Kan localizations, we still need to see that they actually exist.

Proposition 1.1.4.9. For any ∞-category 𝒞 and any set of morphisms W, the Dwyer-Kan localization 𝒞[W−1] exists and the functor

𝒞→𝒞[W−1]

is essentially surjective.

Proof. We can begin by trying the pushout in Cat∞. If we apply Fun(−,𝒟) to this square to obtain the square We need to prove that this is a fiber product in Cat∞. Note that these functor categories (which are not Kan complexes) differ from mapping spaces in Cat∞, which are.

Before we do this, note that note that the essential image of

Fun(⨆WΔ0,𝒟)→Fun(⨆WΔ1,𝒟)

are those functors which send W to equivalences. By general properties of base change, the essential image of

Fun(𝒞′,𝒟)→Fun(𝒞,𝒟)

consists of exactly those functors which take W to equivalences.

To prove the claim about fiber products of functor categories, we will show that for any pushout the diagram is a fiber product. Applying MapCat∞(ℱ,−), we first note that

MapCat∞(ℱ,Fun(𝒟,ℰ))≃MapCat∞(𝒟,Fun(ℱ,ℰ)).

This is because they are both the maximal Kan complex inside of

Fun(ℱ,Fun(𝒟,ℰ))≃Fun(𝒟,Fun(ℱ,ℰ)).

Therefore, we obtain the diagram which is a fiber product. □

Therefore, we see that Cat∞ is really an (∞,2)-category, but we will not discuss this in detail here. We are now ready to define the derived category, however.

Definition 1.1.4.10. Let 𝒲⊆𝒦(𝒜)1 be the set of quasi-isomorphisms, namely morphisms which induce isomorphisms on homology. Now define the derived category 𝒟(𝒜) by the formula

𝒟(𝒜)≔𝒦(𝒜)[W−1].

This is unfortunately extremely non-explicit. For example, it does not tell us how to work with mapping spaces in 𝒟(𝒜).

1.1.5 Slices and filtered colimits

Our goal is now to give a description of mapping spaces in 𝒟(𝒜) as colimits of mapping spaces in 𝒦(𝒜). In many cases, they will even agree with mapping spaces in 𝒦(𝒜). In general, the problem of describing mapping spaces in Dwyer-Kan localizations is very hard.

Definition 1.1.5.1. Let 𝒞 be an ∞-category and x∈𝒞 be an object. We will define the slice category over x 𝒞/x by the fiber product and the slice category under x by the fiber product

Note that objects of 𝒞/x are morphisms c→x and objects of 𝒞x/ are morphisms x→c.

Definition 1.1.5.2. For any chain complex C∈𝒦(𝒜), define the subcategory

𝒦(𝒜)/Cqi⊆𝒦(𝒜)/C

to be the full subcategory on all C′→C which are quasi-isomorphisms. Dually, we can define

𝒦(𝒜)C/qi⊆𝒦(𝒜)C/.

Proposition 1.1.5.3. We have the following description for mapping spaces in 𝒟(𝒜):

Map𝒟(𝒜)(C,D)≃colim(𝒦(𝒜)/Cqi)op⁡Map𝒦(𝒜)(−,D)≃colim(𝒦(𝒜)D/qi)op⁡Map𝒦(𝒜)(D,−).

Warning 1.1.5.4. The mapping spaces as we have defined them are not functors 𝒞op×𝒞→𝒮. In this case, we can get around this by noting that both 𝒦(𝒜) and 𝒮 are homotopy-coherent nerves of ordinary categories, but in general we will need the technique of straightening, which is beyond the scope of these notes.

Because quasi-isomorphisms become equivalences in 𝒟(𝒜), we have a morphism

colim(𝒦(𝒜)/Cqi)op⁡Map𝒦(𝒜)(−,D)→colim(𝒦(𝒜)/Cqi)op⁡Map𝒟(𝒜)(−,D).

Every morphism in 𝒦(𝒜)/Cqi induces an equivalence on mapping spaces in 𝒟(𝒜), so the target of this morphism becomes

Map𝒟(𝒜)(C,D).

Exercise 1.1.5.5. Check that the colimit of a constant functor (𝒦(𝒜)/Cqi)op→𝒮 is given by its value. Hint: first give a description of colimits of constant diagrams 𝒞→𝒮.

Definition 1.1.5.6. A complex C∈𝒦(𝒜) is K-projective if the mapping space functor Map𝒦(𝒜)(C,−) sends quasi-isomorphisms to homotopy equivalences. Similarly, a complex C∈𝒦(𝒜) is K-injective if Map𝒦(𝒜)(−,C) sends quasi-isomorphisms to homotopy equivalences.

Corollary 1.1.5.7. If C is K-projective or D is K-injective, then

Map𝒟(𝒜)(C,D)≃Map𝒦(𝒜)(C,D).

Remark 1.1.5.8. There is a fundamental lemma in homological algebra, which states that bounded below and levelwise projective chain complexes are K-projective. Similarly, bounded above and levelwise injective complexes are K-injective.

Given some C∈𝒦(𝒜) and a quasi-isomorphism C′→C with C′ K-projective, then

Map𝒟(𝒜)(C,D)≃Map𝒦(𝒜)(C′,D).

This is the usual way that Ext groups are computed if 𝒜 has enough projectives. Dually, we can compute mapping spaces by taking a K-injective replacement of D.

Our next goal is to understand limits and colimits in 𝒟(𝒜). Limits are easy to understand if there are enough K-projective objects and colimits are easy to understand if there are enough K-injective objects. In general, we will not need this, but at the cost of introducing filtered colimits.

Definition 1.1.5.9. An ∞-category 𝒞 is filtered if for any finite simplicial set K, every map K→𝒞 extends over the simplicial set

(K×Δ1)⊔K×{1}Δ0.

This is a simplicial set obtained by taking a cone from K out to the right. Dually, we say that 𝒞 is cofiltered if 𝒞op is filtered.

Exercise 1.1.5.10. A 1-category 𝒞 is filtered if and only if for every a,b∈𝒞, there exists an object c∈𝒞 and morphisms a→c and b→c and if for every pair of morphisms a⇉b there exists a morphism b→c such that the two composites are equal. Show that 𝒞 is filtered if and only if N(𝒞) is filtered in the ∞-categorical sense.

We will call colimits indexed over filtered diagrams filtered colimits. Dually, we can also speak of cofiltered limits. Also, being filtered is a weaker property than having colimits.

Lemma 1.1.5.11. If I is a filtered ∞-category and J is a finite simplicial set, then the diagram commutes.

This result only holds for the ∞-category of spaces and is nontrivial even though we only need to check it for J being a fiber product square.

Exercise 1.1.5.12. Prove that filtered colimits commute with finite products in the 1-category Set.

Lemma 1.1.5.13. If K∈𝒮 comes from a finite simplicial set, then the functor

Map(K,−):𝒮→𝒮

commutes with filtered colimits.

The analogous result for finite sets follows by the previous exercise.

Exercise 1.1.5.14. Prove the lemma using the fact that filtered colimits commute with finite limits.

Corollary 1.1.5.15. The functor

[K,−]=π0Map(K,−):𝒮→N(Set)

commutes with filtered colimits.

Proof. This follows from the fact that the functor

π0:𝒮→N(Set)

commutes with all colimits. □

Exercise 1.1.5.16. Prove that

π0:𝒮→N(Set)

commutes with all colimits.

We will now apply this to the discussion of mapping spaces in 𝒟(𝒜).

Lemma 1.1.5.17. The categories 𝒦(𝒜)C/qi and (mcK(𝒜)/Cqi)op are both filtered.

Proof. We will instead note that they have all colimits. More precisely, we have that

K(𝒜)C/qi⊆𝒦(𝒜)C/

is closed under colimits. We will not give the proof of this in full, but first we consider the cofiber functor

𝒦(𝒜)C/→𝒦(𝒜)

which sends a morphism C→C′ to its cofiber, which is the pushout of the diagram Because it is itself a colimit, it commutes with colimits. Now, a morphism C→C′ is a quasi-isomorphism if and only if its cofiber is acyclic (in other words, quasi-isomorphic to 0), so we only need to check that acyclic objects in 𝒦(𝒜) are closed under colimits, which is true by definition. A dual argument gives the result in the over category. □

Proposition 1.1.5.18. The derived category 𝒟(𝒜) has all finite limits and colimits and they are preserved by the functor 𝒦(𝒜)→𝒟(𝒜).

Proof. First, we need to check that 0 is still initial and terminal in 𝒟(𝒜). Note that 0 is K-injective and K-projective, so because mapping spaces can be computed in 𝒦(𝒜), it is still initial and terminal.

Now consider a pushout in 𝒦(𝒜). Therefore, the square is a fiber product in spaces. Then the diagram is a filtered colimit of diagrams of mapping spaces in 𝒦(𝒜) for E′∈𝒦(𝒜)E/qi. Because filtered colimits commute with finite limits in spaces, it is a fiber product. Dually, we see that fiber products are preserved.

Now we need to check that finite limits and colimits actually exist. Consider a diagram

C←A→B

in 𝒟(𝒜). Because π0 commutes with colimits, we see that

π0Map𝒟(𝒜)(A,C)≃colim𝒦(𝒜)C/qi⁡Map𝒦(𝒜)(A,−)

is a filtered colimit of sets. Therefore, there exists a quasi-isomorphism C→C′ such that the morphism A→C→C′ comes from 𝒦(𝒜). Therefore, we have a morphism where the bottom row comes from 𝒦(𝒜). Therefore, we can simply take the colimit of the bottom row. The same trick gives us fiber products. □

Warning 1.1.5.19. The Dwyer-Kan localization producing 𝒟(𝒜) is extremely nice. In general, this is not the case. We will see this in the following statements

Proposition 1.1.5.20. The Dwyer-Kan localization of simplicial sets at weak equivalences

N(sSet)[W−1]≃𝒮

yields the ∞-category of spaces. Note that we have produced highly nontrivial mapping spaces by localizing a category with only discrete mapping spaces and that limits are usually not preserved by this procedure.

Proposition 1.1.5.21. Inverting all quasi-isomorphisms from the 1-category of chain complexes yields the derived category of 𝒜, or in other words,

N(Ch(𝒜))[W−1]≃𝒟(𝒜).

This is very hard to deal with, so the presentation we gave is better. Similarly, if we let W be the set of chain homotopy equivalences, we obtain

N(Ch(𝒜))[W−1]≃𝒦(𝒜).

Therefore, we have in some sense performed a two-step localization.

1.1.6 Derived functors

We will discuss derived functors even when there are not enough injectives or projectives. Also, we will see how these are related to adjunctions and Kan extensions.

Assume that F:𝒜→ℬ is an additive functor, which means that F(0)≅0 and

F(A⊕B)≅FA⊕FB.

This induces a functor

Ch(𝒜)→Ch(F)Ch(ℬ)

given by levelwise applying F. More precisely, it is given by

(⋯→C1→C0→⋯)↦(⋯→F(C1)→F(C0)→⋯)

and is an enriched functor with respect to the dg structure on Ch(𝒜). Therefore, we may apply the dg nerve construction to obtain a functor

𝒦(F):𝒦(𝒜)=Ndg(Ch(𝒜))→Ndg(F)Ndg(Ch(ℬ))=𝒦(ℬ)

which commutes with finite limits and colimits. Our goal now is to induce a functor

𝒟(F):𝒟(𝒜)→𝒟(B).

One thing we might ask is that the square is commutative in Cat∞. Unfortunately, this is too much to ask for in general.

Exercise 1.1.6.1. Prove that the following are equivalent:

1.
There exists a functor 𝒟(𝒜)→𝒟(ℬ) making the square commutative;
2.
The functor 𝒦(𝒜)→𝒦(ℬ) preserves quasi-isomorphisms;
3.
The functor 𝒜→ℬ is exact.

Of course, most functors we would like to derive are not exact, so we need to do something different in general. We could then try to ask for a weaker version of a commutative square, namely that there is a natural transformation Unfortunately, even the zero functor works for LF, so maybe we want some universality property.

Definition 1.1.6.2. The left derived functor LF of F is a functor

LF:𝒟(𝒜)→𝒟(ℬ)

together with a natural transformation

η:LF∘p𝒜→pℬ∘𝒦(F)

such that for any other functor

H:𝒟(𝒜)→𝒟(ℬ),

the map

MapFun(𝒟(𝒜),𝒟(ℬ))(H,LF)→MapFun(𝒦(𝒜),𝒟(ℬ))(H∘p𝒜,pℬ∘𝒦(ℱ))

is an equivalence.

Warning 1.1.6.3. The functor LF might not always exist.

Proposition 1.1.6.4. If LF exists, it preserves finite limits and colimits.

Definition 1.1.6.5. Given a pair (𝒞,W) and a functor G:𝒞→𝒟, the left derived functor LG is given by a diagram such that the induced map

Map(H,LG)→η∗Map(H,G)

is an equivalence for all H:𝒞[W−1]→𝒟. We say that LF is the absolute left derived functor if for any T:𝒟→ℰ, the induced triangle exhibits T∘LG as the left derived functor of T∘G.

Of course, absolute left derived functors are even more rare than left derived functors.

Remark 1.1.6.6. We have used the fact that

Fun(𝒞[W−1],𝒟)≅FunW(𝒞,𝒟)⊆Fun(𝒞,𝒟).

For a given G∈Fun(𝒞,𝒟), we have LG∈FunW(𝒞,𝒟) and

Map(H,LG)≅Map(H,G)

for H∈FunW(𝒞,𝒟), which is an example of coreflection (or a right Kan extension).

The main result of this section is the following.

Theorem 1.1.6.7. For any functor G:𝒦(𝒜)→𝒟, we have

(LG)(C)=lim←Cˆ→C⁡G(Cˆ)

provided that this limit exists for each C∈𝒦(𝒜). This limit is taken over the slice category 𝒦(𝒜)/Cqi.

Example 1.1.6.8. For C=0, we obtain, we have

(LG)(0)=lim←Cˆ→0⁡G(Cˆ)=G(0)

because 0 is initial in the slice category.

Example 1.1.6.9. Assume that there is a K-projective object

p:Cˆ→∼C.

This is in fact initial in 𝒦(𝒜)/Cqi because for any other object Cˆˆ→C, the square is a fiber product. Because Cˆˆ is quasi-isomorphic to C, the right vertical arrow is an equivalence, so the mapping space we want is contractible. Therefore, we have

(LG)(C)=G(Cˆ).

Remark 1.1.6.10. If for every C there exists such a K-projective resolution Cˆ, then

(LG)(C)=G(Cˆ)

for any functor G. This implies that LG is actually an absolute left derived functor, or in other words that every left derived functor is absolute.

Remark 1.1.6.11. Often, people define derived functors by taking projective resolutions, but this of course runs into problems with functoriality of projective resolutions. In addition, our approach generalizes better to the nonadditive setting.

Example 1.1.6.12. Assume that F:𝒜→ℬ is additive, 𝒜 is small, and ℬ has all infinite products and they are exact (Grothendieck’s AB4*). Then 𝒟(ℬ) has all limits and the derived functor

LF:𝒟(𝒜)→𝒟(ℬ)

exists and preserves all finite limits and colimits.

Exercise 1.1.6.13. Prove that the large category 𝒟(ℬ) has all small limits if B satisfies AB3* and AB4*, namely that ℬ has all small products and they are exact. Use as a black box the fact that if a large ∞-category 𝒞 has all small colimits, then 𝒞-indexed colimits in the category of large spaces commute with all small products, not just finite ones.

We have discussed left derived functors until now, but of course there is a dual notion of right derived functors. These are given by diagrams with the appropriate universality property. The dual of our formula for LG reads as

(RG)(C)=colimC→∼Cˆ⁡G(Cˆ),

where the colimit is taken over 𝒦(𝒜)C/qi.

Example 1.1.6.14. We have functors

Map𝒦(𝒜)(A,−):𝒦(𝒜)→𝒮,Map𝒦(𝒜)(−,B):𝒦(𝒜)op=𝒦(𝒜op)→𝒮.

Then the formulae for mapping spaces show that

Map𝒟(𝒜)(A,−)≅RMap𝒦(𝒜)(A,−),Map𝒟(𝒜)(−,B)≅RMap𝒦(𝒜)(−,B).

This is usually written as

Map𝒟(𝒜)=RMap𝒦(𝒜).

Unfortunately, we cannot derive in both variables at the same time, but we will be able to do this when we introduce nonabelian derived functors.

Sketch of proof of Theorem 1.1.6.7. The first step is to prove that defining

(LG)(C)=lim←Cˆ→C⁡G(Cˆ)

defines a functor 𝒦(𝒜)→𝒟.

The next step is to prove that it preserves weak equivalences. This seems obvious because we are taking a limit over weak equivalences, which requires that the pullback functor between slice categories along a weak equivalence has an adjoint.

As a consequence, there is a natural transformation

η:LG→G.

If G already preserves quasi-isomorphisms, then η is an equivalence.The last step is to show that

Map(H,LG)→η∗Map(H,G)→LMap(LH,LG)→η∗Map(H,LG)

is an inverse for η∗. □

We will now discuss adjunctions and cofinality.

Definition 1.1.6.15. Let 𝒞 and 𝒟 be ∞-categories with functors A natural transformation ε:LR→id𝒟 is a counit of an adjunction if for a given pair of objects c∈𝒞 and d∈𝒟, the induced map

Map𝒞(c,Rd)→LMap𝒟(Lc,LRd)→εdMao𝒟(Lc,d)

is a homotopy equivalence. Dually, a natural transformation η:id𝒞→RL is a unit of an adjunction if the induced mao

Map𝒟(Lc,d)→RMap𝒞(RLc,Rd)→ηc∗Map𝒞(c,Rd)

is an equivalence. In either case we say that L is left adjoint to R and write it as L⊣R.

Note that we have given two ways for L to be left adjoint to R, but we will see that they are actually equivalent.

Definition 1.1.6.16. Given functors L,R as before and any natural transformations ε:LR→id and η:id→RL, the zig-zag identities hold if the composites

L=L∘id→ηL∘R∘L→εid∘L=L,R=id∘R→ηR∘L∘R→εR∘id=R

are equivalent to idL and idR, respectively.

Proposition 1.1.6.17. If natural transformations ε and η satisfy the zig-zag identities, then they are unit and counit of an adjunction. Conversely, given a unit of an adjunction η, there is a unique counit ε such that the zig-zag identites hold.

Proof. If ε and η satisfy the zig-zag identities, then

Map𝒞(c,Rd)→LMap𝒟(Lc,LRd)→εMap𝒟(Lc,d),Map𝒟(Lc,d)→RMap𝒟(RLc,Rd)→ηMap𝒞(c,Rd)

are inverse to each other. We omit the proof of the existence of a counit given a unit. □

Exercise 1.1.6.18. Show that if F:𝒞→𝒟 is an equivalence, it is left and right adjoint to its inverse.

We now present some important facts about adjoint functors.

1.
Given a functor L:𝒞→𝒟, then the right adjoint (R,η) is unique if it exists;
2.
The composite of left adjoints is again a left adjoint with the right adjoint given by the composite of right adjoints. A more coherent statement is that we have an equivalence
Cat∞L≃(Cat∞R)op,

where Cat∞L is the ∞-category with ∞-categories as objects and left adjoint functors as morphisms and Cat∞R is defined similarly.

Now let I be a small ∞-category. Consider the functor

Δ:𝒞→Fun(I,𝒞)

given by pulling back along I→pt. Assume that Δ has a left adjoint L. Then for any functor F:I→𝒞, the unit gives a map F→Δ(LF) such that the induced map

Map𝒞(LF,y)→Map(F,Δy)

is an equivalence. In other words, we have

LF=colimI⁡F.

Proposition 1.1.6.19.

  • If 𝒞 has all I-shaped colimits, then Δ admits a left adjoint.

  • Assume that L:𝒞→𝒟 has for any d an object Rd with a map LRd→d such that for all c∈𝒞, the map

    Map𝒞(c,Rd)→Map𝒟(Lc,d)

    is an equivalence. Then L admits a right adjoint R given pointwise by d↦Rd.

Exercise 1.1.6.20. Prove the following statements.

  • Consider the functor π0:𝒮→Set. This has a left adjoint given by the discrete topology.
  • Given a functor forgetful functor 𝒞/x→𝒞 on a slice category, it is a left adjoint if 𝒞 has products.

Adjoint functors behave well with respect to limits and colimits as in the 1-categorical setting.

Proposition 1.1.6.21. Left adjoints preserve colimits and right adjoint preserve limits.

Proof. The proof is left as an exercise. □

Definition 1.1.6.22. Given a functor p:𝒞→𝒞′ and any functor F:𝒞→𝒟, a triangle exhibits RKanF as the right Kan extension of F along p if it is terminal among all such diagrams as in the definition of a left derived functor. In other words, the induced map

Map(H,RKanF)→η∗Map(H∘p,F)

is an equivalence.

Corollary 1.1.6.23. If the right Kan extension RKanF exists for every F:𝒞→𝒟, then the restriction functor

p∗:Fun(𝒞′,𝒟)→Fun(𝒞,𝒟)

admits a right adjoint RKan.

Therefore, we see that derived functors are right Kan extensions.

1.1.7 Nonabelian derived functors

In this section, we will discuss nonabelian derived functors and animation in order to derive non-additive functors. This will be technical, but it will be useful to understand these notions.

First, we will recast derived functors of additive functors F. Assume that 𝒦(𝒜) has enough K-projectives. For example, this is true where 𝒜 is the category of modules over a ring. First, the functor

𝒦(𝒜)K−proj→i𝒦(𝒜)→p𝒟(𝒜)

is an equivalence and i is left adjoint to the projection p. Using this equivalence, the left derived functor LF:𝒟(𝒜)→𝒟 of any functor F:𝒦(𝒜)→𝒟 is simply the restriction along i. In particular, if the target is an abelian category ℬ, the derived functor

LF:𝒟(𝒜)→𝒟(ℬ)

preserves connective objects, or in other words

LF(𝒟(𝒜)≥0)⊆𝒟(ℬ)≥0.

Our goal is now to answer the following questions.

  • How can we universally characterize p∘𝒦(ℱ):𝒦(𝒜)≥0→𝒟(ℬ)?
  • What if F is not additive?

Exercise 1.1.7.1. Given a pointed functor 𝒜→ℬ between abelian categories, prove that if there exists a functor 𝒦(𝒜)≥0→𝒟(ℬ) given on chain complexes representing objects by applying F levelwise, F must already be additive.

Before we proceed, we need to discuss the Yoneda lemma in ∞-categories. Unfortunately, this will require discussing size issues. We will fix three Grothendieck universes

{small sets}⊆{large sets}⊆{very large sets},

which is equivalent to fixing three strongly inaccessible cardinals. This becomes three nested models of ZFC where the set of all small sets is a large set and the set of very large sets is a very large set.

We may discuss categories and ∞-categories in all of these universes:

  • Small categories have small object and morphism sets;
  • Large categories have large object and morphism sets;
  • Very large categories have very large object and morphism sets.

For example, the ∞-category 𝒮 of small spaces is a large ∞-category and the ∞-category 𝒮ˆ of large spaces is a very large ∞-category. For example, if 𝒞 is a large category, then Map𝒞(a,b)∈𝒮ˆ. Another example of this is that if we let Cat∞small be the large ∞-category of small ∞-categories, we can also define Cat∞ to be the very large ∞-category of large ∞-categories. This approach avoids issues involving proper classes, but requires jumping between universes.

Some of our previous constructions can now be discussed more precisely. Here, if 𝒞∈Cat∞, then the Dwyer-Kan localization is still large, or in other words,

𝒞[W−1]∈Cat∞.

Another example is that the formula

Map𝒟(𝒜)(C,D)≃colim(𝒦(𝒜)/Cqi)op⁡Map𝒦(𝒜)(−,D)≃colim(𝒦(𝒜)D/qi)op⁡Map𝒦(𝒜)(D,−)

really lands in the ∞-category 𝒮ˆ of large spaces.

Definition 1.1.7.2. A large ∞-category 𝒞 is locally small if for any pair a,b∈𝒞 of objects, the mapping space

Map𝒞(a,b)∈𝒮ˆ

is equivalent to an object to 𝒮⊆𝒮ˆ, i.e. is essentially small. Equivalently, the functor

Map𝒞(−,−):𝒞op×𝒞→𝒮ˆ

factors through 𝒮⊆𝒮ˆ.

Construction 1.1.7.3. For any large ∞-category 𝒞, we have a functor

j:𝒞→Fun(𝒞op,𝒮ˆ)≕𝒫ˆ(𝒞)

which is given on objects by

c↦c≔Map𝒞(−,c)

called the Yoneda embedding. If 𝒞 is locally small, this factors as

j:𝒞→Fun(𝒞op,𝒮)≕𝒫(𝒮).

Theorem 1.1.7.4 (Yoneda Lemma).

1.
The functor j is fully faithful.
2.
For any F:𝒞op→𝒮ˆ and any X∈𝒞, there is a natural equivalence
MapFun(𝒞op,𝒮ˆ)(X,F)≃F(X).
3.
Every object F∈Fun(𝒞op,Sˆ) is a (large) colimit of objects of the form X for X∈𝒞.

Proof. The proof should be the same as with ordinary categories, but machinery (straightening and unstraightening) is required to handle coherence issues. We will omit this. Of course, the second part implies the first by the equation

Map𝒫ˆ(𝒞)(x,y)≃y(x)≅Map𝒞(x,y).

For the last item, we consider the pullback The category 𝒞/F is actually large, not very large. We now claim that

F≃colimx∈𝒞/F⁡x.
□

Exercise 1.1.7.5. For any F∈Fun(𝒞op,𝒮ˆ), prove that

F≃colimx∈𝒞/F⁡x.

Because of our keeping track of size constraints, note that if 𝒞 is small, then every

F:𝒞op→𝒮

is a small colimit of representables.

Now let 𝒞→𝒟 be a functor where 𝒞 is small and 𝒟 is possibly large.

Proposition 1.1.7.6. Assume that 𝒟 admits all small colimits. Then

1.
There exists an essentially unique colimit-preserving functor
𝒫(𝒞)=Fun(𝒞op,𝒮)→𝒟

extending F. In other words, there is a left Kan extension of F.

2.
If 𝒟 is locally small, then this is left adjoint to the restricted Yoneda embedding
𝒟→Fun(𝒟op,𝒮)→F∗Fun(𝒞op,𝒮).

Corollary 1.1.7.7. There is an equivalence

Funcolim(𝒫(𝒞),𝒟)≃Fun(𝒞,𝒟).

In other words, 𝒫(𝒞) is the universal ∞-category obtained from 𝒞 obtained from 𝒞 be freely adjoining colimits.

This is really just a restatement of the proposition.

Construction 1.1.7.8. Let K be any class1 of small colimit shapes, for example all colimits, all finite colimits, all filtered colimits, or all geometric realizations. We form the category

𝒫K(𝒞)⊆𝒫(𝒞)

as the smallest full subcategory which contains representables and which is closed under K-indexed colimits.

Proposition 1.1.7.9. For any large ∞-category 𝒟 which admits K-indexed colimits, restriction along j:𝒞→𝒫K(𝒞) is an equivalence

FunK−colim(𝒫K(𝒞),𝒟)→j∗Fun(𝒞,𝒟)

whose inverse is given by left Kan extension.

Example 1.1.7.10. If 𝒞 is any ∞-category, we can define the Ind-category

Ind(𝒞)=𝒫filtered(𝒞).

We claim the following:

1.
Objects in Ind(𝒞) are given by functors F:I→𝒞, where I is filtered. These objects are denoted
colimi∈I⁡Fi∈Ind(𝒞).
2.
For any pair F,G, we have
MapInd(𝒞)(colimi∈I⁡Fi,colimj∈J⁡Gj)≃limi∈Icolimj∈J⁡Map𝒞(Fi,Gj).

In particular, if 𝒞 is a 1-category, so is Ind(𝒞).

We are finally now able to return to nonabelian derived functors.

Proposition 1.1.7.11 (Dold-Kan, Quillen, …). Assume that 𝒜 has enough compact projective objects (compact means that Hom𝒜⁡(A,−) preserves filtered colimits). Then we have an equivalence

𝒟(𝒜)≥0≅𝒦(𝒜proj)≥0≅𝒫Δop,filtered(𝒜cp)≅FunΠ((𝒜cp)op,𝒮).

Corollary 1.1.7.12. A functor

𝒟(𝒜)≥0→ℰ

which preserves geometric realizations and filtered colimits is uniquely determined by its restriction to 𝒜cp.

This is precisely a nonabelian derived functor, which is given by taking the Kan extension in the diagram In other words, for any object in 𝒟(𝒜)≥0, we resolve it by simplicial diagrams of compact projectives and then evaluate the functor termwise.

We conclude by giving the categorical incarnation of nonabelian derived functors.

Definition 1.1.7.13. Let 𝒞 be a category which admits small colimits and is generated under small colimits by 𝒞cp. Here, an object x∈𝒞 is projective if Map𝒞(x,−) commutes with geometric realizations (if 𝒞 is a 1-category, we replace geometric realizations with split coequalizers). Then the animation Ani(𝒞) is defined as

𝒫Δop,filtered(𝒞cp)⊆FunΠ((𝒞cp)op,𝒮).

Example 1.1.7.14. If 𝒞=Set, we obtain

Ani(Set)≃𝒮.

1.2 Higher algebra

One of the most important objects in homotopy theory is the ∞-category of spectra. Studying spectra will give us a homotopy-enriched version of algebra.

1.2.1 Spectra

Let 𝒮∗ be the ∞-category of pointed spaces. There are functors

Σ,Ω:𝒮∗→𝒮∗,

where Σ is given by the pushout and Ω is given by the fiber product

Exercise 1.2.1.1. Prove that Σ⊣Ω.

Definition 1.2.1.2. A spectrum is a sequence of (pointed) spaces Xi for i≥0 together with homotopy equivalences

Xi→∼ΩXi+1.

Definition 1.2.1.3. The ∞-category Sp of spectra is the infinite fiber product

Sp≔Eq(𝒮∗)×𝒮∗Eq(𝒮∗)×𝒮∗,

where Eq(𝒮∗)⊆𝒮∗Δ1 is the full subcategory on equivalences, the rightward morphisms Eq(𝒮∗) take an arrow to its target, and the leftward morphisms take an arrow to the loop space of its source.

Note that objects in Sp are exactly given by lists of

Xi→∼ΩXi+1.

Maps in Sp are lists of maps

f:Xi→Yi

together with homotopies

Remark 1.2.1.4. We can write Sp as a colimit

Sp=lim(⋯→Ω𝒮∗→Ω𝒮∗→Ω𝒮∗).

Using this, mapping spaces can be described as

MapSp(X,Y)=limMap𝒮∗(Xi,Yi).

Example 1.2.1.5. If A is an abelian group, there is a spectrum HA given by

(HA)i≔K(A,i).

By definition, we have equivalences

K(A,i−1)≃ΩK(A,i).

Example 1.2.1.6. Let X∈𝒮∗ be a pointed space. Then there is a spectrum Σ∞X given by

(Σ∞X)i≔colimk⁡ΩkΣk+iX.

Here, we are using the fact that the loop space is a fiber product, so forming it commutes with filtered colimits. In particular, if X=S0, we define Σ∞S0≕𝕊.

Lemma 1.2.1.7. If X is a space, then

MapSp(Σ∞X,Y)≃Map𝒮∗(X,Y0)

for any spectrum Y.

Proof sketch. Consider a map

X→Y0≃Ωk+iYk+i.

By the adjunction, it is adjoint to a morphism

Σk+iX→Yk+i.

Applying Ωk, we obtain a morphism

ΩkΣk+iX→Yi.

This yields a map

(Σ∞X)i=colimk⁡ΩkΣk+iX→Yi.

Going in the other direction is given by restricting to (Σ∞X)0 and restricting to the first term in the colimit. □

Definition 1.2.1.8. Define the functor Ω∞:Sp→𝒮∗ by

Ω∞Y≔Y0.

Using this definition, the previous lemma becomes the statement that Ω∞ and Σ∞ are adjoint.

Example 1.2.1.9. For a finite K∈𝒮∗, we have

MapSp(Σ∞K,Σ∞X)≃Map𝒮∗(K,Ω∞Σ∞X)≃MapS∗(K,colimk⁡ΩkΣkX)≃colimk⁡Map𝒮∗(K,ΩkΣkX)≃colimk⁡Map𝒮∗(ΣkK,ΣkX).

For example, if X=S0, we see that

πnMapSp(𝕊,Σ∞X)=πnS(X)

are the stable homotopy groups.

We will now see that Sp is well-behaved.

Lemma 1.2.1.10. The ∞-category Sp has all limits, filtered colimits, and a zero object.

Proof. The zero object is given by Xi=pt. Limits and colimits both commute with Ω, so we can take them pointwise and still get a spectrum. By the formula for mapping spaces, they satisfy the universal properties. □

Lemma 1.2.1.11. The functor Ω:Sp→Sp is an equivalence.

Proof. Applying Ω to a spectrum is given by

(X0,X1,…)↦(ΩX0,X0,X1,…).

This is just a shift, and its inverse is given by shifting down. □

Proposition 1.2.1.12. The ∞-category Sp has all colimits and pushout squares are the same as pullback squares (and vice versa).

Very rough proof sketch. The proof is surprisingly elementary but quite tricky. The key idea is that ∞-category with all finite limits, a zero object, and where Ω is an equivalence has pushouts. These pushouts are determined by the fact that pushout squares are the same as pullback squares. □

We will call ∞-categories with zero objects and all finite limits and colimits where pushout and pullback squares are the same stable. Another example of a stable ∞-category is the derived category 𝒟(𝒜).

Remark 1.2.1.13. The suspension functor Σ:Sp→Sp is inverse to Ω. Therefore, it is simply the left shift functor. Also note that Yi is equivalent to Ω∞ΣiY.

Example 1.2.1.14. Note that

[Σ∞X,ΣnHA]Sp=[X,K(A,n)]𝒮∗=Hn(X,A).

Similarly, we have

[Σn𝕊,Y]𝕊=[Sn,Ω∞Y]𝒮∗=πn(Ω∞Y).

Therefore, we can obtain both cohomology and stable homotopy groups. Because Sp is stable, we get long exact sequences in both cohomology and in stable homotopy.

Unfortunately, not every spectrum is a suspension spectrum. However, this is close to being true.

Lemma 1.2.1.15. For all Y∈Sp, we have

Y≃colimi⁡Σ−iΣ∞Yi.

Proof. We will prove that they have the same mapping spaces. In particular, we compute

MapSp(Y,Z)=limiMap𝒮∗(Yi,Zi)=limiMapSp(Σ∞Yi,ΣiZ)=limiMapSp(Σ−iΣ∞Yi,Z)=MapSp(colimi⁡Σ−iΣ∞Yi,Z).
□

Our goal is now to make sense of homology, To do this correctly requires us to talk about symmetric monoidal structures, but we can give a different construction.

Construction 1.2.1.16. We will define a functor Sp→𝒟(ℤ) given by

Y↦colimi⁡C∗(Yi)[−i].

This functor is characterized by preserving colimits and taking Σ∞X↦C∗(X). In particular, we have

𝕊↦ℤ[0].

We want to view spectra as modules over 𝕊 and the homology functor as a base change to 𝒟(ℤ). We will now attempt to make this precise.

Definition 1.2.1.17. Define the category Spfin⊆Sp of finite spectra to be the full subcategory of all spectra of the form Σ−iΣ∞K for K a finite space.

Exercise 1.2.1.18. Prove that Spfin is closed under finite colimits.

Proposition 1.2.1.19. We have Sp=Ind(Spfin).

Proof. There are a natural functor Ind(Spfin)→Sp. The objects in Spfin are compact objects in Sp. This is because

MapSp(Σ−nΣ∞K,colimj⁡Yj)≃Map𝒮∗(K,Ω∞Σncolimj⁡Yj)≃colimj⁡Map𝒮∗(K,Ω∞ΣnYj).

Therefore, the functor is fully faithful. To prove that it is essentially surjective, we write a spectrum Y as

Y=colim⁡Σ−iΣ∞Yi

and then write Yi as a filtered colimit of finite spaces. □

Note that in the derived category 𝒟(R), the subcategory Perf(R) of perfect complexes consists exactly of the compact objects. This is analogous to the fact that every finite spectrum is a finite limit of shifts of 𝕊. In addition, we actually have

𝒟(R)=Ind(Perf(R)),

so we will think of Sp as the derived category 𝒟(𝕊) if such a thing existed (this requires a way to think about 𝕊 as a ring). However, a point of non-analogy is that the mapping space

MapSp(𝕊,𝕊)

is not discrete (and in fact it contains all stable homotopy groups of spheres, so is extremely complicated).

We will now make abelian groups a full subcategory of spectra.

Definition 1.2.1.20. A spectrum X∈Sp is n-connective if

πi(X)=[Σi𝕊,X]Sp=0

for all i<n. Dually, X is n-coconnective if πiX=0 for all i>n. We will denote the full subcategories as Sp≥n and Sp≤n.

Proposition 1.2.1.21. The inclusion

Sp≤n→Sp

has a left adjoint τ≤n.

Proof. Denote Xn≔X. We will build Xi as follows:

  • Choose generators of πi(Xi−1) and consider the corresponding map

    ⨁Σi𝕊→Xi−1.
  • Considering the cofiber of this morphism, we obtain a pushout
  • Let τ≤n≔colimi⁡Xi.

This satisfies the property that τ≤nX∈Sp≤n and that πiτ≤nX=πiX for all i≤n. This uses the fact that 𝕊 is connective. Another property is that every map

X→Y∈Sp≤n

factors through all of these pushouts because Y has no homotopy groups for i>n and therefore through τ≤nX. □

Definition 1.2.1.22. Let τ≥nX denote the fiber of the morphism X→τ≤n−1X.

Lemma 1.2.1.23. If X∈Sp≥n and Y∈Sp≤n−1, then

Map(X,Y)≃0.

In addition, there is an equivalence

Sp≥n∩Sp≤n≃Ab.

Proof. Any map X→Y factors through τ≤n−1X→Y. But now τ≤n−1X is weakly contractible, so it must be 0.

For the latter statement, note that πn gives a functor. In addition, note that mapping spaces are discrete because

Map(X,Y)=Map(ΣiX,Y)≃0

for i>0. If πn(X) is free, choose a map

⨁Σn𝕊→X

which is an isomorphism on πn and therefore an equivalence on τ≤n. This gives us an isomorphism

Map(X,Y)≃Map(⨁Σn𝕊,Y)≃∏πn(Y).

If πn(X) is not free, we choose a map

⨁Σn𝕊→X

which is surjective on πn. The fiber has free πn, so we use the exact sequence for π∗Map(−,Y) to conclude. □

We will now discuss the Postnikov tower. For ever X, we have a tower such that X is actually the limit of this sequence. Unfortunately, to actually reconstruct X from its truncations requires a lot of gluing data.

1.2.2 Symmetric monoidal ∞-categories

Our goal is to explain why Sp and 𝒟(R) have canonical symmetric monoidal structures.

Recall that an ordinary symmetric monoidal category consists of a category 𝒞 with a tensor product

⊗:𝒞×𝒞→𝒞,

a unit object 𝟏𝒞∈𝒞, and natural isomorphisms

(a⊗b)⊗c≃a⊗(b⊗c),a⊗𝟏𝒞≃a≃𝟏𝒞⊗a,a⊗b≃b⊗a

satisfying a number of coherence conditions. One of them is the pentagon identity, which says that the diagram commutes.

In this setting, a lax symmetric monoidal functor between symmetric monoidal categories 𝒞 and 𝒟 is a functor

F:𝒞→𝒟

together with natural morphisms

F(c)⊗𝒟F(c′)→F(c⊗𝒞c′)

for all c,c′∈𝒞 and a natural morphism

𝟏𝒟→F(𝟏𝒞).

These must be compatible with the associativity, unit, and symmetry isomorphisms. Such a lax symmetric monoidal functor is strong symmetric monoidal if the above natural morphisms are isomorphisms.

Also recall that a symmetric monoidal category (𝒞,⊗) is closed if for all c∈𝒞, the functor −⊗c admits a right adjoint Hom(c,−) and in particular preserves colimits. Our goal is to generalize the following result to ∞-categories.

Proposition 1.2.2.1. Let R be a commutative ring. Then the category ModR of R-modules admits an essentially unique symmetric closed symmetric monoidal structure with unit R.

Proof sketch. Existence is clear, so we will consider uniqueness. Note that because R is the tensor unit, we must have

R⊗M≅M.

Because the tensor product is assumed to preserve colimits, we obtain

(⨁IR)⊗M≅⨁I(R⊗M)=⨁IM.

For an arbitrary R-module N, we write N as the cokernel

⨁JR→f⨁IR↠N

of a morphism of free R-modules. This implies that N⊗M is the cokernel of

f⊗M:⨁JM→⨁IM.

This must be equal to N⊗M. □

Exercise 1.2.2.2. Give an actual proof of the proposition.

For any morphism R→S of commutative rings, we obtain a functor

−⊗RS:ModR→ModS,

which is symmetric monoidal.

In the land of ∞-categories, we will state the following theorem, which gives some examples of symmetric monoidal ∞-categories and symmetric monoidal functors.

Theorem 1.2.2.3.

1.
The ∞-categories Sp and 𝒟(R) admit essentially unique closed symmetric monoidal structures with units 𝕊 and R, respectively. We will denote the tensor products by ⊗𝕊 and ⊗R𝕃, respectively.
2.
The functors C∗:Sp→𝒟(ℤ), Σ+∞:𝒮→Sp, and ⊗R𝕃S:𝒟(R)→𝒟(S) have canonical strong symmetric monoidal structures.

This will require us to define symmetric monoidal ∞-categories such that N𝒞 is an example for any symmetric monoidal category and to define lax and strong symmetric monoidal functors.

The very rough idea of the proof of the theorem for Sp is as follows. If X∈Sp, then we must have 𝕊⊗X≅X. Secondly, tensoring with the suspension spectrum of a space gives

(Σ+∞Y)⊗X≅Σ+∞(colimy⁡pt)⊗X≅colimy⁡(Σ+∞pt)⊗X≅colimy⁡X.

We then obtain (Σ−nY)⊗X≅Σ−n(Y⊗X) because Σ is an equivalence and is clearly symmetric monoidal. Finally, we use the fact that every spectrum is a colimit of its constituent parts Σ∞−nYn. This determines the tensor product Y⊗X up to equivalence.

Let Fin∗ be the category of finite pointed sets ⟨n⟩={0,…,n} with 0 as a basepoint. For every 1≤i≤n there is a map

ρi:⟨n⟩→⟨1⟩k↦{1k=i0otherwise.

Definition 1.2.2.4 (First definition, Segal). A symmetric monoidal ∞-category is a functor

𝒞:NFin∗→Cat∞

such that the induced maps

𝒞(⟨n⟩)→(ρi)∏i=1n𝒞(⟨1⟩)

are equivalences for all n=0,1,…

The underlying category of such an object is 𝒞≔𝒞(⟨1⟩). The tensor product is simply the map

⊗:𝒞⊗𝒞←∼𝒞(⟨2⟩)→m∗𝒞(⟨1⟩)=𝒞,

where m:⟨2⟩→⟨1⟩ is given by 0↦0 and 1,2↦1. The tensor unit is given by the map

𝟏:pt=𝒞(⟨0⟩)→𝒞(⟨1⟩)=𝒞,

which is equivalent to an object in 𝒞. The idea is that all of the higher values of the functor encode all coherences like associativity, and symmetry.

Exercise 1.2.2.5. For an ordinary symmetric monoidal 1-category 𝒞, construct a functor

Fin∗→Cat∞

which takes a pointed set S⊔∗ to 𝒞×S.

Definition 1.2.2.6. A strong symmetric monoidal functor 𝒞→𝒟 is a natural transformation 𝒞→𝒟.

In particular, we could define a full subcategory

SymMonCat∞⊆Fun(NFin∗,Cat∞).

The reader could take this as a definition of the ∞-category of symmetric monoidal ∞-categories, but it has some shortcomings. The main shortcoming is that we don’t really have a way to discuss lax symmetric monoidal functors.

Definition 1.2.2.7 (Lurie). A symmetric monoidal ∞-category is a functor

𝒞⊗→NFin∗

satisfying the following conditions:

1.
It is a cocartesian fibration.2 In particular, we can consider the fibers and compute them as ordinary fiber products of simplicial sets. In addition, for any morphism f:⟨n⟩→⟨m⟩ in Fin∗, we obtain a pushforward
f!:𝒞⟨n⟩⊗→𝒞⟨m⟩⊗.
2.
The induced maps
𝒞⟨n⟩⊗→(ρi)!∏𝒞⟨1⟩⊗

are equivalences for all n=0,1,…

We will call 𝒞≔𝒞⟨1⟩⊗ and the tensor product is given by

⊗:𝒞⊗𝒞←∼𝒞⟨2⟩⊗→m!𝒞⟨1⟩⊗=𝒞.

Theorem 1.2.2.8 (Lurie). The two definitions agree in that for a symmetric monoidal ∞-category 𝒞⊗→NFin∗, we get an induced functor NFin∗→Cat∞ given by ⟨n⟩↦𝒞⟨n⟩⊗ and vice versa.

We will discuss how to get a fibration from a copresheaf of ∞-categories, but only do it for an ordinary symmetric monoidal category (𝒞,⊗). We define 𝒞⊗ as follows:

  • Objects are given by lists c1,…,cn in 𝒞 for ⟨n⟩∈Fin∗;

  • Morphisms from c1,…,cn to d1,…,dm are given by the data of

    • A map f:⟨n⟩→⟨m⟩ in Fin∗;

    • For each k∈⟨m⟩∖0, a map

      ⨂i∈f−1(k)ci→dk;
  • Composition is defined in the obvious way;
  • The forgetful functor takes c1,…,cn to ⟨n⟩.

Taking the nerve of this gives a symmetric monoidal ∞-category.

We will now start defining lax symmetric monoidal functors. We will call a morphism

f:⟨n⟩→⟨m⟩

inert if the induced map

f|f−1(⟨m⟩∖0):f−1(⟨m⟩∖0)→⟨m⟩∖0

is a bijection.

Definition 1.2.2.9. A lax symmetric monoidal functor between symmetric monoidal ∞-categories 𝒞⊗→NFin∗ and 𝒟⊗→NFin∗ is a functor such that F⊗ sends cocartesian lifts of inert morphisms to cocartesian lifts.

Exercise 1.2.2.10. Prove that for 1-categories, a lax symmetric monoidal functor 𝒞→𝒟 induces a functor 𝒞⊗→𝒟⊗.

1.2.3 𝔼n-algebras

𝔼n-algebras interpolate between associative (𝔼1-) algebras and commutative (𝔼∞-) algebras. In this section, 𝒞 will be a symmetric monoidal ∞-category.

Definition 1.2.3.1. An associative algebra in 𝒞 is a symmetric monoidal functor

N(Assact⊗)→𝒞,

where objects of Assact⊗ are finite sets, morphisms are morphisms of finite sets with a chosen linear order on preimages of points, composition is given by the lexicographic order, and the tensor product is given by disjoint union. We will denote the ∞-category of associative algebras in 𝒞 by

Alg(𝒞)≔Fun⊗(N(Assact⊗),𝒞).

Definition 1.2.3.2. A commutative algebra in 𝒞 is a symmetric monoidal functor

N(Commact⊗)→𝒞,

where Commact⊗ is just the category of finite sets. We will denote the ∞-category of commutative algebras in 𝒞 by

CAlg(𝒞)≔Fun⊗(N(Commact⊗),𝒞).

Warning 1.2.3.3. In a 1-category 𝒞, we have an inclusion

CAlg(𝒞)⊆Alg(𝒞).

This is completely false in ∞-categories, even if there is a functor.

We will now interpolate between commutative and associative algebras.

Definition 1.2.3.4. Let 0≤n<∞. We define a symmetric monoidal ∞-category (𝔼n⊗)act as the homotopy-coherent nerve of the topologically enriched category given by the following:

  • Objects are disjoint unions Dn⊔⋯⊔Dn of (poly)disks Dn=(0,1)n;

  • Morphisms from Dn⊔⋯⊔Dn to Dn⊔⋯⊔Dn are given by rectilinear embeddings. These are simply embeddings of topological spaces which on each disk is given by an affine linear map with matrix of the form

    (α1⋱αn),αi∈ℝ>0.

    An example would look something like Figure 1.1.

  • Composition is simply composition of embeddings.

This category is clearly topologically enriched and has a symmetric monoidal structure given by disjoint union.

Definition 1.2.3.5. An 𝔼n-algebra in a symmetric monoidal ∞-category 𝒞 is a symmetric monoidal functor

(𝔼n⊗)act→𝒞.

We will denote the ∞-category of 𝔼n-algebras in 𝒞 by

Alg𝔼n(𝒞)≔Fun⊗((𝔼n⊗)act,𝒞).

Note that all mapping spaces in (𝔼n⊗)act are determined by

Map(𝔼n⊗)act(Dn⊔⋯⊔Dn,Dn).

This has a map

Map(𝔼n⊗)act(Dn⊔⋯⊔Dn,Dn)→Confk(Dn)⊆Dn

given by evaluation at the center of each disk. Here, Confk(Dn)⊆Dn is the configuration space and is simply the locus where no two points agree.

Exercise 1.2.3.6. Prove that the evaluation map we just defined is a homotopy equivalence.

As an example, it is clear that

Map(𝔼n⊗)act(Dn,Dn)≃Conf1(Dn)≃pt.

The next example is

Map(𝔼n⊗)act(Dn⊔Dn,Dn)≃Conf2(Dn)≃Sn−1.

Now suppose we have an 𝔼n-algebra A:(𝔼n⊗)act→𝒞 with underlying algebra A(Dn)=A. We also have a morphism

Sn−1→Map(A⊗A,A)

and other morphisms. Restricting to the 0-cell, this is a multiplication morphism.

To try to understand 𝔼n-algebras, we may try to begin with n=1.

Proposition 1.2.3.7. There is an equivalence

NAss𝒶𝒸𝓉⊗→(𝔼1⊗)act

of symmetric monoidal ∞-categories which sends a finite set S to disjoint union ⨆SD1.

Proof. First, we show that all mapping spaces in (𝔼1⊗)act are discrete. Up to homotopy, a map D1⊔⋯⊔D1→D1 is simply an ordering of the indexing set of connected components of the source. This is precisely the set of maps in Assact⊗. This functor sends disjoint unions to disjoint unions, and finally a symmetric monoidal functor between symmetric monoidal ∞-categories is an equivalence in the ∞-category of symmetric monoidal ∞-categories if and only if the underlying functor is an equivalence. □

Corollary 1.2.3.8. We have an equivalence

Alg𝔼1(𝒞)≅Alg(𝒞).

Exercise 1.2.3.9. Figure out what 𝔼0-algebras are in an arbitrary symmetric monoidal ∞-category. Next, figure out what 𝔼2-algebras in the ∞-category Cat of 1-categories are (you should get braided monoidal categories).

There are functors

(𝔼0⊗)act→(𝔼1⊗)act→⋯

given by taking the Cartesian product with D1. These are symmetric monoidal functors, so we have induced functors

⋯→Alg𝔼1(𝒞)→Alg𝔼0(𝒞).

Definition 1.2.3.10. The ∞-category of 𝔼∞-a;gebras is the inverse limit of the diagram

⋯→Alg𝔼1(𝒞)→Alg𝔼0(𝒞)

in Cat∞.

Theorem 1.2.3.11. We have an equivalence

Alg𝔼∞(𝒞)≅CAlg(𝒞).

Sketch of proof. First, note that

Alg𝔼∞(𝒞)≅lim←⁡Alg𝔼n(𝒞)≃lim←⁡Fun⊗((𝔼n⊗)act,𝒞)≃Fun⊗(colim⁡(𝔼n⊗)act,𝒞).

Proving that this colimit is equivalent to NCommact⊗ is left as an exercise. □

We will now state a very important result. The proof is very hard, but the statement should be understandable. Let (𝒞,⊗) be a closed symmetric monoidal category or at least have the property that −⊗c commutes with filtered colimits and geometric realizations. We will also assume that 𝒞 has all limits and colimits.

Theorem 1.2.3.12 (Lurie).

1.
The ∞-category Alg𝔼n(𝒞) admits all limits and colimits for any 0≤n≤∞. The forgetful functor
Alg𝔼n(𝒞)→𝒞

preserves filtered colimits, geometric realizations, and all limits. Moreover, it detects equivalences.

2.
When n=∞, the coproduct and tensor product coincide.
3.
The ∞-category Alg𝔼n(𝒞) admits a symmetric monoidal structure such that Alg𝔼n(𝒞)→𝒞 is symmetric monoidal.

Exercise 1.2.3.13. Do the 1-categorical analogue of the theorem in the category Ab of abelian groups.

We will now discuss 𝔼n-algebras in the ∞-category of spaces 𝒮 equipped with symmetric monoidal structure given by the Cartesian product. Then Alg(𝒮) is the category of “monoids” in 𝒮. For any such space X, the set of connected components π0(X) is a monoid.

Definition 1.2.3.14. We say X is grouplike if π0(X) is a group. This is equivalent to saying that the shear map

X×X→X×X(a,b)↦(ab,b)

is a homotopy equivalence. In addition, we say an 𝔼n-algebra is grouplike if the underlying 𝔼1-algebra is grouplike.

For every pointed space X∈𝒮∗, the iterated loop space

ΩnX≃Map𝒮∗(Sn,X)≅Map((Dn,∂Dn),(X,∗))

is canonically an 𝔼n-algebra in 𝒮.

Exercise 1.2.3.15. Make this 𝔼n-algebra structure precise by giving a functor (𝔼n⊗)act→𝒮 of topologically enriched categories.

Theorem 1.2.3.16 (Boardman-Vogt). The functor

Ωn:𝒮∗n−conn→Alg𝔼n(𝒮)

is fully faithful with essential image the grouplike 𝔼n-algebras for any 0≤n<∞.

Corollary 1.2.3.17. For any 𝔼n-algebra A in 𝒮 and any connected pointed space X∈𝒮∗conn, we have that

Map𝔼n(ΩnΣnX,A)≅Map𝒮∗(X,A).

Proof. We can consider the subspace A′⊆A consisting of the unit component π0(A′)⊆π0(A). Then

Map𝔼n(ΩnΣnX,A)≃Map𝔼n(ΩnΣnX,A′).

Similarly, we have

Map𝒮∗(X,A)≃Map𝒮∗(X,A′).

Therefore, we may assume that A is grouplike. But this means that A=ΩnY for some pointed n-connected space Y. This implies that

Map𝔼n(ΩnΣnX,ΩnY)≅Map𝒮∗(ΣnX,Y)≅Map𝒮∗(X,ΩnY)≅Map𝒮∗(X,A).
□

Sketch of proof of Theorem 1.2.3.16. We begin with the case of n=1. Here, we have the functor

Ω:𝒮∗conn→Alg𝔼1gp(𝒮).

We will construct an inverse using the bar construction, which is given by 

 \ms {Bar}(G) \coloneqq \colim _{\Delta ^{\op }} \left( \cdots G \times G \triple {\to } G \rightrightarrows \pt  \right) .

The result we need is that ΩBar(G)≃G is an equivalence of spaces. This is usually done by constructing a fiber sequence

G→EG→BG.

The general step is now to induct on n. For example, if we consider 𝒮∗2−conn, its image in Alg𝔼1Sp(𝒮∗conn). Therefore we have a chain This is actually the same as 𝔼2-algebras, and the general case works the same way and the desired result follows from Theorem 1.2.3.18. □

Theorem 1.2.3.18 (Dunn additivity). For any symmetric monoidal ∞-category 𝒞, we have

Alg𝔼n+m(𝒞)≅Alg𝔼m(Alg𝔼n(𝒞))

for all n,m≥0.

Note that the 1-categorical version of this is the Eckmann-Hilton argument.

Corollary 1.2.3.19. Suppose that 𝒞 has sifted colimits and ⊗ commutes with them in both variables separately. Then

Bar:Alg𝔼n(𝒞)/𝟏→Alg𝔼n−1(𝒞)

given by 

 A \mapsto \colim \left( \cdots A \otimes A \triple {\to } A \rightrightarrows \1 \right)

is well-defined.

Proof. Note that it is simply given by

Alg𝔼n≅Alg𝔼1(Alg𝔼n−1(𝒞))→Alg𝔼1(𝒞).
□

1.2.4 p-adic completion

We will generalize the process of going from ℤ to ℤp in the world of spectra. In addition, we will see how spectra can be recovered from their p-completions and their rationalizations.

Recall that an abelian group A is p-complete if it is complete (and separated) with respect to the p-adic topology on A. This is the topology which has a neighborhood basis of 0 given by pnA⊆A. Equivalently, this says that

A→∼lim←⁡A/pn≕Ap∧.

Definition 1.2.4.1. For a spectrum X∈Sp and an integer n∈ℤ, define X/n to be the cofiber of the map X→nX given by the addition of identity morphism n times. Equivalently, we have

X/n≃X⊗𝕊𝕊/n.

As we would expect, if n∣m, then there is a canonical map

X/m→X/n

defined as the cofiber of

Definition 1.2.4.2. For a spectrum X∈Sp, we define its p-completion to be the spectrum

Xp∧≔lim←⁡(⋯→X/p3→X/p2→X/p).

Note that there is a canonical map X→Xp∧ induced from the projections X→X/pn.

Remark 1.2.4.3. All of these constructions are well-defined up to contractible choice.

Definition 1.2.4.4. A spectrum X is p-complete if the map X→Xp∧ is an equivalence. Denote the ∞-category of p-complete spectra by Spp∧.

Theorem 1.2.4.5.

1.
For every spectrum X, the spectrum Xp∧ is p-complete.
2.
The functor (−)p∧:Sp→Spp∧ is left adjoint to the inclusion Spp∧↪Sp.
3.
The ∞-category Spp∧ has all limits and colimits.

Sketch of proof. We will first prove that Xp∧ is p-complete. First, note that Spp∧ is closed under limits and finite colimits. This is true because the functor −/p is a cofiber and so commutes with all limits and colimits and the limit functor commutes with limits and finite colimits. The second step is to prove that for any X, X/p is p-complete. This implies that X/pn is p-complete by using the fiber sequence

X/p→pn−1X/pn→X/pn−1.

This implies that Xp∧ is p-complete.

First, note that the functor (−)p∧ is idempotent. This means that

(Xp∧)p∧≃Xp∧.

If Y is a p-complete spectrum, we can construct an inverse to

Map(X,Y)←Map(Xp∧,Y)

by applying p-completion to everything.

We know already that limits and finite colimits exist. For an arbitrary colimit of a functor I→XSpp∧, the colimit is simply given by

(colimISp⁡Xi)p∧.
□

Exercise 1.2.4.6. Prove that a spectrum X is p-complete if and only if

lim(⋯→X→pX→pX)≃0.

Moreover, prove that X/p is p-complete for any spectrum X.

Definition 1.2.4.7. A map f:X→Y of spectra is a p-adic equivalence if the induced map

fp∧:Xp∧→Yp∧

is an equivalence.

Note that if X and Y are p-complete, then f is a p-adic equivalence if and only if f is an equivalence.

Proposition 1.2.4.8.

1.
A map f:X→Y is a p-adic equivalence if and only if the map
f/p:X/p→Y/p

is an equivalence.

2.
A map f:X→Y between connective X,Y is a p-adic equivalence if and only if the induced map
X⊗𝕊H𝔽p→Y⊗𝕊H𝔽p

is an equivalence (in other words, we can check equivalence on homology).

Proof. The proof is left as an exercise to the reader. □

Now we know that p-adic equivalences have nice properties, but it is not clear how to tell whether a spectrum is p-complete.

Proposition 1.2.4.9. Let A be an abelian group. If A is p-complete, then so is HA∈Sp.

For example, we see that Hℤp is p-complete. The converse unfortunately fails in general, but it does hold if A has bounded order of p∞-torsion.

Definition 1.2.4.10. An abelian group A is derived p-complete if the Eilenberg-Maclane spectrum HA is p-complete.

Remark 1.2.4.11. There is also a notion of p-completeness in 𝒟(ℤ). Everything works exactly as in Sp. Then A is derived p-complete if and only if it is p-complete as an object of 𝒟(ℤ). This is equivalent to the condition that there is a quasi-isomorphism

A≃Rlim←⁡Cone(A→pnA)∈𝒟(ℤ).

Theorem 1.2.4.12.

1.
A spectrum X is p-complete if and only if πn(X) is derived p-complete for all n.
2.
Assume that πn(X) has bounded order of p∞-torsion for each n. Then
π∗(Xp∧)=π∗(X)p∧.

Example 1.2.4.13. The most important example of a p-complete spectrum is the p-adic completion 𝕊p∧ of the sphere. We can compute

π∗(𝕊p∧)={ℤp∗=0{p∞-torsion in π∗(𝕊)}>00∗<0.

Another example is simply (Hℚ)p∧=0 because multiplication by p is an isomorphism on ℚ.

There are some nice monoidal properties associated to p-complete spectra which are listed below. We will not prove these.

  • The category Spp∧ of p-complete spectra admits a closed symmetric monoidal structure given by

    X⊗ˆpY≔(X⊗𝕊Y)p∧.

    In particular, the p-completion functor is strong symmetric monoidal.

  • If R is an 𝔼n-algebra, then so is Rp∧ and R→Rp∧ is an 𝔼n-map exhibiting Rp∧ as the initial p-complete 𝔼n-algebra under R.

It is much easier to deal with p-complete spectra than to deal with spectra. However, this is only useful if we can recover spectra from their p-completions.

Question 1.2.4.14. Can we recover any spectrum X from its p-completions Xp∧ as p ranges over all primes?

The answer to this question must be no by the example of Hℚ. In order to even attempt to have an affirmative answer, we will also need to consider rationalization. Here, recall that an abelian group A is rational if it is uniquely divisible. Equivalently, it is a ℚ-vector space.

Definition 1.2.4.15. A spectrum X is rational if πn(X) is rational for each n. We denote the full subcategory of rational spectra by Spℚ⊆Sp.

This is actually even better-behaved than p-completeness.

Theorem 1.2.4.16.

1.
A spectrum is rational if and only if it admits the structure of an Hℚ-module.
2.
For any spectrum X, the spectrum X⊗𝕊Hℚ≕Xℚ is rational and π∗(Xℚ)=π∗(X)ℚ.
3.
The functor −⊗𝕊Hℚ:Sp→Spℚ is left adjoint to the inclusion Spℚ⊆Sp.
4.
The category Spℚ⊆Sp is closed under limits and colimits.
5.
We have an equivalence
Spℚ≅ModHℚ≃𝒟(ℚ).
6.
The category Spℚ is symmetric monoidal with tensor product
X⊗𝕊Y=X⊗HℚY

and unit Hℚ.

Exercise 1.2.4.17. Prove this theorem using the fact that Hℚ⊗𝕊Hℚ=Hℚ.

We can now refine our question.

Question 1.2.4.18. Can we recover any spectrum X from its p-completions Xp∧ as p ranges over all primes together with its rationalization Xℚ?

Our slogan will be that the answer to this question is yes if we also include the data of a certain “gluing map.” This uses something known as the Hasse square.

For every spectrum we have maps

X→Xp∧andX→Xℚ.

In addition, rationalizing the p-completion map, we have maps

Xℚ→(Xp∧)ℚ≕Xℚp.

By naturality properties of rationalization, we obtain a commutative square This is called the Hasse square or the fracture square.

Theorem 1.2.4.19. For any spectrum X, this square is a fiber product.
