This theorem is proved by noting that p is invertible on the fiber of X→Xp∧. Therefore, the fiber of the top row is rational (because all primes are invertible), so it equals its rationalization, which is the fiber of the bottom row.

The theorem can be refined to the categorical level. In particular, we have a pullback diagram of ∞-categories. This means that we can decompose the entire ∞-category of spectra.

Unfortunately, this morphism is not symmetric monoidal, but it at least behaves well with respect to 𝔼n-algebras. More precisely, there is a pullback square of ∞-categories, where the arrows are given by restriction from the previous square.

1.2.5 Tate construction

Let G be a group object in 𝒮. In particular, this means that G is a group-like 𝔼1-space. These can in fact be modeled by topological groups, but the correct generality is that of group-like 𝔼1-spaces. There is a classifying space BG∈𝒮 given by the bar construction. If 𝒞 is any ∞-category, we will let

𝒞BG=Fun(BG,𝒞)

denote the category of objects in 𝒞 with a G-action.

Construction 1.2.5.1. We will consider G as an object in 𝒮G×G by letting G×G act on G by the action

(g,h)⋅h≔gxh−1.

Definition 1.2.5.2 (Klein). We define a spectrum DG∈SpBG called the dualizing spectrum of G as

DG≔(Σ+∞G)h(G×1)

with its remaining G=1×G-action.

The name dualizing spectrum needs a justification, which will be given in the remainder of this section. Before we do this, we give some examples.

Example 1.2.5.3. Assume G is a finite group. Then

Σ+∞G=⨁g∈G𝕊.

Computing the homotopy fixed points, we obtain

(Σ+∞G)hG=(⨁g∈G𝕊)hG≃𝕊.

More precisely, the map

(⨁g∈G𝕊)hG→⨁g∈G𝕊→𝕊

is an equivalence.

To see this, consider the homotopy fixed point spectral sequence

H∗(G,⨁g∈Gπ∗𝕊)⟹π∗((⨁g∈G𝕊)hG).

It is a classical result that

H∗(G,⨁g∈GA)={A∗=00∗≠0.

Therefore the spectral sequence degenerates and yields the result. This implies that DG=𝕊 with the trivial action.

Now suppose that G is a compact Lie group.

Theorem 1.2.5.4. If G is a compact Lie group, then

DG=𝕊𝔤≔Σ∞(𝔤+)

where G acts by the adjoint representation.

For example, let 𝕋=U(1)=S1. Then because the adjoint representation of an abelian group is trivial, we have D𝕋=𝕊1 with the trivial action.

Now assume that BG≃(M,m0) for some closed smooth manifold M. For example, if G=ℤ, then BG≃S1. Alternatively, we can consider any closed manifold (M,m0) and let G=ΩM.

Theorem 1.2.5.5 (Atiyah duality). The dualizing spectrum is given by

DG=𝕊−Tm0M≃𝕊−dim⁡M,

where we extend the construction 𝕊V for any representation of G to a virtual representation. As a functor

BG≃M→Sp,

it sends

m↦𝕊−TmM.

Remark 1.2.5.6. For any space X (in place of BG), we can define a dualizing spectrum

DX:X→Sp.

For example, we can define this functor on connected components because

X≃⨆BGi.

In particular, we assign DGi to BGi.

Construction 1.2.5.7. Let 𝒞 be a stable ∞-category which has all limits and colimits. For any E∈Sp and X∈𝒞, there is an object

E⊗X∈𝒞

defined such that the functor

−⊗X:Sp→𝒞

preserves colimits and the composite

𝒮→Σ+∞Sp→−⊗X𝒞

is given by the functor

M↦M⊗X=colimM⁡cX.

Definition 1.2.5.8. Let G∈Alg𝔼1gp(𝒮) and X∈BG. We define the norm map

NmG:(DG⊗𝕊X)hG→XhG

as the composite

Exercise 1.2.5.9. Prove that

((Σ+∞G⊗𝕊X)h(1×G))h(G×1)≃XhG.

This is quite an abstract construction, so we will try to get our hands on it with some examples.

Example 1.2.5.10. If G is finite and X∈𝒞BG, then the norm map is

(DG⊗X)hG≃XhG→XhG.

For example, if 𝒞=Sp and X=HM for an abelian group M with a G-action, then this map is a map and is induced from the classical norm map

MG→MG[m],↦∑g∈Ggm

from coinvariants to invariants. This follows from the fact that for a general X, the composite

X→XhG→NmGXhG→X

is the sum over all g∈G of the maps ρg:X→X given by multiplication by g.

Exercise 1.2.5.11. Prove that if G is finite, the composite

X→XhG→NmGXhG→X

agrees with the map

∑g∈Gρg:X→X.

Example 1.2.5.12. When G=𝕋, we get a map

ΣXh𝕋=(D𝕋⊗X)h𝕋→Xh𝕋.

Theorem 1.2.5.13. The norm map (DG⊗X)hG→XhG is an equivalence provided that one of the following conditions holds:

1.
BG is a finite CW complex;
2.
X is induced, which means that X≃Σ+∞G⊗Y where G acts only on Σ+∞G.

Sketch of proof. In the first case, all limits in the interchange maps are finite. Because all functors in the composite are exact, we are done.

In the second case, the limits and colimits are still close enough to being finite, so we are done. □

Example 1.2.5.14. Let BG be a closed manifold M, 𝒞=Sp, and X=Hℤ with the trivial action of G. In this case, the norm is a map

(DG⊗X)hG→∼XhG=HℤBG.

The target has homotopy groups given by

π∗(HℤBG)=H−∗(M,ℤ).

The source is explicitly given by

(DG⊗X)hG≅(𝕊−tM⊗Hℤ)hG≃(Hℤ[−n])hG,

where G acts on HZ[−n] non-trivially. This has homotopy groups

π∗((Hℤ[−n])hG)=H∗+n(M,ℤw1)

given by homology with coefficients in the orientation cover. On homotopy groups, this map

H∗+n(M,ℤw1)→∼H−∗(M,ℤ)

is simply Poincaré duality (at least if M is orientable).

If we replace Hℤ by any spectrum, we get Poincaré duality in arbitrary cohomology theories. If X=BG is a finite CW complex, the norm equivalence is a generalized version of Poincaré duality

H∗(X,DX)→H−∗(X).

This can be thought of as being analogous to Serre or Verdier duality in algebraic geometry. If DX is a parameterized sphere (DX=𝕊[n] as underlying spectra), then this is equivalent to X being a Poincaré duality space.

Theorem 1.2.5.15 (Klein). The natural transformation (called the assembly map)

(DG⊗−)hG→(−)hG

exhibits the functor (DG⊗−)hG as the universal functor over (−)hG which preserves colimits.

Note that this uniquely determines the spectrum DG as an object of SpBG.

Definition 1.2.5.16. For an object X∈𝒞BG, we define the Tate object as the cofiber

XtG≔cofib(NmG).

Example 1.2.5.17. If BG is finite, then XtG=0 for all X. If G is finite and X=HM for an abelian group M with a G-action, then (HM)tG has homotopy groups given by the Tate cohomology

π∗((HM)tG)=Hˆ−∗(G,M)

of G with coefficients in M.

Exercise 1.2.5.18. Work out what Tate cohomology is in terms of usual homology and cohomology.

Example 1.2.5.19. Suppose that 𝒞 is a symmetric monoidal ∞-category such that the tensor product commutes with colimits in both variables separately. Then the functor

(−)tG:𝒞BG→𝒞

admits a (unique) lax symmetric monoidal structure such that the natural transformation

(−)hG→(−)tG

admits a refinement to a symmetric monoidal transformation.

Corollary 1.2.5.20. If A∈Alg𝔼n(𝒞BG)≃Alg𝔼n(𝒞)BG, then AhG→AtG is a morphism of 𝔼n-algebras.

1.2.6 Tate diagonal

The Tate diagonal is a surprising feature of the world of spectra. Before we discuss it, we will motivate it by discussing abelian groups.

Let A be an abelian group. If we try to write a map of sets

A→A⊗A,x↦x⊗x,

this is not a homomorphism. For example, note that

(x+y)⊗(x+y)=x⊗x+y⊗y+(x⊗y+y⊗x).

Recall now that if Cp is the cyclic group with p elements, there is a norm map

N:(A⊗p)Cp→(A⊗p)Cp,x1⊗⋯xp↦∑σ∈Cpxσ(1)⊗⋯⊗xσ(p).

Note here that the error term of the map x↦x⊗x is in the image of the norm map. Therefore, the “diagonal” x↦x⊗⋯⊗x induces a homormorphism

A→(A⊗p)Cp/N((A⊗p)Cp).

This homomorphism in fact exhibits

(A⊗p)Cp/N((A⊗p)Cp)≅A/p.

Exercise 1.2.6.1.

1.
Prove that x↦x⊗p induces a homomorphism
A→(A⊗p)Cp/N((A⊗p)Cp).
2.
Prove that this homomorphism factors through an isomorphism
A/p→∼(A⊗p)Cp/N((A⊗p)Cp).

We will now discuss the analogous construction for spectra.

Theorem 1.2.6.2. There is a unique lax symmetric monoidal natural transformation

X→(X⊗p)tCp.

In the rest of this section, we will attempt to see where this comes from and understand some of its properties.

Lemma 1.2.6.3. The Singer construction

X↦(X⊗p)tCp

is an exact functor.

This result is particularly surprising because the p-th tensor power functor is not even additive.

Proof. First, suppose Y≃X⊕Z. By the binomial theorem, we have

(X⊕Z)⊗p=X⊗p⊕Z⊗p⊕⨁p(X⊗(p−1)⊗Z)⊕⨁(p2)(X⊗(p−2)⊗Z⊗2)⊕⋯

On all of the non-pure terms, the action of Cp on the connected components is free, so these terms are all induced modules over Cp. These terms vanish after taking Tate fixed points.

In general, consider a cofiber sequence X→Y→Z as a “two-stage filtration” on Y of the form where Z appears as the associated graded term. We then obtain a filtration on Y⊗p of the form

X⊗p→⨁X⊗(p−1)⊗Y→⋯→⨁X⊗Y⊗(p−1)→Y⊗p.

There is a monoidal structure on filtered objects called the Day convolution structure which produces this diagram from our filtered object. The associated graded terms are given by

X⊗p,…,⨁pX⊗Z⊗(p−1),Z⊗p.

Applying Tate fixed points, the associated graded terms are now of the form

(X⊗p)tCp,0,…,0,(Z⊗p)tCp.

This implies that we have a cofiber sequence

(X⊗p)tCp→(Y⊗p)tCp→(Z⊗p)tCp.
□

Remark 1.2.6.4. The Singer construction commutes with suspension as

((ΣX)⊗p)tCp≃Σ(X⊗p)tCp.

We can write

(ΣX)⊗p≃𝕊p⊗X⊗p,

but the action of Cp involves a nontrivial action on 𝕊p, where we take the suspension spectrum of the one-point compactification of the regular representation of Cp. In fact, we have (𝕊p)tCp≃(𝕊1)tCp, where S1 has the trivial action.

Lemma 1.2.6.5 (Stable Yoneda Lemma). Let 𝒞 be a stable ∞-category. We consider the stable ∞-category Funex(𝒞,Sp) of exact functors to Sp. Taking mapping spectra, there exists a natural equivalence

mapFunex(𝒞,Sp)(map(X,−),F)≃F(X).

Proof sketch. We will reduce this to the 1-categorical Yoneda lemma. A natural transformation Map(X,−)→F is simply a sequence of natural transformations on the n-th underlying spaces with some compatibility conditions. More precisely, we have natural transformations

map(Σ−nX,−)→Ω∞ΣnF(−),

which by the ordinary Yoneda lemma yields a sequence of points in

Ω∞ΣnF(Σ−nX)≃Ω∞F(X).

In other words, we have an equivalence of spaces

MapFunex(𝒞,Sp)(map(X,−),F)≃Ω∞F(X).
□

Natural transformations X→(X⊗p)tCp correspond to maps 𝕊→(𝕊⊗p)tCp≃𝕊tCp. There is a natural choice of map like this given by

𝕊≃map(Σ+∞pt,𝕊)→𝕊hCp≃map(Σ+∞Cp,𝕊)→𝕊tCp.

Note that there are other maps 𝕊→𝕊tCp, for example the zero map. However, we need a map which preserves the lax symmetric monoidal structure, and the unique such map is the one we have just given.

Lemma 1.2.6.6. The functor map(𝕊,−) is initial among all lax symmetric monoidal exact functors Sp→Sp.

We are now ready to discuss some properties of the Tate diagonal. In particular, we will not prove anything.

Theorem 1.2.6.7. For a bounded below X, the morphism

X→(X⊗p)tCp

exhibits (X⊗p)tCp as Xp∧. In particular, (X⊗p)tCp is bounded below.

In particular, we see that 𝕊tCp≃𝕊p∧. This is completely different from Tate cohomology for abelian groups and is a special form of the Segal conjecture. Proofs of these results rely on the Adams spectral sequence because the Tate spectral sequences is too messy.

The Tate construction also allows us to define a version of Frobenius on 𝔼∞-ring spectra.

Definition 1.2.6.8. For an 𝔼∞-ring spectrum R, we have the Tate-valued Frobenius

R→Δ(R⊗p)tCp→μtCpRtCp

using the fact that multiplication R⊗p→R is equivariant. This follows from the fact that a morphism (R⊗p)hCp→R is encoded in the definition of an 𝔼∞-algebra.

We should think about this as an analogue of the morphism

R→R/p,x↦xp

for an ordinary commutative ring R.

Exercise 1.2.6.9. Prove that it is necessary that R is commutative and that the target is reduced by p. Also prove that x↦xp is a ring homomorphism R→R/p.

Applying the Tate-valued Frobenius to

map(Σ+∞X,E)

for some space X and 𝔼∞-algebra E, we obtain power operations. For example, Steenrod operations and Adams operations arise in this way.

2 (Topological) cyclic homology

2.1 Classical Hochschild and cyclic homology

In this section, we discuss Hochschild homology, (negative, periodic) cyclic homology, the HKR theorem, and related topics.

2.1.1 Hochschild homology

Let k be a field and R be a k- algebra.

Definition 2.1.1.1. The Hochschild homology of R is the homology of the complex

HH(R/k)≔(⋯→∂R⊗kR→∂R),

where the differential is given by

∂(a0⊗⋯⊗an)≔a0a1⊗⋯⊗an−a0⊗a1a2⊗⋯⊗an⋯+(−1)nana0⊗⋯⊗an−1.

Remark 2.1.1.2. This seems related to what happens when you multiply elements placed on an S1 as in Figure 2.1. In fact, we will see later that there is a connection to the actual S1.

Example 2.1.1.3. For now, set R=k. In this case, we have

HH(k/k)=(⋯→k→k),

where the differentials are alternating sums of 1 and −1. In fact, we see that the complex is

HH(k/k)=(⋯→0k→idk→0k),

and therefore the Hochschild homology is

HH∗(k/k)={k∗=00otherwise.

Example 2.1.1.4. Because the last differential is given by a⊗b↦ab−ba, we see that

HH0(R/k)=R/[R,R].

In particular, if R is commutative, we have

HH0(R/k)=R.

In this case, we have

HH1(R/k)=R⊗kRIm⁡∂≅ΩR/k1.

We will now recall the definition of the module of Kähler differentials.

Definition 2.1.1.5. The module of Kähler differentials of a commutative ring R is the module ΩR/k1 generated by dx for all x∈R subject to the following relations:

1.
For all x,y∈R, we have d(x+y)=dx+dy;
2.
For all x,y∈R, we have d(xy)=xdy+ydx;
3.
For all x∈k, we have dx=0.

Therefore, we see that ΩR/k1 receives a universal k-linear derivation from R.

There is at most one map

HH1(R/k)→ΩR/k1x⊗y↦x⋅dy.

Exercise 2.1.1.6. Check that this is an isomorphism.

We will now prove some more properties of Hochschild homology.

Lemma 2.1.1.7. If R is commutative, then HH∗(R) has the structure of a strictly graded-commutative ring. Here, this means that x2=0 for any x of odd degree, which is only relevant in characterisic 2.

Proof. The Hochschild complex HH(R/k) in fact comes from a simplicial commutative ring where the face maps are the components of the differential ∂. The desired result then follows by Theorem A.1.0.2. □

On the de Rham side, there is also a multiplicative structure.

Definition 2.1.1.8. The de Rham complex is the exterior algebra

ΩR/k∗≔ΛR∗ΩR/k1=⨁k≥0ΛRkΩR/k1=SymR⁡ΩR/k1[1]x2=0,x∈ΩR/k1.

By extending from degree 1, we obtain a map ΩR/k∗→HH∗(R/k).

Theorem 2.1.1.9 (Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg). If R/k has cotangent complex concentrated in degree 0, then the map

ΩR/k∗→HH∗(R/k)

is an isomorphism.

We will discuss the cotangnet complex later, but for now we may think that R is a smooth or ind-smooth k-algebra.

Remark 2.1.1.10. The differential on ΩR/k∗ does not play a role here. Studying what it corresponds to on the Hochschild side will leade us to cyclic homology.

Exercise 2.1.1.11. Find an explicit description of Ωk[x1,…,xn]/k∗ and in particular show that it is concentrated in degrees at most n.

We will now extend to the case when k is an arbitrary commutative ring. This will lead to flatness issues, so we will fix this by taking derived tensor products. For now, we will let R be a dg-algebra over k which is K-flat. This is a flatness condition, but when R is bounded below, it agrees with levelwise flatness. Over ℤ, it always agrees with levelwise flatness. For such an R, we define the Hochschild complex by

HH(R/k)≔Tot⁡(⋯→R⊗kR→R).

If R is not K-flat, we will simply replace it by a K-flat resolution R♭ and define

HH(R/k)≔HH(R♭.k).

This is well-defined up to quasi-isomorphism.

Proposition 2.1.1.12. For a dg-algebra R, there is a quasi-isomorphism

HH(R/k)≃R⊗R⊗k𝕃Rop𝕃R.

Remark 2.1.1.13. This is usually called Shukla homology, but we will not make this distinction here.

Proof. Replacing R by a flat resolution, we consider the complex

Tot⁡(⋯→R⊗kR⊗kR→R⊗kR)≃R.

The differentials are given by multiplying adjacent terms, but without the ana0 term (think configurations on an interval). This complex is usually called the bar complex. Applying −⊗R⊗kRopR, the resulting total complex computes the desired complex R⊗R⊗kRop𝕃R, but it also computes HH∗(R/k). □

Lemma 2.1.1.14. If R is a dg-algebra which arises from a simplicial commutative k-algebra, then HH(R/k) also comes from a simplicial commutative k-algebra. In particular, the Hochschild homology groups HH∗(R/k) form a strictly graded-commutative k-algebra.

Proof. We replace R by a flat simplicial commutative k-algebra. Then HH(Rn/k) gives a bisimplicial commutative k-algebra. The total complex is then quasi-isomorphic to the diagonal, which is clearly simplicial. □

Lemma 2.1.1.15. If A,B are dg-algebras, then

HH(A⊗𝕃B/k)≃HH(A/k)⊗k𝕃HH(B/k).

Remark 2.1.1.16. If R is commutative, then setting A=B=R gives a multiplication map on HH via the multiplication of R.

Proof. Because HH(A/k) and HH(B/k) are simplicial dg-algebras, the tensor product

HH(A/k)⊗k𝕃HH(B/k)

is a bisimplicial dg-algebra. Taking the total complex in all three directions, the result is quasi-isomorphic to the diagonal, which is precisely

HH(A⊗k𝕃B).
□

We are now ready to prove the HKR theorem for polynomial rings. As we will see later, we will reduce the general case to this one.

Proof of Theorem 2.1.1.9 for polynomial rings. In the case of R=k[x], we have

Ωk[x]/k∗=k[x]⊗Λ(dx).

Then we only need to check that HH(k[x]/k) vanishes in degree greater than 1. This is given by

HH(k[x]/k)=k[x]⊗k[x]⊗kk[x]𝕃k[x]=k[x]⊗k[a,b]𝕃k[x].

We have the resolution

k[a,b]→⋅(a−b)k[a,b]

of k[x], and this gives the desired result.

For R=k[x1,…,xn] This is simply a tensor product

R=k[x1]⊗k⋯⊗kk[xn],

so because both sides of the HKR theorem commute with tensor products, we obtain the desired result.

Finally, if R=k[xi∣i∈I], we write R as a filtered colimit of finitely-generated polynomial algebras by writing the set {xi∣i∈I} of generators as a filtered colimit of its finite subsets. Because both sides commute with filtered colimits, we are done. □

We will now turn to an extremely non-smooth example.

Proposition 2.1.1.17. We have

HH∗(𝔽p/ℤ)=𝔽p⟨x⟩,

where the ⟨x⟩ means the free divided power algebra generated by x.

Proof. We will compute the derived tensor product

𝔽p⊗𝔽p⊗𝕃𝔽p𝔽p.

We will resolve 𝔽p by the dg-algebra

ℤ[ε]/ε2,∂ε=p,|ε|=1.

The tensor product is then given by

A≃𝔽p⊗𝕃𝔽p≃𝔽p[ε]/ε2.

We will resolve 𝔽p as an A-algebra by

A⟨x⟩=A[x1,x2,…]xixj=(i+ji)xi+j,∂xi=εxi−1,|xi|=2i,

and the desired result follows by taking the tensor product. □

2.1.2 The Connes operator

We will describe an operator on HH which corresponds to the de Rham differential. Recall that the de Rham differential

d:ΩR/k∗→ΩR/k∗+1

is induced from the universial derivation d:R→ΩR/k1 by the Leibniz rule.

Definition 2.1.2.1. Let R be an associative k-algebra. We define a k-linear map

B:HH(R/k)n→HH(R/k)n+1

by the formula

r0⊗⋯⊗rn↦∑σ∈Cn+1(−1)nσ(0)(1⊗rσ+(−1)nrσ⊗1),

where we define

rσ≔rσ(0)⊗⋯⊗rσ(n).

This formula is related to the cyclic objects introduced by Connes, and there is a way to think about it systematically in the topological setting, which we will discuss later.

Exercise 2.1.2.2. Check that

1.
B2=0;
2.
dB+Bd=0.

The operator B equips HH(R/k) with the structure of a dg-module over the dg-algebra

A≔k[b]/b2,|b|=1,∂=0.

Note that if 𝕋=U(1) is the circle group, then we have

A=H∗(𝕋,k).

We then see that HH∗(R/k) is a graded module over k[b]/b2, and in particular that there is an operator

B:HH∗(R/k)→HH∗+1(R/k)

satisfying B2=0.

Warning 2.1.2.3. One might object that we only defined the Connes operator only for algebras concentrated in degree 0, but with some careful thought we can define B for dg-algebras R/k.

We need the following fact.

Lemma 2.1.2.4. If R is commutative, then B is a derivation. In particular, it satisfies the graded Leibniz rule

B(xy)=B(x)y+(−1)|x|xB(y).

Warning 2.1.2.5. The Connes operator is not true on the complex HH(R/k). It is true up to coherent homotopy, but proving this is very hard. Instead, we will later use the topological enhancement to understand this.

Proposition 2.1.2.6. The map

ΩR/k∗→HH∗(R/k)

sends the de Rham differential d to the Connes operator B. In other words, the diagram commutes.

Proof. The map ΩR/k∗→HH∗(R/k) is determined by its effect in degrees 0 and 1. In degree 0, it is given by the identity

R→HH0(R/k)=R,

and in degree 1, it is given by

ΩR/k1→HH1(R/k)=R⊗kR∼xdy↦[x⊗y].

Therefore, it is enough to check that the diagram commutes. Note that for any r∈R, we see that all signs in the definition of B are +1, so we have

B(r)=[1⊗r]+[r⊗1].

This corresponds to the element

1⋅dr+r⋅d1=dr∈ΩR/k1.

We conclude by using the fact that the de Rham differential is uniquely determined by being a derivation and its effect on R. □

Remark 2.1.2.7. Sometimes in the rest of these notes, we will denote the Connes operator by d. If this causes confusion, we will call it B.

Example 2.1.2.8. For HH∗(𝔽p/ℤ)=𝔽p⟨x⟩ with x in degree 2, the Connes operator acts trivially for degree reasons.

Question 2.1.2.9. Does this mean that it acts trivially (maybe up to homotopy or quasi-isomorphism) on HH(𝔽p,ℤ)?

The answer to this question is in fact no, and we will see this by taking a (derived) reduction mod p. This means that we will consider

HH(𝔽p)⫽p≔HH(Fp)⊗ℤ𝕃𝔽p.

Letting A act trivially on 𝔽p, we obtain a structure of an A-module on HH(𝔽p)⫽p. We compute

HH(𝔽p)⫽p≃HH(Fp)⊗ℤ(Λℤ(ε),|ε|=1,∂ε=p)≃HH(𝔽p)⊗𝔽pΛ𝔽p(ε).

This implies that

H∗(HH(𝔽p)⫽p)≃HH∗(𝔽p)⊗𝔽pΛ𝔽p(ε)≃𝔽p⟨x⟩⊗𝔽pΛ𝔽p(ε).

Proposition 2.1.2.10. Writing the divided power γn(x) as x[n], we have B(x[n])=0 and B(ε)=x.

Note that this implies that

B(εx[n])=xx[n]=(n+1)x[n+1].

Proof. The map HH(𝔽p)→HH(𝔽p)⫽p is compatible with B, and therefore we obtain B(x[n])=0 in homology.

Now recall that we computed

HH∗(𝔽p)=𝔽p⟨x⟩

by replacing 𝔽p by (Λℤ(ε),∂ε=p), so we write the complex

⋯→∂Λℤ(ε)⊗Λℤ(ε)→∂Λℤ(ε).

Writing out the full double complex, we obtain The class x is given by 1⊗ε−ε⊗1. Applying B, we obtain

B(ε)=1⊗ε−ε⊗1.

After reducing mod p, we can replace all copies of ℤ by 𝔽p and ε becomes a cycle, and we obtain B(ε)=x. □

2.1.3 Periodic and cyclic homology

In the anology between Hochschild homology and the de Rham complex, we will now discuss cyclic homology, which will be analogous to algebraic de Rham cohomology.

We will work with derived functors in the category DGModA. The homotopy theory we will work with is inverting quasi-isomorphisms, which means we will consider the ∞-category

ModA(𝒟(k)).

Definition 2.1.3.1. Let R be a k-algebra.

1.
The cyclic homology of R is
HC∗(R/k)≔H∗(k⊗A𝕃HH(R/k))=Tor∗A⁡(k,HH(R/k)).

This will not play any role in these notes.

2.
The negative cyclic homology of R is
HC∗−(R/k)≔RHomA⁡(k,HH(R/k))=ExtA−∗⁡(k,HH(R/k)).

This is more important than cyclic homology, and topological cyclic homology will be an analog of this rather than of cyclic homology. Also, note that HC∗−(R/k) is a module over ExtA∗⁡(k,k)=k[t], where |t|=−2.

3.
The periodic cyclic homology (or periodic homology) of R is
HP∗(R/k)=HC∗−(R/k)[t−1].

Exercise 2.1.3.2. Show that ExtA∗⁡(k,k)≅k[t], where |t|=−2.

Note that the definition we gave is not the standard one in the literature, which involves double complexes. We may wonder if these definitions are equivalent.

Proposition 2.1.3.3. For any k-algebra R, we have

HC−(R/k)≃(HH(R/k)⟦t⟧,∂+tB),

where ∂+tB is defined as

xti↦(∂x)ti+(Bx)ti+1

for x∈HH(R/k) (this is basically saying that ∂(t)=0). Moreover, we have

HP(R/k)≃(HH(R)⦇t⦈,∂+tB).

Proof. We will resolve k as an A-algebra by

C=A{x0,x1,…},|xk|=2k,

where we declare that

∂(xk)=bxk−1.

Note that C also has the structure of a coalgebra with coproduct given by

Δ(xk)=∑i+j=k∑i+j=kxi⊗xj.

This implies that

RHomA⁡(k,HH(R/k))=HomA(C,HH(R/k))=(HH(R/k)⟦t⟧,∂+tB).

Here, we use the fact that ti is the dual of the element xi, and therefore because the differential on C is just b and lowers the x-degree by 1, dually it will be B and raise the t-degree by 1. The formula for HP(R/k) follows by inverting t. □

Remark 2.1.3.4. This argument works more generally to obtain RHom⁡(k,H) for an arbitrary H∈DGModA.

Remark 2.1.3.5. A is a Hopf algebra with couint

ε:A→kε(b)=0

and coproduct Δ:A→A⊗A given by

Δ(b)=1⊗b+b⊗1.

This implies that RHomA(k,−) is a lax symmetric monoidal functor (here, note that k is the unit in the category of dg A-modules) and as such is given by

H↦(H⟦t⟧,∂+tB)

as a lax symmetric monoidal functor. Moreover, if C is an algebra object in DGModA, i.e. C is a dg algebra and B satisfies the Leibniz rule, then RHomA(k,C) is a dg algebra.

Warning 2.1.3.6. Even if R is commutative, B is not a derivation on HH(R), so we cannot simply argue that negative cyclic and periodic homology have products. This is true up to chain homotopy, however, but this is still not enough to obtain a product. We will see that B is a derivation up to coherent homotopy, but we run into issues with the formality of A, which will require working with S1 to resolve.

Instead of doing all of that, we will use the hack that (HH(R/k)⟦t⟧,∂+tB) has a product up to chain homotopy. This implies that HC∗−(R/k) and HP∗(R/k) are graded commutative algebras.

Our goal now is to enhance the HKR theorem (Theorem 2.1.1.9). For this, we will need de Rham cohomology.

Definition 2.1.3.7. Let R be a commutative k-algebra. The de Rham cohomology of R relative to k is defined as

HdR∗(R/k)≔H∗(Ω∗(R/k),d).

Remark 2.1.3.8. Since we are working with commutative rings (equivalently, affine schemes), every term in the de Rham complex is acyclic by vanishing of higher cohomology on affines, so we are just taking global sections. However, this invariant is more interesting for schemes X/k by upgrading the de Rham complex to a complex of sheaves.

Theorem 2.1.3.9. Assume that ℚ⊆k and that LR/k is flat and concentrated in degree 0. Then there are natural isomorphisms

HP∗(R/k)≅HdR∗(R/k)⦇t⦈,

where |t|=−2 and

HCn−(R/k)≅ZdRn(R/k)⊕∏i≥1HdRn+2i(R/k).

Exercise 2.1.3.10. Describe the map HC∗−→HP∗ in this case and check that it exhibits

HP∗≅HC∗−[t−1].

Remark 2.1.3.11. Because this is again relatively boring for rings, the interesting statement is that for a scheme X/k with LX.k being flat and concentrated in degree 0, we have

HP∗(X/k)≅HdR∗(X,k)⦇t⦈.

Remark 2.1.3.12. We can drop the flatness assumption on R if we replace de Rham cohomology with a Hodge-completed derived de Rham cohomology following Bhatt-Morrow-Scholze, but this is of course extremely complicated.

Remark 2.1.3.13. The statement of Theorem 2.1.3.9 is false if k is not characteric 0.

Proof. We will give a classical proof. It is possible to give a fancier proof using nonabelian derived functors.

Consider a chain-level map

μ:HH(R/k)→ΩR/k∗

given by

r0⊗r1⊗⋯⊗rn↦1n!r0dr1⋯drn.

Lemma 2.1.3.14. This μ is an A-linear map of commutative dg algebras

(HH(R/k),∂,B)→(ΩR/k∗,0,d).

Proof of Lemma. We compute

μ(∂(r0⊗⋯⊗rn))=μ(r0r1⊗r2⊗⊗rn−r0⊗r1r2⊗⋯⊗rn+⋯±rnr0⊗r1⊗⋯⊗rn−1)=r0r1dr2⋯drn−r0d(r1r2)dr3⋯drn+⋯=r0r1dr2⋯drn−r0r1dr2⋯drn+⋯=0.

Compatibility with B and d is given by the equation

μ(B(r0⊗⋯⊗rn))=∑σ∈Cn+1(−1)nσ(0)μ(1⊗rσ±rσ⊗1)=1(n+1)!∑σ∈Cn+1sign⁡(σ)drσ(0)⋯drσ(n)=1n!dr0⊗⋯⊗drn=d(1n!r0dr1⋯drn)=d(μ(r0⊗⋯⊗rn)).

We conclude with the following exercise.

Exercise 2.1.3.15. Check that μ is multiplicative with respect to the shuffle product on the left and the wedge product of forms on the right. □

Using the lemma, we see that

ΩR/k∗→HH∗(R/k)→H∗(μ)ΩR/k∗

is the identity, so the statement follows from Theorem 2.1.1.9. □

We are now ready to prove Theorem 2.1.3.9.

Proof of Theorem 2.1.3.9. We simply compute

HP∗(R/k)=H∗(HH(R/k)⦇t⦈,∂+tB)≃H∗(ΩR/k∗⦇t⦈,td)≅HdR∗(R/k)⦇t⦈.

Applying the same strategy to negative cyclic homology, we obtain

HC∗−(R/k)≅H∗(ΩR/k∗⟦t⟧,td).
□

We still want to deal with arbitary k (so not in characteristic 0).

Construction 2.1.3.16. We have the Postnikov filtration

τ≥∙HH(R/k)

of HH(R/k) as an A-module, which is compatible with B and leads to a filtration of

(τ≥∙HH(R/k)⦇t⦈,∂+tB).

HP(R/k).

This leads to a multiplicative, conditionally convergent spectral sequence

E2=HH∗(R/k)⦇t⦈⟹HP∗(R/k).

The E3-page is given by

H∗(HH∗(R/k),B)⦇t⦈⟹HP∗(R/k).

If R has flat cotangent complex, then this is

E3=HdR∗(R/k)⦇t⦈⟹HP∗(R/k).

We will now return to the example of 𝔽p over ℤ. First, we need to upgrade divided powers to divided power series.

Definition 2.1.3.17. Let R be a commutative ring. We define the divided power series algebra R⟨⟨x⟩⟩ as the completion of R⟨x⟩ at the filtration generated by the divided powers of x (note this is not an adic completion).

Proposition 2.1.3.18. For R=𝔽p, we have

HC∗−(𝔽p/ℤ)≅ℤp[t]⟨⟨x⟩⟩/(xt−p),|x|=2,|t|=−2.

In addition, we have

HP∗(𝔽p/ℤ)≅ℤp[t±]⟨⟨x⟩⟩/(xt−p)≅(ℤp⟨⟨y⟩⟩/(y−p))[t±],

where y has degree 0.

Remark 2.1.3.19. Note that we have

HP0(𝔽p/ℤ)≅HC0−(𝔽p/ℤ)≅ℤp⟨⟨y⟩⟩/(y−p),

which is obtained by adjoining divided powers of p to ℤp. Because ℤp already has divided powers of p, the element y[p]−ppp! is p-torsion. In fact, we have

ℤp⟨y⟩/(y−p)≅ℤp⟨z⟩/z,

where we should think of z as y−p.

What we have seen is that the negative cyclic and periodic cyclic homology of 𝔽p is very unpleasant. The situation will improve when we consider the topological version of everything. Also, in fact, HP∗(𝔽p/ℤ) is the 2-periodic derived de Rham cohomology of 𝔽p.

Proof. Recall that HH∗(𝔽p/ℤ)≅𝔽p⟨x⟩. We also recall the spectral sequence coming from the Postnikov filtration, which reads

𝔽p⟨x⟩[t]⟹HC∗−(𝔽p/ℤ).

The E2-page of the spectral sequence is given below, where the horizontal direction is powers of t and the vertical direction is divided powers of x. We also use dots to denote copies of 𝔽p.

Because everything is in even degree, the spectral sequence collapses at the E2-page. Therefore, HC∗−(𝔽p/ℤ) has a filtration with associated graded given by 𝔽p⟨x⟩[t].

There is an additive extension problem and a multiplicative extension problem. We will obtain a copy of ℤp by using the diagonal (with slope 1) entries, and we also need to check that divided powers lift from the associated graded.

The connective cover of HC−(𝔽p/ℤ) can be represented by a simplicial commutative ring. Later, we will study everything using homotopy theory and see that the Connes operator comes from an S1-action on animated rings, so we can just take homotopy fixed points to obtain HC−. In any case, the connective cover admits divided powers on positive degree homotopy groups. In particular, every choice of x,t∈HC∗−(𝔽p/ℤ) yields a map

ℤ⟨x⟩[t]→HC∗−(𝔽p/ℤ).

If we can find x,t such that HC∗−(𝔽p/ℤ), then this map induces an isomorphism on associated gradeds of the map

ℤ⟨x⟩/(xt−p)→HC∗−(𝔽p/ℤ).

Because the filtration on HC∗−(𝔽p/ℤ) is complete, completing ℤ⟨x⟩/(xt−p) yields the desired result.

Now we will recall the computation of HH(𝔽p/ℤ). We first resolved 𝔽p by

𝔽p≃(Λℤ(ε),∂ε=p).

In HH(𝔽p/ℤ), we have x=Bε, ∂x=0, and Bx=0. It follows that in HH(𝔽p/ℤ), we have a cycle x representing x∈HH∗(𝔽p/ℤ). Using the fact that

HC−(𝔽p/ℤ)=(HH(𝔽p/ℤ)⟦t⟧,∂+tB),

we calculate

(∂+tB)εp+tx,

and therefore p=tx in HC∗−(𝔽p/ℤ). □

Remark 2.1.3.20. One can also deduce this entire computation using the fact that

(HH(𝔽p/ℤ),∂,B)≃(ℤ[ε]ε2⟨x⟩,∂ε=p∂x=0,Bε=xBx=0).

Remark 2.1.3.21. We have not talked at all about cyclic homology, but there is a long exact sequence which computes HC(R/k). This comes from a cofiber sequence, or distinguished triangle.

2.1.4 The HKR theorem

We will now discuss the cotangent complex using nonabelian derived functors and prove the HKR theorem.

Let 𝒞 be a 1-category, which is generated by compact projective objects. Here, an object K in compact projective if

Hom⁡(K,−)

preserves filtered colimits and reflexive coequalizers, which are diagrams of the form Note that this notion doesn’t really make sense for ∞-categories. Being generated by compact projective objects means that all

Hom⁡(K,−)

detect isomorphisms.

We can now pass from 𝒞 to the full subcategory on compact projective objects. If 𝒞=Set, then we get finite sets, and if C=ModR, then we get finitely generated projective modules. We can then construct the animation of 𝒞, which is given by

Ani(𝒞)=FunΠ((𝒞cp)op,𝒮),

where 𝒮 denotes the ∞-category of anima (spaces or simplicial sets). Some properties of this include the following:

  • The category 𝒞cp of compact projective objects is a full subcategory of Ani(𝒞), and so is the ind-category Ind(𝒞cp).
  • A general object of 𝒞 can be represented as the geometric realization of a simplicial diagram with entries in Ind(𝒞cp).

  • If X is compact projective object of 𝒞 and Yj are any ind-compact projective objects, then the mapping space

    MapAni(𝒞)(X,colimj∈Δop⁡Yj)=colimj∈Δop⁡MapAni(𝒞)(X,Yj)

    is a simplicial set, so taking the geometric realization gives us a space.

Example 2.1.4.1. If 𝒞=Set, functors are determined by their effect on the singleton set, so we just get Ani(Set)=Spaces.

Example 2.1.4.2. The non-negative derived category 𝒟(𝒜)≥0 of an abelian category with enough compact projectives is equivalent to the animation Ani(𝒜). One advantage of this description is that any functor out of Ani(𝒜) preserving filtered colimits and reflexive coequalizers is simply a functor out of the 1-category 𝒞cp. For example, if we have a nonadditive functor

F:𝒜→ℬ(↪Ani(ℬ)),

this will extend to a functor preserving filtered colimits and geometric realizations denoted by

LF:Ani(𝒜)→Ani(ℬ).

Example 2.1.4.3. For any commutative ring R, there is a functor

ΛRn:ModR→ModR

taking a module to its n-th exterior power. This is clearly nonadditive, but there is a derived functor

LΛRn:𝒟(R)≥0→𝒟(R)≥0.

We cannot compute by resolving chain complexes, so instead we will represent an object by a simplicial diagram of projective modules and then applying ΛRn levelwise.

For example, consider R=ℤ. We will attempt to resolve ℤ/n, and this is resolved by the chain complex

ℤ→nℤ.

Applying the Dold-Kan correspondence, we obtain a simplicial object

Exercise 2.1.4.4.

1.
Find a levelwise projective simplicial abelian group whose complex is quasi-isomorphic to ℤ/n[0].
2.
Compute LΛℤ2(ℤ/n). Hint: compute Hi for i≤2 by hand and then find a different reason for the vanishing for higher i.

If we apply Λℤ2 to this, we obtain a simplicial diagram which is simply given by which is equivalent to ℤ/n[1]. Note that this is not equivalent to applying Λℤ2 levelwise to the chain complex we started with, and that a functor commutes with Dold-Kan only if it is additive.

One advantage of this animation language is that we can discuss animation for categories which have no linear structure. For example, we have

Ani(cRing)=FunΠ((cRingcp)op,𝒮)≅FunΠ((Polyfg)op,𝒮).

Clearly we see that the ind-compact projective objects

Ind(cRingcp)=Poly

are simply all polynomial rings. Therefore, we will represent objects by simplicial diagrams of polynomial rings. For example, we have

MapAni(cRing)(ℤ[x],colimΔop⁡Yi)=colimΔop⁡Yi

extracts the underlying simplicial set (in fact a simplicial abelian group). This give some version of non-negative complexes with ring structure.

Warning 2.1.4.5. This does not agree with commutative ring objects in 𝒟(ℤ).

The universal property is that

Fungeom,filtered(Ani(cRing),𝒟)=Fun(Polyfg,𝒟)=Funfiltered(Poly,𝒟).

This allows us to define nonabelian derived functors by defining functors on polynomial rings which preserve filtered colimits.

Example 2.1.4.6. The functor HH(−/ℤ):Poly→𝒟(ℤ)≥0 commutes with filtered colimits. Therefore, it extends to a functor

LHH:Ani(cRing)→𝒟(ℤ)≥0.

If we apply it to an ordinary commutative ring, this agrees with our previous definiion of Hochschild homology. In fact, it agrees for all animated rings by considering the associated dg-algebra.

Remark 2.1.4.7. There is a way to define Hochschild homology in ∞-categories in much greater generality which does not require animated rings.

Question 2.1.4.8. Is there a way to extend the HKR theorem to general rings using non-abelian derived functors?

Construction 2.1.4.9. For any C∈𝒟(ℤ), we can cut off homology groups using the functor τ≥n:𝒟(ℤ)→𝒟(ℤ). This produces a map

τ≥nC→C

which has the following properties:

  • The map is an isomorphism on Hi for i≥n;
  • For all i<n, we have Hi(τ≥nC)=0.

One explicit construction of this is to replace everything in degree <n by 0 and to replace the degree n part with the cycles.

Exercise 2.1.4.10. Construct the functor τ≥n:𝒟(ℤ)→𝒟(ℤ) using an adjunction.

We in fact have a map τ≥n+1C→τ≥nC, and the cofiber is given by

Cofiber⁡(τ≥n+1C→τ≥nC)≃Hn(C)[n].

For polynomial rings R, we have a diagram Therefore, we can try to compute Hochschild homology using the machinery of nonabelian derived functors by levelwise using the HKR theorem for this “filtration.”

Definition 2.1.4.11. We define

FHKRnHH(−/ℤ):Ani(cRing)→𝒟(ℤ)≥0

as the geometric realization preserving extension of τ≥nHH(−/ℤ) from Poly.

We see that there is a cofiber sequence

FHKRnHH(R/ℤ)→FHKRn(R/ℤ)→LΩR/ℤn[n]

for any animated ring R.

Lemma 2.1.4.12. The nonabelian derived functor FHKRn(−/ℤ) lands in 𝒟(ℤ)≥n. More precisely, for any animated ring R, we have

FHKRnHH(R/ℤ)∈𝒟(ℤ)≥n.

Proof. The lemma clearly holds for polynomial rings, and the extension to everything else follows from the fact that 𝒟(ℤ)≥n is closed under filtered colimits. □

Lemma 2.1.4.13. If a functor F:cRing→Ab commutes with reflexive coequalizers, then

H0(LF(R))=F(R).

Proof. We resolve R by a simplicial diagram of polynomial rings as and note that R is the reflexive coequalizer of Therefore, LF(R) is the total complex of so taking H0, we obtain the reflexive coequalizer of □
