2.
The functor cRing→Ab given by R↦ℤ[R×n];
3.
The functor Ω−/ℤi:cRing→Ab. Hint: think about the generators and relations presentation for ΩR/ℤ1.

We are now ready to give an enhanced version of Theorem 2.1.1.9.

Theorem 2.1.4.15. If LΩR/ℤn is concentrated in degree 0 for each n, then Theorem 2.1.1.9 holds for R.

Proof. Using the long exact sequence in homology associated to

FHKRn+1→FHKRn→LΩR/ℤn[n],

This implies that

Hn(FHKRn)→H0(LΩR/ℤn)=ΩR/ℤn

is an isomorphism and that for all i>n, the induced map

Hi(FHKRn+1)→Hi(FHKRn)

is an isomorphism. Descending to R0, we obtain

ΩR/ℤn≃HnFHKRn≃HnFHKR0=HHn(R/ℤ).

We will omit checking that this is compatible with multiplication, and that in fact it is the map we had before. □

To better understand this, we need to better understand LΩR/ℤn. This will in fact agree with the value on R of the nonabelian derived functor

Ani(cRing/R)→𝒟(R)≥0→𝒟(ℤ)≥0

which is given by

A↦R⊗AΩA/ℤn

for A∈Poly/R. By definition, we have

R⊗AΩA/ℤn≃ΛRn(R⊗AΩA/ℤ1).

Exercise 2.1.4.16. Check that A↦R⊗AΩA/k1 takes compact projective objects in k−Alg/R to compact projective objects in ModR.

Applying nonabelian derived functors, we obtain

LΩR/ℤn=LΛRn(LΩR/ℤ1).

Proposition 2.1.4.17. If LΩR/ℤ1 is concentraded in degree 0 and ΩR/ℤ1 is a flat R-module, then LΩR/ℤn is also concentrated in degree 0.

Proof. If ΩR/ℤ1 is projective, then

LΛRn(ΩR/ℤ1)=ΛRn(ΩR/ℤ1).

In the general case, we use Lazard’s theorem, which states that every flat R-module is a filtered colimit of finitely generated projective modules. □

We are now able to state the correct form of Theorem 2.1.1.9.

Theorem 2.1.4.18 (Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg, ultimate version). If LΩR/k1 is concentrated in degree 0 and ΩR/ℤ1 is a flat R-module, then

HHn(R/ℤ)=ΩR/ℤn.

Remark 2.1.4.19. For simplicity, we worked over ℤ, but everything still holds if we replace ℤ be an arbitrary commutative ring k.

2.1.5 Hochschild homology of schemes

Let k be a commutative ring and X be a scheme over k. We could in principle allow the base to be non-affine, but for simplicity we will ignore this. There are two approaches:

1.
Extending from the affine case (by a right Kan extension);
2.
Generalize the functor HH(−/k) to k-linear dg categories (or stable ∞-categories) and then define define
HH(X/k)=HH(Perf(X)/k).

This is essentially an approach in the spirit of non-commutative geometry and is actually better in many cases (for example, we see that Hochschild homology is really an invariant of a stable ∞-category), but we will take the first approach in these notes since it is closer to the case of rings.

Definition 2.1.5.1. For a scheme X, we define its Hochschild homology by

HH(X/k)=limU⊆XU affine openHH(𝒪(U)/k)∈𝒟(k).

Note that if X=Spec⁡R is affine, then

HH(Spec⁡(R)/k)=limU⊆Spec⁡RHH(𝒪(U),k)=HH(𝒪(Spec⁡R)/k)=HH(R/k)

because U=Spec⁡R is terminal in the poset of affine open subsets of Spec⁡R.

Remark 2.1.5.2. We can also define Hochschild homology for stacks. For simplicity, we will not do this.

We will now discuss an example of a non-affine scheme. Let X=ℙk1. It has an open cover by

(𝔸k1)+=Spec⁡k[x]and(𝔸k1)−=Spec⁡k[y],

whose intersection is given by

(𝔸k1)+∩(𝔸k1)−=𝔾m=Spec⁡k[x±].

We will hope for some kind of descent of Mayer-Vietoric sequence.

Theorem 2.1.5.3. For any pair of open subsets U,V⊆X such that X=U∪V, the square is a pullback in 𝒟(k). In other words, Hochschild homology satisfies Zariski descent.

Remark 2.1.5.4. Later, we will see that HH(−/k) satisfies fpqc descent.

Corollary 2.1.5.5. There is a long exact sequence

Lemma 2.1.5.6. For any commutative ring R and x∈R, we have

HH(R[x−1]/k)≅HH(R/k)⊗RR[x−1].

Exercise 2.1.5.7. Prove this.

In the example of ℙ1, we have a pullback This becomes the long exact sequence Therefore, it is easy to compute

HH1(ℙ1/k)=0,HH0(ℙ1/k)=k⊕k,andHH−1(ℙ1/k)=0.

Proof of Theorem 2.1.5.3. We always have the square For any open set U⊂X, a cofinality argument gives

HH(U)=limA⊆XHH(A∩U).

Therefore, without loss of generality that X is affine. Unfortunately, affine schemes can have non-affine open subsets, but another cofinality argument allows us to assume that U and V are affine and are standard opens. Therefore, we have reduced to the case of where 1∈(x,y). Using the fact that Hochschild homology commutes with localization, this becomes Therefore, it suffices to prove that which is a standard fact. This is true because

R[x−1]/R≅R[x−1,y−1]/R[y−1],

which is true because y acts invertibly on R[x−1]/R. This is true because x is invertible on R/y. □

Our goal now is to prove an analog of Theorem 2.1.4.15 and Theorem 2.1.4.18 for schemes. We begin by defining a filtration on HH(X/k) by the formula

FHKRnHH(X/k)=limU⊆Xaffine openFHKRn(HH(𝒪(U)/k)).

Remark 2.1.5.8. Note that this cannot be done using the non-commutative approach.

Proposition 2.1.5.9. This defines a complete filtration on HH(X/k), namely that

lim→n⁡FHKRnHH(X/k)=0.

Moreover, the associated graded is given by

limU⊆XLΩU/kn[n]=RΓ(X,LΩX/kn)[n],

which is usually called the derived Hodge cohomology of X.

Note that if X is smooth, we just get the usual Hodge cohomology.

Proof. Completeness follows from the fact that it is true for affines and that inverse limits commute with inverse limits. The assertion about (derived) Hodge cohomology follows again from the fact that cofibers commute with limits. □

Using the proposition, we obtain a spectral sequence

RΓ(X,LΩX/kn[n])⟹HH∗(X/k).

Corollary 2.1.5.10. If ℚ⊆k, then there is a canonical isomorphism

HH(X/k)≅∏RΓ(X,LΩX/kn[n]).

Proof. This is clearly true if X=Spec⁡k[x1,…,xn]. Using non-abelian derived functors, this is also true for any affine X. The general case follows. □

Remark 2.1.5.11. This isomorphism is in fact compatible with the B operator, so we get the desired results for periodic and negative cyclic homology.

2.2 Topological Hochschild and cyclic homology

2.2.1 Hochschild homology in ∞-categories

Hochschild homology can be constructed in an arbitrary symmetric monoidal ∞-category.

Recall that Assact⊗ is a 1-category with objects being finite sets and morphisms being maps of finite sets with a linear order on each preimage. Also recall that composition is given by the lexicographic order and that this category is symmetric monoidal with respect to the disjoint union.

In Assact⊗, the object ⟨1⟩ is an associative algebra object, which means it comes with a multiplication map

⟨1⟩⊔⟨1⟩→⟨1⟩

given by the left copy of ⟨1⟩ being smallest. The unit is the unique morphism from the empty set, and it is clear that multiplication is associative and unital. Therefore, we should think of Assact⊗ as a kind of free symmetric monoidal category on one associative algebra object, so as before, we define an associative algebra in an ∞-category 𝒞 to be a symmetric monoidal functor

N(Assact⊗)→𝒞.

Of course, the underlying object is simply the image of ⟨1⟩.

Exercise 2.2.1.1. Prove that the category of symmetric monoidal functors Assact⊗→Ab is equivalent to the category of rings.

Recall that Hochschild homology was defined by writing a simplicial diagram. However, this is very hard to do by hand in an ∞-category, so we need a systematic way of handling ∞-categories.

Definition 2.2.1.2. For a finite, nonempty totally ordered set S, define the set of cuts to be

Cut⁡(S)={(S0,S1)∣S0,S1⊆S,S0<S1,S0⊔S1=S}.

We form the closely related set of cyclic cuts

Cutcyc⁡(S)=Cut⁡(S)/(S,∅)∼(∅,S).

Exercise 2.2.1.3. Check that the functor Cut:Δop→Set and CutCyc:Δop→Set are represented by the simplicial sets Δ1 and S1.

The functor Cutcyc actually defines a functor Δop→Assact⊗. For a map f:S→T of totally ordered sets and a cut (S0,S1)∈Cutcyc⁡(S), the preimage

(f∗)−1(S0,S1)⊆Cutcyc⁡(T)

consists of all cuts on T “between” the images f(S0) and f(S1) if the cut is nontrivial. If (S0,S1) is trivial, then the preimage consists of all cuts outside of f(S). To give this an order, in the first case we simply order the cuts from left to right. In the second case, we start with the cuts to the right of f(S) and then go to the cuts to the left of f(S).

Definition 2.2.1.4. For an algebra A:Assact⊗→𝒞, the Hochschild object is defined by

HH(A/𝒞)≔colimΔop⁡(A∘Cutcyc).

Lemma 2.2.1.5. For an ordinary ring (or dg algebra), we obtain an algebra A in 𝒟(ℤ). Then there is an equivalence

HH(A/𝒟(ℤ))≃HH(A/ℤ)

between the Hochschild complex of A as an algebra in 𝒟(ℤ) and the Hochschild complex of A defined previously.

Proof. The functor Ch(ℤ)→𝒟(ℤ) preserves tensor products of K-flat chain complexes. Therefore, if we take our dg algebra to be K-flat, the two sides of the lemma are computing the same object by the fact that in 𝒟(ℤ), a colimit of a simplicial diagram is computed by a total complex. □

Exercise 2.2.1.6. For an ordinary ring R, prove that the composite

Δop→CutcycAssact⊗→RAb

agrees with the cyclic bar complex of R.

Definition 2.2.1.7. For a ring spectrum A, define its topological Hochschild homology by

THH(A)≔HH(A/Sp).

Recall that ordinary rings R have Eilenberg-Maclane spectra HR, so we can take their topological Hochschild homology and denote it by THH(R).

Example 2.2.1.8. Because 𝕊 is the unit in Sp, we have THH(𝕊)=𝕊 for the same reason that HH∗(ℤ)=ℤ.

This example suggests that we can view THH as HH(−/𝕊), but it will take some work to make this precise. Before we do this, we will consider things like modules over algebras.

Definition 2.2.1.9. Define the 1-category LModact⊗ in the following way:

  • Objects are finite sets with elements labelled (“colored”) by {a,m};

  • Morphisms are maps S→T together with a total ordering on preimages subject to the conditions that

    • Preimages of a-colored elements are completely a-colored;
    • Preimages of m-colored contain precisely one m-colored element and this element is the maximum.

We can define an analogous category RModact⊗ by the same definition, except the m-colored element of a preimage must be the minimum.

Definition 2.2.1.10. A left module in a symmetric monoidal ∞-category 𝒞 is a symmetric monoidal functor

LModact⊗→𝒞.

Note that if we only considered a-colored sets, we obtain the underlying algebra of the left module. Now recall that we can tensor left and right modules over a ring R to obtain an abelian group.

Definition 2.2.1.11. Define a category LRModact⊗ by the following:

  • Objects are finite sets with colors given by {r,a,ℓ};

  • Morphisms are maps f:S→T of finite sets with a total ordering on preimages such that

    • Preimages of a-colored elements are entirely a-colored;
    • Preimages of r-colored elements have precisely one r-colored element at the minimum and the rest are a-colored;
    • Preimages of ℓ-colored elements have precisely one ℓ-colored element at the maximum and the rest are a-colored.

Because the r and ℓ-colored elements do not interact, we see that a symmetric monoidal functor LRModact⊗→𝒞 is simply a pair of functors LModact⊗→𝒞 and RModact⊗→𝒞 which agree on Assact⊗.

Definition 2.2.1.12. Define the tensor product N⊗AM to be the colimit of the composite

Δop→CutLRModact⊗→(N,A,M)𝒞.

Here, the cut functor colors (∅,S) as r, (S,∅) as ℓ, and everything else as a.

There are variants of this theory, including bimodules. In this case, we relax the restriction on preimages of m-colored elements by dropping the condition that it must be either the minimum or maximum. Then Cutcyc factors through the category BiModact⊗ by assigning the color m to the trivial cuts and the color a to everything else. Therefore, if M is a bimodule over A, we have

HH(A/𝒞;M),

which is Hochschild homology of A with coefficients in M.

We can also discuss commutative algebras. Recall that Commact⊗=Fin, which lets is define commutative algebras in 𝒞.

Lemma 2.2.1.13. For a commutative algebra A, its Hochschild homology HH(A/𝒞) has a commutative algebra structure.

We will now study THH for ordinary rings. Eilenberg-Maclane spectra extend to a functor

H:𝒟(ℤ)→Sp

coming from the Dold-Kan correspondence. It has the property that

π∗(H(C))=H∗(C).

This functor is lax symmetric monoidal and preserves colimits, so we obtain a canonical map

THH(HR)→H(HH(R)).

On homotopy groups, we obtain a morphism

THH∗(HR)→HH∗(R).

The functor H canonically factors through an equivalence

𝒟(ℤ)→Mod(Hℤ),

which is symmetric monoidal. Therefore, we see that

H(HH(R))=HH(HR/Mod(Hℤ))=THH(HR/Hℤ).

Example 2.2.1.14. If R is a ℚ-algebra, then the map THH∗(R)→HH∗(R) is an isomorphism. This follows from the fact that

𝕊⊗Hℚ≃Hℤ⊗Hℚ=Hℚ.

This implies that

S⊗HR≃Hℤ⊗HR,

so we obtain

HR⊗𝕊HR≃HR⊗HℤHR.

Proposition 2.2.1.15. For an ordinary ring R, the map

THHi(R)→HHi(R)

is an isomorphism for i≤2 and surjective for i≥3.

Proof. The fiber of the map

THH(R)→HH(R)

is the geometric realization of a simplicial diagram of the form The last term is 0 and the other terms are all 2-connective by a study of the effect of 𝕊→Hℤ on homotopy groups. A technical argument (which we will not give here) shows that homotopy groups come from the last term, the suspension of the second-to-last term, the double suspension of the third-to-last term, and so on, so the geometric realization must be 3-connective. □

If we consider the ordinary ring 𝔽p, we see that

THH2(𝔽p)≅HH2(𝔽p)≅𝔽p

with generator x.

Theorem 2.2.1.16 (Bökstedt). There is an isomorphism

THH∗(𝔽p)≅𝔽p[x].

In particular, we have no divided power structure. In addition, the map

𝔽p[x]→𝔽p⟨x⟩

is zero in degree ≥p.

2.2.2 Bökstedt periodicity

We will now study the spectrum THH(𝔽p).

Theorem 2.2.2.1 (Bökstedt). As an 𝔼1-algebra over 𝔽p, THH(𝔽p) is free on one generator of degree 2. More explicitly, we have

THH(𝔽p)≃H𝔽p⊗Σ∞ΩS3.

Note that THH(𝔽p) is actually an 𝔼∞-algebra, but we are forgetting some of the structure in this theorem. Also, note that ΩΣS2 is the free 𝔼1-algebra on S2, so

Map𝔼1/H𝔽p(H𝔽p⊗Σ∞ΩS3,R)≃Map𝔼1(ΩS3,Ω∞R)≃Map𝒮(S2,Ω∞R)≃MapSp(Σ∞S2,R)≃MapH𝔽p(Σ2H𝔽p,R)

by a chain of adjunctions.

We should first prove that the two versions of Bökstedt’s theorem are equivalent. If we consider the element x∈THH2(𝔽p), then we obtain a map of 𝔼1-algebras

H𝔽p⊗Σ∞ΩS3→THH(𝔽p).

This map is an equivalence if and only if it is an equivalence on homotopy groups. Finally, note that the homotopy groups of the source are simply

𝔽p[x],

where x has degree 2. This is because

π∗(H𝔽p⊗Σ∞ΩS3)≃H∗(ΩS3,𝔽p).

Using the Serre spectral sequence, this is 𝔽p in every even degree. Because ΩS3 is an 𝔼1-algebra, we obtain the desired product structure.

Exercise 2.2.2.2. Prove that π∗(H𝔽p⊗Σ+∞X) agrees with H∗(X,𝔽p) for any space X.

Lemma 2.2.2.3. We have an equivalence

THH(R)≃R⊗R⊗𝕊RopR.

Sketch of proof. Write R≃R⊗RR. This becomes Therefore, we have

R⊗R⊗𝕊Rop=colimΔop⁡R⊗R⊗𝕊RopR⊗(s+1).

This construction identifies the rightmost and leftmost copies of R, so it gives us exactly the cyclic bar complex of R. □

We would like to apply this description to 𝔽p. First, we need to understand the spectrum

H𝔽p⊗𝕊H𝔽p.

This is quite difficult (because the homotopy groups of spheres are extremely difficult), but it does have an interpretation as the homology groups of the Eilenberg-Maclane spectrum H𝔽p, which form the dual Steenrod algebra.

Theorem 2.2.2.4 (Milnor). As an algebra, we have

π∗(H𝔽p⊗𝕊H𝔽p)={𝔽2[ζ1,ζ2,…]|ζi|=2i−1p=2Λ𝔽p(τ0,τ1,…)⊗𝔽p[ξ1,ξ2,…]|τi|=2pi−1,|ξi|=2pi−2p>2.

This is a very large description of the homotopy groups. Fortunately, there is a direct description of the spectrum H𝔽p⊗𝕊H𝔽p, which is an 𝔼∞-algebra over 𝔽p.

Lemma 2.2.2.5. As an 𝔼2-algebra over H𝔽p, H𝔽p⊗𝕊H𝔽p is free on one generator of degree 1. More explicitly, there is an equivalence

H𝔽p⊗Σ+∞Ω2S3≃H𝔽p⊗𝕊H𝔽p.

Proof of Theorem 2.2.1.16. Write

THH(𝔽p)≃H𝔽p⊗H𝔽p⊗𝕊H𝔽pH𝔽p≃H𝔽p⊗H𝔽p⊗𝕊Σ+∞Ω2S3H𝔽p.

The three terms in the tensor products come from the spaces pt and Ω2S3, so we can form a bar construction with Ω2S3 acting on two copies of a point. Therefore, we obtain

THH(𝔽p)≃H𝔽p⊗Σ+∞Bar(∗,Ω2S3,∗)≃H𝔽p⊗Σ+∞ΩS3.

Because we formed the bar construction with an 𝔼2-algebra, we still have an 𝔼1-algebra structure. □

Remark 2.2.2.6. The description of H𝔽p⊗H𝔽p is equivalent to Bökstedt’s theorem. This is because a map A→B of connected H𝔽p-algebras is an equivalence if and only if the map

H𝔽p⊗AH𝔽p→H𝔽p⊗BH𝔽p

is an equivalence. We simply apply this to the map

H𝔽p⊗Σ+∞Ω2S3→H𝔽p⊗𝕊H𝔽p,

which is given by specifying an element of π1.

Exercise 2.2.2.7.

1.
Let A be a connected H𝔽p-algebra. Prove that a map N→M of connective A-modules is an equivalence if
H𝔽p⊗AN→H𝔽p⊗AM

is.

2.
Let A→B be a map of connected H𝔽p-algebras with an equivalence
H𝔽p⊗AH𝔽p→H𝔽p⊗BH𝔽p.

Prove that H𝔽p⊗AB≃H𝔽p and that A→B is an equivalence.

If p is odd, there are Dyer-Lashof operations

Qi:πn(R)→πn+2(p−1)i(R),βQi:πn(R)→πn+2(p−1)i−1(R)

for any 𝔼∞-algebra over H𝔽p. For any element of degree n, then

Qn2x=xp.

In addition, we have

Qix=0

whenever i<n2. Similarly, when i≤n2, we have

βQix=0.

These should be viewed as coming from the homology of configuration spaces. On 𝔼2-algebras, we already have Qn2x whenever n is even and Qn+12x, βQn+12x when n is odd. The first is simply the p-th power, but the existing power operations for odd n are an additional structure on 𝔼2-algebras.

Theorem 2.2.2.8 (Dyer-Lashof, Araki-Kudo). We have

H∗(Ω2S3,𝔽p)=Λ𝔽p(a,Q1a,QpQ1a,…)⊗𝔽p[βQ1a,βQpQ1a,…].

Note that this is very similar to Milnor’s result. All of the elements given by Dyer-Lashof have the same degrees as Milnor’s elements, so we might try to compare them.

Theorem 2.2.2.9 (Steinberger). On π∗(H𝔽p⊗𝕊H𝔽p), we have

τi=Qpi−1Qpi−2…Q1τ0

and

ξi=βQpi−1Qpi−2⋯Q1τ0.

Now it remains to try to construct a map realizing our desired isomorphism on homotopy groups.

Proof of Lemma 2.2.2.5. We have a map

π1(H𝔽p⊗𝕊H𝔽p)→π1(H𝔽p⊗HℤH𝔽p).

The target is simply Tor1ℤ⁡(𝔽p,𝔽p)≃𝔽p. This map is actually an isomorphism (because the map 𝕊→Hℤ is 1-connected). Therefore, we obtain a map

H𝔽p⊗Σ+∞Ω2S3→H𝔽p⊗𝕊H𝔽p

of 𝔼2-algebras over H𝔽p. This is an isomorphism on π1, but both sides are generated in the same way by the 𝔼2 Dyer-Lashof operations, so it is an isomorphism on all homotopy groups. □

Exercise 2.2.2.10. Prove that π1(H𝔽p⊗𝕊H𝔽p)≃𝔽p.

2.2.3 Properties of THH

We will now consider formal properties of topological Hochschild homology. These include base change results, universality, and more.

Proposition 2.2.3.1. The functor THH:Alg(Sp)→Sp is a (strong) symmetric monoidal functor. In particular, there is a natural equivalence

THH(A⊗𝕊B)≃THH(A)⊗𝕊THH(B).

More generally, the functor

HH(−/𝒞):Alg(𝒞)→𝒞

is symmetric monoidal.

Proof. Consider the forgetful functor U:Alg(Sp)→Sp as an object in the symmetric monoidal category Fun(Alg(Sp),Sp). This is in fact an algebra object. Then we obtain

THH(−)≅HH(U/Fun(Alg(Sp),Sp)).
□

Corollary 2.2.3.2. If R is an 𝔼n-algebra, then THH(R) is an 𝔼n−1-algebra.

Proof. Recall that

Alg𝔼n(Sp)≅Alg𝔼n−1(Alg𝔼1(Sp)).

Applying THH and using the fact that it depends only on the underlying 𝔼1-algebra structure, we land in Alg𝔼n−1(Sp). □

In particular, if R is an 𝔼∞-algebra, so is THH(R). However, there is a more canonical description. First recall that if A,B∈CAlg(Sp), then A⊗𝕊B is the coproduct in CAlg(Sp).

Proposition 2.2.3.3. For R∈CAlg(Sp), we have

THH(R)≅colimS1⁡R≕R⊗S1,

where we are considering the constant diagram on R.

Exercise 2.2.3.4. Prove this.

Warning 2.2.3.5. This colimit is different from the colimit in the category of all spectra, which is given by

We will now prove a base change formula for THH.

Proposition 2.2.3.6. For any lax symmetric monoidal functor F:𝒞→𝒟 and A∈Alg(𝒞), we get a canonical map

HH(FA/𝒟)→F(HH(A/𝒞)).

If F is strong symmetric monoidal and preserves geometric realizations, then this map is an equivalence.

Proof. We need to compare the cyclic bar constructions and The latter receives a map from and this receives a map from the first colimit. The second part follows from the additional assumptions on F. □

Example 2.2.3.7. Consider the Eilenberg-Maclane functor H:𝒟(ℤ)→Sp which is lax symmetric monoidal. Therefore, we obtain a map

THH(R)→H(HH(R/ℤ))

for any Hℤ-algebra R.

Example 2.2.3.8. If k→k′ is a map of commutative ring spectra, we have the functor

−⊗kk′:Modk→Modk′.

This is symmetric monoidal and preserves all colimits, so we have

THH(R/k)⊗kk′≃THH(R⊗kk′/k′).

We will now prove a more general version of Bökstedt periodicity. First, recall that an 𝔽p-algebra is perfect if the Frobenius morphism is an isomorphism. Examples include finite fields 𝔽pn and the ring

𝔽p[x1/p∞]=colim⁡(𝔽p[x]→φ𝔽p[x]→⋯).

By definition, we have a map

Hk→THH(k)

inducing a map k→THH∗(k) on homotopy groups. We can then precompose this with a map THH(𝔽p)→THH(k), so we obtain a map

Hk⊗H𝔽pTHH(𝔽p)→THH(k).

On homotopy groups, this gives us a map

k[x]→THH∗(k).

Theorem 2.2.3.9 (Bökstedt periodicity for perfect rings). For any perfect 𝔽p-algebra k, the map

k[x]→THH∗(k)

is an isomorphism of commutative rings. Equivalently, THH(k) is the free 𝔼1-algebra on a degree 2 element x over Hk.

Proof. For every perfect ring k, there is a commutative ring spectrum 𝕊W(k) called the spherical Witt vectors such that

𝕊W(k)⊗𝕊H𝔽p≃k.

This should be thought of as a lift of k along 𝕊→H𝔽p. This implies that

THH(k)≃THH(𝕊W(k)⊗𝕊HFp)≃THH(𝕊W(k))⊗𝕊THH(𝔽p)≃THH(𝕊W(k))⊗𝕊𝔽p⊗H𝔽pTHH(𝔽p)≃THH(k/H𝔽p)⊗H𝔽pTHH(𝔽p)≃HH(k/𝔽p)⊗H𝔽pTHH(𝔽p).

Therefore, it suffices to prove that

HH∗(k/𝔽p)=0

for all ∗≥1. This is left as an exercise. □

We will conclude with one more base change formula for THH. Recall that if k is an 𝔼∞-ring, then THH(k)=k⊗S1, so we get a map THH(k)→k of 𝔼∞-rings by

THH(k)=k⊗S1=colimS1⁡k→colimpt⁡k=k

along the projection S1→pt. In particular, the composition k→THH(k)→k is the identity.

Remark 2.2.3.10. This retract THH(k)→k does not exist if k is only 𝔼n for any finite n.

Theorem 2.2.3.11. If k is a commutative ring spectrum and R is an associative k-algebra, then

THH(R/k)≃THH(R)⊗THH(k)k.

Sketch of proof. We can rewrite □

2.2.4 The circle action on THH

We will now consider the origin of the Connes operator on Hochschild homology from an actual action of §1 on topological Hochschild homology.

Recall that a group action on an object of a 1-category 𝒞 is a functor

BG→𝒞,

where BG is a category with a single object and automorphisms given by G.

Definition 2.2.4.1. A group action of a group G on an object of a category 𝒞 is a functor

N(BG)→𝒞.

Note that N(BG) is a Kan complex with Ω(N(BG))≃G. This means that the space associated N(BG) is the classifying space of G.

Example 2.2.4.2. Note that Bℤ≃S1.

Definition 2.2.4.3. For any grouplike 𝔼1-algebra G in 𝒮 and an ∞-category 𝒞, the category of objects of 𝒞 with G-action is the functor category

Fun(BG,𝒞).

Definition 2.2.4.4. Define the homotopy orbits of an object X with G-action as the colimit

XhG=colimBG⁡X.

Similarly, define the homotopy fixed-points by the limit

XhG=limBGX.

In the category of spaces, if X has the trivial G-action, then we have

XhG≃X×BGandXhG≃Map(BG,X).

Exercise 2.2.4.5. Prove this.

The homotopy orbits should be thought of as a derived version of a quotient construction. For example, if the action of G is free, then we get an actual quotient.

Proposition 2.2.4.6. Objects in 𝒟(ℤ) with an action of S1 are equivalent to A=Λℤ(ε)-modules in 𝒟(ℤ), where ε has degree 1.

Sketch of proof. We use the fact that

Fun(BS1,𝒟(ℤ))≃ModC∗(S1).

We now need to compare C∗(S1) to its homology A, or more precisely to prove that C∗(S1) is formal. Here, we have maps These maps are isomorphisms on homology in degrees 0 and 1 and they both factor through τ≤1Free𝔼1(ε). Because τ≤1 is lax symmetric monoidal on 𝒟(ℤ)≥0, we are done. □

Remark 2.2.4.7. This equivalence is not compatible with monoidal structures on both sides. It does not give the correct answer ∞-categorically when we consider HC− and HP, but it is fine on homology.

Theorem 2.2.4.8. On HH(R/𝒞), there is a natural S1-action. More precisely, the Hochschild homology functor refines to a functor

HH:Alg𝔼1(𝒞)→Fun(BS1,𝒞)

which agrees with the S1-action on HH(R/ℤ) obtained from the Connes operator.

Definition 2.2.4.9. The paracyclic category Λ∞ is a 1-category with objects given by totally ordered sets with a ℤ-action which are equivalent to sets of the form 1nℤ and morphisms given by equivariant order-preserving maps.

There is an S1≃Bℤ-action on Λ∞ given by the map

Bℤ×Λ∞→Λ∞

acting trivially on objects and by the map

ℤ×HomΛ∞⁡(1nℤ,1mℤ)→HomΛ∞⁡(1nℤ,1mℤ)

given by translation.

Definition 2.2.4.10. The cyclic category Λ is the 1-category with the same objects as Λ∞ and morphisms given by

HomΛ⁡(1nℤ,1mℤ)=HomΛ∞⁡(1nℤ,1mℤ)/ℤ.

Lemma 2.2.4.11. We have N(Λ)=N(Λ∞)hS1.

This follows from the fact that the ℤ-action is free.

Lemma 2.2.4.12. We have an equivalence

Fun(N(Λ),𝒞)≃Fun(N(Λ∞),𝒞)hS1.

Proof. We compute mapping spaces. We need to prove that

Map(𝒟,Fun(N(Λ),𝒞))≃Map(𝒟,Fun(N(Λ∞),𝒞))hS1.

If we recall that mapping spaces were the maximal Kan complexes in functor categories, we can apply exponential laws. Therefore, it suffices to show that

Map(N(Λ),Fun(𝒟,𝒞))≃Map(N(Λ∞),Fun(𝒟,𝒞)),

which is just the definition of the colimit. □

Definition 2.2.4.13. A cyclic object in 𝒞 is a functor N(Λop)→𝒞. There is a functor Δ→Λ∞ sending [n−1] to the set ℤ×[n−1]≅1nℤ with the lexicographic order. The underlying object of a cyclic object is defined via the restriction

Fun(N(Λop),𝒞)→Fun(N(Λ∞op),𝒞)→Fun(N(Δop),𝒞).

It is natural to wonder what the geometric realization of a cyclic object is.

Lemma 2.2.4.14. The diagram commutes. More precisely, the functor Δ→Λ∞ is cofinal.

Lemma 2.2.4.15. For a cyclic object X, the object

colimΛ∞op⁡X≃colimΔop⁡X

admits an S1-action.

Proof. Recall that

Fun(N(Λ),𝒞)≃Fun(N(Λ∞),𝒞)hS1.

Taking the colimit, we obtain a functor

Fun(N(Λ∞op),𝒞)hS1→colimhS1𝒞hS1≃Fun(BS1,𝒞).
□

Exercise 2.2.4.16. For an ∞-category 𝒞 with a trivial G-action, prove that

𝒞hG≃Fun(BG,𝒞).

Proof of Theorem 2.2.4.8. We now show that the cyclic bar complex is a cyclic object. Let

Cutℤ:Λ∞op→Assact⊗

be the functor which sends a totally-ordered set S to the set of ℤ-equivariant cuts, which are just partitions of S of the form

S=⋯⊔S−1⊔S0⊔S1⊔⋯

such that each Si is a fundamental domain for the ℤ-action. We need to consider preimages along morphisms f:S→T in Λ∞. These are simply given by the set of all cuts between f(S0) and f(S1) ordered from left-to-right. The functor Cutℤ is ℤ-invariant on morphisms, so it factors through

Λ→Assact⊗.

Restricting to Δop, we obtain Cutcyc. □

Exercise 2.2.4.17. Prove that Cutℤ restricts to Cutcyc.

2.2.5 THH of the integers

In this slight digression, we will compute the topological Hochschild homology of the integers.

Theorem 2.2.5.1 (Bökstedt). We have an isomorphism

THH∗(ℤ)={ℤ∗=0ℤ/n∗=2n−10else.

In fact, THH∗(ℤ) is the homology of the dg algebra

ℤ[x]⊗Λ(e),

where |x|=2, |e|=1, and the differential is given by ∂x=e and ∂e=0.

Note that we can compute the differentials as

⋯→ℤx2→2ℤex→0ℤx→1ℤe→0ℤ→0.

Remark 2.2.5.2. In fact, as an 𝔼1-algebra over Hℤ, THH(ℤ) is the Eilenberg-Maclane functor applied to the above dg algebra.

As a consequence of this, we see that

THH(ℤ)/p=THH(ℤ)⊗HℤH𝔽p

is isomorphic on homotopy groups to the homology groups of the dg-algebra given by 𝔽p[x]⊗Λ(e) with ∂x=e and ∂e=0.

Exercise 2.2.5.3. Compute the homology of the dg-algebra 𝔽p[x]⊗Λ(e) with ∂e=x and show that it has a nontrivial ring structure.

Definition 2.2.5.4. For a ring spectrum R, define the p-completion THH(R,ℤp)≔THH(R)p∧, the rationalization THH(R,ℚ)≔THH(R)ℚ, and the ℚp version THH(R,ℚp)≔THH(R,ℤp)ℚ.

By definition, we can use the Hasse square to recover THH(R).

Lemma 2.2.5.5. We have an equivalence

THH(R,ℤp)≃THH(Rp∧,ℤp)≃HH(Rp∧/Spp∧).

Moreover, we have

THH(R,ℚ)≃THH(Rℚ/Hℚ)≃HH(Rℚ/ℚ).

Proof. First, we note that The second statement follows for a similar reason. We calculate

THH(R,ℚ)=THH(R)⊗𝕊Hℚ≃THH(R⊗𝕊Hℚ/Hℚ)≃THH(Rℚ/Hℚ).
□

As an example, we see that THH(ℤ,ℚ)=HH(ℚ/ℚ)=Hℚ. We then turn our attention to THH(ℤ,ℤp).

Theorem 2.2.5.6. We have

THH∗(ℤ,ℤp)≃{ℤp∗=0ℤp/nℤp∗=2n−10else.

This is the homology of the the dg-algebra ℤp[x]⊗Λ(e) with the differential ∂x=e.

Proof of Theorem 2.2.5.1 assuming Theorem 2.2.5.6. Using Theorem 2.2.5.6, we get that THH(ℤ,ℚp)=Hℚp. Therefore the fracture square takes the form It is easy to see now that THH0(ℤ)=ℤ and

THH2n−1(ℤ)=∏pTHH2n−1(ℤ,ℤp)=∏pℤp/nℤp=ℤ/nℤ

whenever n is nonzero. □

Definition 2.2.5.7. We define an 𝔼∞-ring spectrum

𝕊[z]≔𝕊[ℕ]=Σ+∞ℕ.

To give a discrete commutative ring R the structure of an 𝕊[z]-algebra is equivalent to giving an element π∈R (so we spend z→π). This is because any map 𝕊[z]→HR factors through Hℤ[x]. We will now consider ℤ as an 𝕊[z]-algebra by sending z to p.

Warning 2.2.5.8. If we consider a commutative ring spectrum R instead of a discrete ring, then an 𝔼∞-map 𝕊[z]→R is not the same as an element z∈π0R, or in other words 𝕊[z] is not the free 𝔼∞ algebra on a single generator. However, it is free as an 𝔼1-algebra.

Theorem 2.2.5.9 (Relative Bökstedt periodicity). We have

THH∗(ℤ/𝕊[z],ℤp)≃ℤp[x].

This has appeared in the work of Lurie, Bhatt-Morrow-Scholze, Antieau-Mathew-Nikolaus, and Krause-Nikolaus.

Proof. We first note that

THH(ℤ/𝕊[z],ℤp)/p≃THH(ℤ/𝕊[z],ℤp)⊗HℤH𝔽p.≃THH(ℤ/𝕊[z],ℤp)⊗𝕊[z]𝕊≃THH(ℤ⊗𝕊[z]𝕊/𝕊,ℤp)≃THH(𝔽p,ℤp)≃THH(𝔽p).

Now we study the long exact sequence and deduce that the homotopy groups THH∗(ℤ/𝕊[z],ℤp) are p-torsion-free and concentrated in even degrees. Therefore, there exists an element x∈THH2(ℤ/𝕊[z],ℤp) lifting x∈THH2(𝔽p). This gives us a map

ℤp[x]→THH∗(ℤ/𝕊[z],ℤp)

which is an isomorphism after mod-p reduction. Because these groups are p-torsion-free and p-complete, so this map is an isomorphism on the nose. □

Exercise 2.2.5.10. Prove that THH∗(ℤ/𝕊[z],ℤp) is p-torsion-free and concentrated in even degrees.

Recall that by the base change formula, we have

THH(R/𝕊[z])=THH(R)⊗THH(𝕊[z])𝕊[z]=THH(R)⊗Hℤ⊗𝕊THH(𝕊[z])(Hℤ⊗𝕊[z])≃THH(R)⊗HH(ℤ[z]/ℤ)ℤ[z].

We can now consider the HKR filtration on THH(ℤ[z]/ℤ), which induces a filtration on THH(R) and thus a multiplicative spectral sequence.

Proposition 2.2.5.11. There is a convergent, multiplicative spectral sequence

THHn(R/𝕊[z])⊗ℤ[z]Ωℤ[z]/ℤm⟹THHn+m(R).

Note that by definition, we have an equivalence

THH∗(R/𝕊[z])⊗ℤ[z]Ωℤ[z]/ℤ∗≃THH∗(R/𝕊[z])⊗ℤΛ(dz).

In addition, there is a similar spectral sequence in the p-complete world.

Proof of Theorem 2.2.5.6. The spectral sequence takes the form

ℤp[x]⊗ℤpΛ(dz)⟹THH∗(ℤ,ℤp).

Using homological Serre grading, the only differentials are d2.

By the Leibniz rule, it is determined by

d2(x)=α⋅dz∈ℤp⋅dz.

We see that THH1(ℤ,ℤp)=ℤp/αℤp. However, this is equal to

HH1(ℤ/ℤ;ℤp)=0,

so α is a unit in ℤp. Up to changing x by a unit, we may assume that ∂x=dz. Because each degree has a single contribution, there are no extension problems. □

2.2.6 Negative topological cyclic homology

Definition 2.2.6.1. We define negative topological cyclic homology as homotopy fixed points with respect to the S1-action on topological cyclic homology by the formula

TC−(R)≔THH(R)hS1.

Recall that an ∞-category is stable if it has finite limits and colimits and all pushout squares are also pullback squares.

Lemma 2.2.6.2. If 𝒞 is stable, there is a unique lift whoch is exact in both arguments.

In particular, objects in stable ∞-categories have mapping spectra.

Sketch of proof. In 𝒞, we write

Y≃ΩΣY≃Ω2Σ2Y≃⋯,

and therefore we have

Map(X,Y)≃ΩMap(X,ΣY)≃Ω2Map(X,Σ2Y)≃⋯,

which defines a spectrum. □

The proof of the following lemma is left as an exercise to the reader.

Lemma 2.2.6.3. If I is a small ∞-category, then

1.
The functor category Fun(I,Sp) is stable;
2.
For any such functor, we have
limIF≃mapFun(I,Sp)(𝕊,F).

We will now compare TC− to the negative cyclic homology HC−.

Proposition 2.2.6.4. We have

HC−(R)≃HH(R)hS1.

Proof. We will identify 𝒟(ℤ) with ModHℤ. In particular, we have

HH(R)hS1≃mapFun(BS1,Sp)(𝕊,HH(R))≃mapFun(BS1,ModHℤ)(Hℤ,HH(R))≃mapFun(BS1,𝒟(ℤ))(ℤ,HH(R))≃MapModC∗(S1)(ℤ,HH(R))≃MapModA(ℤ,HH(R))≃RHomA⁡(ℤ,HH(R))≃HC−(R).
□

Unfortunately, the formality result we used does not behave well with respect to monoidal structures.

Lemma 2.2.6.5. The functor (−)hS!:Fun(BS1,Sp)→Sp is lax symmetric monoidal and the §1-action on THH(R) (or HH(R)) is compatible with the product structure if R is an 𝔼∞-algebra. In particular, there is an 𝔼∞-algebra structure on TC−(R) (and HC−(R)) if R is an 𝔼∞-algebra.

If we want to do calculations, it would be helpful to understand how to compute with homotopy fixed points.

Lemma 2.2.6.6. Let BS1→Sp be an S1-action on HA for an abelian group A. Then we have

π∗(HA)hS1=A[t]

with t of degree −2.

Proof. The full subcategory of spectra on all Eilenberg-Maclane spectra (in degree 0) is a 1-category. In particular, we simply have

Map(A,B)≃Hom⁡(A,B)

where we put the discrete topology on Hom⁡(A,B). Therefore, a functor BS1→Sp which takes the basepoint to HA is actually constant. Now we are looking for homotopy fixed points for a constant action, so they are given by

HAhS1≃map(Σ+∞BS1,HA).

This has homotopy groups given by H∗(BS1,A), which gives the desired result. □

Exercise 2.2.6.7. For a spectrum X, prove that

XhS1≃map(Σ+∞BS1,X).

For a general spectrum, we can decompose it into its Postnikov tower. Unfortunately, we lose track of extension problems, but there is at least a spectral sequence.

Theorem 2.2.6.8 (Homotopy fixed points spectral sequence). There is a multiplicative, conditionally convergent spectral sequence

π∗(X)[t]⟹π∗(XhS1).

Using negative Serre grading, this spectral sequence lives completely in the second quadrant and looks like the below.

Sketch of proof. We consider the Whitehead tower

⋯τ≥2X→τ≥1X→τ≥0X→⋯

Applying homotopy fixed points, we obtain a sequence

⋯→(τ≥1X)hS1→(τ≥0X)hS1→⋯

which is not the same as taking the Whitehead tower of the homotopy fixed points. The homotopy cofibers are simply Eilenberg-Maclane spectra, so after taking homotopy fixed points they become of the form (HπiX)hS1. Therefore we obtain a filtration on XhS1, which yields a spectral sequence. □

An S1-action on X gives us a map Σ+∞S1⊗X→X. This uses the fact that S1 is a monoid in spaces, so Σ+∞S1 is a ring spectrum. The canonical map

Σ+∞S1→Σ+∞pt≃𝕊

splits, so we have a decomposition

Σ+∞S1≃𝕊⊕Σ∞S1≃𝕊⊕𝕊1.

Restricting the action to the second summand, we obtain a map

ΣX≃𝕊1⊗X→X,

or in other words a map

b:πn(X)→πn+1(X).

Lemma 2.2.6.9. In the homotopy fixed points spectral sequence, the differential d2 is determined by the formula

d2α=bα⋅t

for any α∈π∗(X) and d2t=ηt2.

Our goal is now to calculate TC−(𝔽p). The 𝔼2-page of the spectral sequence looks like

and therefore the spectral sequence degenerates at the 𝔼2-page. Therefore, TC2k−(𝔽p) are complete filtered groups with associated graded a sequence of 𝔽ps.

Now choose lifts t˜∈TC−2− and x˜∈TC2− which lift t and x, respectively. Then TC0−(𝔽p)↠𝔽p is surjective and the kernel is generated as an ideal by t˜x˜. Therefore, we have a relation

p=a⋅t˜x˜.

In order to compute a, we have a map, recall that we have a map

THH(𝔽p)→HH(𝔽p)

which is an isomorphism on τ≤2. Therefore we have an equivalence

(τ≤2THH(𝔽p))hS1→(τ≤2HH(𝔽p))hS1.

The spectral sequence for HC− showed that t˜x˜=p, and thus a is a unit. Therefore, we may assume that a=1, so t˜x˜=p, so we obtain a map

ℤp[t˜,x˜]/(p−t˜x˜)→TC∗−(𝔽p).

Theorem 2.2.6.10. This map is an isomorphism.

Corollary 2.2.6.11. We have

TC−2k(𝔽p)≃ℤp

and is generated by x˜k when k≥0 and t˜−k when k≤0.

2.2.7 Topological periodic homology

We will now define a topological version of periodic homology. As a warning, this is not defined by inverting something and may not even be periodic.

Definition 2.2.7.1. Define the topological periodic homology of a ring spectrum R as Tate fixed points by

TP(R)≔THH(R)tS1.

Because taking Tate fixed points is lax symmetric monoidal in a way that is compatible with taking homotopy fixed points, we see that TP(R) is a TC−(R)-algebra if R is commutative. The homotopy groups of this spectrum can be computed using a spectral sequence.

Proposition 2.2.7.2. For a spectrum X with G-action, there is a multiplicative, conditionally convergent spectral sequence

πp((Hπq(X))tG)⟹πp+q(XtG).

Proof sketch. Consider the Whitehead filtration τ≥∙X on X. Applying Tate fixed points, it does commute with this limit even though it does not commute with limits or colimits in general. □

If we want to use this to calculate anything, we need to understand Tate fixed points of Eilenberg-Maclane spectra with respect to S1-actions. This can also be generalized to cyclic groups, but we will not pursue this direction.

For the spectrum Hℤ, we can consider the cofiber sequence

ΣHℤhS1≃(𝕊adS1⊗Hℤ)hS1→HℤhS1→HℤtS1.

Because the first term has only nonnegative homotopy groups and the second has only nonpositive homotopy groups, we can read off the homotopy groups of the Tate fixed points. In particular, we obtain

π∗(HℤtS1)={ℤ∗ is even0else.

Lemma 2.2.7.3. We have the ring structure

π∗HℤtS1≅ℤ[t±].

Proof. Consider the Tate spectral sequence for Hℤ⊗Σ+∞S1. Because this has a free action, we have

(Hℤ⊗Σ+∞S1)tS1=0.

The spectral sequence takes the form

and so the only way for the spectral sequence to yield zero is for all maps d2 to be isomorphisms. Using the multiplicative structure, we do not get a ring but instead a module over the Tate construction on Hℤ.

Fix generators xi of π2iHℤtS1 with x−i=ti. Also fix generators σ0 and σ1 of H∗(S1), so that the generator in degree (2i,j) is xi⋅σj. We then compute

d2(σ0)=±x−1t⋅σ1,

where the sign depends on our previous choices. This implies that

d2(xiσ0)=±xi⋅tσ1=±xi−1⋅σi.

Therefore, up to a sign, we have xi⋅t=xi−1. We may choose the xi such that all signs are positive, but this now determines the ring structure. □

Exercise 2.2.7.4. Using a similar approach to the one given here, compute π∗(HℤtCm) as a ring. Hint: use a free action of Cm on a space with easy homology groups.

Remark 2.2.7.5. If we run the same argument with HA⊗Σ+∞S1 as an Hℤ-module, then we obtain

π∗HAtS1=A[t±].

When A is a ring, this is also true as a ring.

Proposition 2.2.7.6. If X is an object of Fun(BS1,ModHℤ) (equivalently a module over Hℤ in Fun(BS1,Sp)), then we have

XtS1≃XhS1⊗HℤhS1HℤtS1.

In a weaker form, on homotopy groups we have

π∗XtS1≃π∗XhS1[t−1].

Sketch of proof. We have an expression

HℤtS1≃colim⁡(HℤtS1→tΣ2HℤtS1→t⋯)

as HℤhS1-modules. Therefore, we need to prove that XtS1 is the same kind of colimit, or in other words that

XtS1≃colim⁡(XtS1→tΣ2XtS1→t⋯).

This clearly works when X is an Eilenberg-Maclane spectrum. Both sides are compatible with fiber sequences, which gives us the case when X has finitely many nonzero homotopy groups. To extend to arbitrary X, we need some connectivity arguments, which we will omit here. □

Exercise 2.2.7.7. Prove that

HℤtS1≃colim⁡(HℤtS1→tΣ2HℤtS1→t⋯)

as HℤhS1-modules.

Given that we are calling TP topological periodic homology, we would like to see how it is related to the usual periodic homology.

Proposition 2.2.7.8. We have

HP(R)=HH(R)tS1.

Proof. Because HH(R) is an Hℤ-module, we see that HH(R)tS1 is obtained from HH(R)hS1=HC−(R) by inverting t. This is exactly how we defined periodic cyclic homology. □

We will now return to topological periodic homology.

Proposition 2.2.7.9. The Tate spectral sequence for Tate fixed points of S1-actions takes the form

π∗(X)[t±]⟹π∗(XtS1).

Applying this to topological Hochschild homology gives us a spectral sequence

THH∗(R)[t±]⟹TP∗(R).

We are now ready to apply it to compute TP(𝔽p).

Theorem 2.2.7.10. We have

TP∗(𝔽p)=ℤp[t±].

Proof. Note that the Tate spectral sequence is simply a periodized of the homotopy fixed points spectral sequence, at least on the 𝔼2-page. Therefore, it degenerates at the 𝔼2-page. The spectral sequence looks like

and therefore we have just periodized all of the extension problems. Using the map from TC−, we see that

π−2kTP(𝔽p)=π−2kTC−(𝔽p)≃ℤpt˜k.

We will also choose a lift t−1˜ of t−1. But now we see that

t˜⋅t−1˜=1(modhigher filtration),

so it must be a unit. But then t˜ is invertible and its negative powers t˜−k generate π2k(TP(𝔽p)). □

Warning 2.2.7.11. If the Tate spectral sequence has differentials, then topological periodic homology may not be periodic. There are even examples with infinitely many differentials where TP becomes connective.

2.2.8 The cyclotomic structure

There is an additional structure on topological Hochschild homology which does now exist on ordinary Hochschild homology. This is a map

THH(R)→THH(R)tCp.

Construction 2.2.8.1. Assume we have a fiber sequence

X→Y→Z

of pointed connected spaces. Because these are bar constructions of group objects, we write it as

BH→BG→BG/H.

Then there is a functor

B(G/H)→𝒮

which sends pt↦BH which classifies BG, i.e. G/H acts on BH such that

(BH)hG/H≃BG.

Exercise 2.2.8.2. For a normal subgroup H⊆G of a finite group, describe the G/H-action on BH obtained from the fiber sequence

BH→BG→B(G/H).

As a consequence, for any ∞-category 𝒞, we have an equivalence

Fun(BG,𝒞)≃Fun(BH,𝒞)hG/H.

With some additional work, this implies that the functors

(−)hH,(−)tH:Fun(BH,𝒞)→𝒞

induce functors

(−)hH,(−)tH:Fun(BG,𝒞)≃Fun(BH,𝒞)hG/H→Fun(pt,𝒞)hG/H≃Fun(BG/H,𝒞).

In particular, this means that for any normal subgroup H⊆G, if X has a G-action, then XhH and XtH have residual G/H-actions such that

(XhH)hG/H≃XhG.

Example 2.2.8.3. Let G=𝕋=U(1)=S1 and H=Cp⊆𝕋 be a cyclic group of prime order embedded as p-th roots of unity. For an object X∈𝒞B𝕋, we see that XhCp and XtCp have residual 𝕋/Cp-actions. We identify 𝕋/Cp≃𝕋 by the map z↦zp.

Definition 2.2.8.4. A cyclotomic structure on a spectrum X∈SpBS1 is given by maps

φp:X→XtCp

which are 𝕋-equivariant for every prime p. We refer to φp as the cyclotomic Frobenius. A cyclotomic spectrum is a spectrum with a 𝕋-action and cyclotomic structure.

The main fact about cyclotomic spectra that we will discuss is the following.

Theorem 2.2.8.5. For every ring spectrum R, THH(R) admits a natural cyclotomic structure.

Remark 2.2.8.6. The cyclotomic structure on THH(R) is induced from the Tate diagonal

Δp:Id→Tp

on spectra. It does not exist for HH(R/𝒞) where 𝒞 is an arbitrary stable symmetric monoidal ∞-category. In fact, one can prove that on 𝒟(ℤ) there is no natural map

X→(X⊗ℤ⋯⊗ℤX)tCp.

Therefore, HH(R/ℤ) does not admit any kind of cyclotomic structure.

We will now construct the cyclotomic structure. We will first give a construction in the case of an 𝔼∞-ring. First, we will need to discuss induction of G-objects. Let 𝒞 be an ∞-category with all small colimits. Then we have a forgetful functor

𝒞BG→𝒞

for any group G.

Proposition 2.2.8.7. This functor has a left adjoint given by

c∈𝒞↦colimG⁡(constc)=c⊗G

with the G-action on G.

Proof. Note that

Map𝒞BG(c⊗G,d)≃Map𝒞(c⊗G,d)hG≃Map𝒮(G,Map𝒞(c,d))hG≃Map𝒞(c,d).
□

Example 2.2.8.8. Suppose that 𝒞=Sp and G is finite. Then

⨁g∈Gc

is the “free” object.

Example 2.2.8.9. If G=𝕋, the free 𝕋-object is

c⊗𝕋=c⊕c[1].

Example 2.2.8.10. This is the important example for the construction we want to perform. Let 𝒞=CAlg(Sp) and G be a finite group. If R∈CAlg(Sp), then

colimG⁡(R)=R⊗⋯⊗R⏟|G| times=R⊗G.

Proposition 2.2.8.11. For R∈CAlg(Sp), the map

R→THH(R)

exhibits THH(R) as the free 𝔼∞-ring with an S1-action under R.

Proof. By our general formula, the free object is given by

colimS1⁡(R)=R⊗S1.

As discussed previously, this colimit is THH(R). We will omit the proof of the property that the S1-action agrees with the one previously constructed. □

Construction 2.2.8.12. For every R∈CAlg(Sp), the map R→THH(R) is a map of 𝔼∞-rings. The target has an action of 𝕋, so we obtain an induced Cp-action. Therefore, there is a unique extension a Cp-equivariant map

R⊗⋯⊗R⏟p times→THH(R).

Taking Tate fixed points, we obtain a map

(R⊗⋯R)tCp→THH(R)tCp.

Also recall that the Tate diagonal is a map

R→(R⊗⋯⊗R)tCp

of 𝔼∞ rings.

Exercise 2.2.8.13. Check that the map R⊗p→THH(R) agrees with the inclusion of the degree p part of the cyclic bar complex.

Using the universal property of THH(R), we obtain the cyclotomic Frobenius.

Proposition 2.2.8.14. There is a unique 𝕋-equivariant map

THH(R)→THH(R)tCp

of 𝔼∞-rings fitting into the diagram

We will now move on to the case when R is only an 𝔼1-algebra. Recall that by definition, we had

THH(R)=colimΔop⁡(R⊗(n+1))≕colim∙∈Δop⁡(THH(R)∙),

where THH(R)∙:Λ→Sp is a cyclic object. This can be written as where R⊗n+1 carries an action of Cn+1. There is another cyclic object (sdp⁡THH(R))tCp given by and the cyclotomic structure on THH(R) arises by taking the levelwise Tate diagonal. The main complication comes from the way of viewing the target as a cyclic object.

Exercise 2.2.8.15. For an ordinary ring R, explicitly describe a cyclic object whose underlying simplicial object has degree k part (R⊗(k+1)p)Cp.

As a result, we obtain a map

THH(R)→colimΔop⁡((sdp⁡THH(R))tCp)→(colim[n]∈Δop⁡(R⊗(n+1)p))tCp=THH(R)tCp.

2.2.9 The definition of TC

We are finally ready to define topological cyclic homology. In fact, we will give two equivalent definitions, one of which is useful for theoretical purposes and one of which is useful for calcuations.

Definition 2.2.9.1. The ∞-category of cyclotomic spectra is the fiber product In particular, a map (X,φp)→(Y,φp′) is given by the data of

1.
A 𝕋-equivariant map f:X→Y;
2.
A 𝕋-equivariant homotopy filling the square for every prime p.

In the ∞-category of cyclotomic spectra, the mapping spaces are given by the equalizer In fact, more is true. We will leave the following proposition as an exercise.

Proposition 2.2.9.2. The ∞-category CycSp of cyclotomic spectra is a stable ∞-category and the mapping spectra are given by the equalizer Moreover, CycSp has all limits and colimits. In addition, CycSp has a symmetric monoidal structure given by

(X,φp)⊗(Y,φp′)=(X⊗𝕊Y,X⊗𝕊Y→XtCp⊗𝕊YtCp→(X⊗𝕊Y)tCp).

In this monoidal structure, a commutative algebra in CycSp is given by

1.
A commutative ring spectrum X∈CAlg(Sp)B𝕋 with 𝕋-action;
2.
A 𝕋-equivariant map of commutative algebras
φp:X→XtCp

for all primes p.

In particular, if R is an 𝔼∞-ring, then THH(R) is a commutative algebra in CycSp.

Now recall that negative topological cyclic homology was defined by

TC−(R)=THH(R)hS1=MapSpB𝕋(𝕊,THH(R)).

We will now give a similar description for TC. In order to do this, we need to give 𝕊 the structure of a cyclotomic spectrum.

Example 2.2.9.3. The sphere spectrum 𝕊 (with the trivial action) is naturally an 𝔼∞ cyclotomic spectrum.

  • The underlying spectrum with 𝕋-action is 𝕊 with the trivial action;

2.2.11 TC of perfect rings

Our goal is now to generalize the computation of TC(𝔽p) to any perfect ring of characteristic p. In this generality, we will need to replace ℤp by the Witt vectors. Recall that if k is a perfect 𝔽p-algebra, then

THH∗(k)=k[x].

Recall that there is a commutative ring W(k) called the p-typical Witt vectors of k which is p-torsion free, p-complete, and has W(k)/p≃k. Moreover, it is uniquely determined by these properties.

Theorem 2.2.11.1. Let R be any derived p-complete ring. Then the reduction mod p map

HomCRing⁡(W(k),R)→HomCRing⁡(k,R/p)

is a bijection.

Proof. If R=lim←⁡R/pn is p-complete, then we use obstruction theory to inductively lift maps through the square-zero extension R/pn+1→R/pn. For more details, see Section A.2.2. If R is derived p-complete, then

R=lim←⁡R⫽pn

as an animated ring. Therefore, as in the first step we can reduce to R⫽p. We conclude by using the fact that R⫽p→R/p is a square-zero extension. □

The following corollary is left as an exercise.

Corollary 2.2.11.2. We have an equivalence of categories

F:W(k)→W(k)

called the Witt vector Frobenius such that

F/p:k→k

is the Frobenius.

TC∗−(k)≅W(k)[x,t]/(xt−p)andTP∗(k)≅W(k)[t±].

Remark 2.2.11.5. Note that W(𝔽p)=ℤp, so this matches our previous computation.

xt=p∈TC0−(k).

However, xt cannot be a zero divisor because this is true on the spectral sequence, so TC0−(k) is p-torsion free and p-complete with mod-p reduction k. Therefore, we have

TC0−(k)≅W(k).

The rest follows because the spectral sequences are functorial. Periodizing the spectral sequences, we obtain the result for TP. □

We will now need to understand the maps

can,φ:TC−(k)→TP(k).

We know that can⁡(x)=pt−1, can⁡(t)=t, and can⁡(r)=r for r∈W(k). We also know that φ(x)=t−1 and φ(t)=pt. It remains to study its effect on W(k).

Remark 2.2.11.6. For any connective ring spectrum, the map π0can:TC0−(R)→TP0(R) is an isomorphism for degree reasons. Thus we can consider π0φ as an endomorphism of TC0−(R)=TP0(R). This is one of the beginnings of the theory of prismatic cohomology.

2.2.12 Frobenius lifts and group rings

We will now study cyclotomic spectra with Frobenius lifts, i.e. spectra where the Frobenius factors through homotopy fixed points. Some examples are Xtr, but more interesting examples are spherical group rings. In these cases, we will give a more explicit formula for TC.

Definition 2.2.12.1. A p-cyclotomic spectrum with Frobenius lift is a p-cyclotomic spectrumm X with a 𝕋-equivariant factorization

X→ψpXhCp→XtCp

of the Frobenius.

Example 2.2.12.2. By definition, the cyclotomic spectrum Xtr with the trivial action has a Frobenius lift because φp was defined as the composite

X→XhCp→XtCp.

This can be viewed as the map

map(Σ+∞pt,X)→map(Σ+∞BCp,X).

If X has a Frobenius lift, the map φ:Xh𝕋→Xt𝕋 factors as In particular, the map φ−can:Xh𝕋→Xt𝕋 factors as We may now try to use this formula to study TC.

Proof sketch. Recall that TC is the homotopy fiber of the map φ−can. Therefore, we have a diagram so the square on the left is a pullback. The proof that the bottom square is a pullback is omitted. □

TC(Xtr)=X⊕(X⊗fib⁡(Σ𝕊h𝕋→tr𝕊)).

The spectrum fib⁡(Σ𝕊h𝕋→tr𝕊) is usually called Σℂℙ−1∞. Here, if we desuspend it, it has cells in even degrees starting in degree −2, hence the name.

We will now turn to the case of spherical group rings. Let G be an 𝔼1-group in 𝒮. Recall that Ω and B give an equivalence between these and pointed connected spaces. We will define the group ring to be the spectrum

𝕊[G]≔Σ+∞G.

In order to understand TC, we will need to understand THH.

Lemma 2.2.12.6. We have the formula

THH(𝕊[G])=Σ+∞LBG,

where L denotes the free loop space.

Proof. Because THH(𝕊[G]) was defined by the cyclic bar construction, we can pull the suspension out of the colimit and obtain

THH(𝕊[G])=Σ+∞|Barcyc(G)|.

We now compare Barcyc(G) with the cyclic object Fun(S∙,BG), where Sn is the groupoid given by a cycle on {0,…,n}. Unfortunately, Fun(Sn,BG) is not G×n, so there is no levelwise isomorphism. However, it is equivalent to GhG×n×n, where G×n acts by conjugation on adjacent factors.

This implies that |Fun⁡(S∙,BG)| is obtained from |Barcyc(G)| by taking orbits under where the boundary maps are projections. This is contractible. Now we have

Fun(Sn,BG)=Map(|Sn|,BG)≃Map(S1,BG)≃LBG.
□

Exercise 2.2.12.7. Prove that for a space X, the simplicial space has contractible realization.

1.
The 𝕋-action on THH(𝕊[G])=Σ+∞LBG comes from the 𝕋-action on LBG given by rotating loops.
2.
The Frobenius morphism Σ+∞LBG→Σ+∞LBGtCp admits a lift Σ+∞LBG→Σ+∞LBGhCp coming from the Cp-invariant map LBG→LBG defined by precomposition with the degree p endomorphism of S1.

The proof of this uses the fact that the Tate diagonal 𝕊[G]→(𝕊[G]⊗p)tCp lifts through the actual diagonal G→G⊗p.

Σ+∞LBG→ψp−idΣ+∞LBG

Proof. It suffices to p-complete the cofibers of the two rows and check that they are equivalent. They are given by (Σ+∞LBG)hℕ≃Σ+∞(ψp−1LBG)hℤ and (Σ+∞BG)hℕ≃(Σ+∞BG)hℤ, respectively. Therefore, it suffices to prove that

ψp−1LBG→BG

To prove this, we will consider fiber sequences in spaces. More precisely, consider the sequence of fiber sequences. In the colimit, we obtain the fiber sequence1

p−1G≃p−1G0→ψp−1LBG→BG.

Now the homology H∗(G0,𝔽p) is a connected Hopf algebra and p induces the map

H∗(G0)→ΔH∗(G0)⊗p→μH∗(G0).

This map is not necessarily zero, but it is degreewise nilpotent. □

is degreewise nilpotent.

Appendix A
Simplicial rings and cotangent complexes

A.1 Simplicial rings and divided power structures

Definition A.1.0.1. The category scRing of simplicial commutative rings is defined to be the functor category

scRing≔Fun(Δop,cRing).

More precisely, this is a diagram satisfying the usual conditions for face and degeneracy maps.

Theorem A.1.0.2 (Eilenberg-Zilber). The functor

sAb→Ch

sending a simplicial abelian group to the associated chain complex is lax symmetric monoidal with respect to the pointwise tensor product on simplicial abelian groups and the usual tensor product on chain complexes.

This implies that every simplicial commutative ring produces a commutative dg algebra. We will now make this product structure explicit.

Definition A.1.0.3. An (m,n)-shuffle is a function

(μ,ν):[m+n]→[m]×[n]

satisfying the following conditions:

  • Both μ and ν are surjective and order preserving;

  • The maps μ and ν jump at disjoint positions. For example, consider the case when m=n−2, as in Figure A.1.

    We can see that an (m,n)-shuffle is simply a way to shuffle m red and n blue cards together. There is a unique permutation which takes the configuration having all red cards on top to our given shuffle.

Proposition A.1.0.4. Let R∈scRing. Then there is a map Rm⊗Rn→⋅Rm+n given by the formula

x⋅y=∑(μ,ν)sign⁡(μ,ν)sμ(x)sν(y),

where sμ(x) and sν(y) correspond to applying the degeneracies making up μ and ν to obtain elements of Rm+n. This gives R the structure of a strict cdga.

Proof. We will not go through all of the combinatorics explicitly.

  • To prove associativity, we can express both (xy)z and x(yz) as a sum

    ∑(λ,μ,ν)sign⁡(λ,μ,ν)sλ(x)sμ(y)sν(z).

  • To check commutativity, the fact that R was a simplicial commutative ring means we can exchange the roles of μ and ν up to

    sign⁡(μ,ν)sign⁡(ν,μ)=(−1)mn,

    which is exactly what we desire.

  • A variant of this argument also gives strictness. When we compute x2, the summands corresponding to (μ,ν) and (ν,μ) appear with opposite signs, so we see that x2=0.
  • The differential is given by the alternating sum of the face maps. Applying this to x⋅y will decompose the result into (m−1,n)-shuffles and (m,n−1)-shuffles, which yields the desired result. □

We will now discuss divided power structures. In fact, every simplicial commutative ring will give us one of these.

Proposition A.1.0.5. Let R∈scRing be a simplicial commutative ring. Then there exist maps γk:Rn→Rnk for all n,k≥1 such that

  • We have γ1(x)=x for all x∈R;

  • We also have

    γk(x)γℓ(x)=(k+ℓℓ)γk+ℓ(x)

    for all k,ℓ. This means that we should think that xk=k!γk(x);

  • For all x,y∈Rn, we have

    γk(x+y)=∑i+k=kγi(x)γj(y);

  • Similarly, we have

    γk(xy)=xkγk(y);

  • We have the identity

    γk(γℓ(x))=(kℓ)!k!(ℓ!)kγkℓ(x).

Proof. If x is odd, we define γ1(x)=x and γk(x)=0 for all k≥2. This is fine because x2=0 already. If x is even, we have

xk=∑(μ1,…,μk)sign⁡(μ1,…,μk)sμ1(x)⋯sμk(x).

We can permute the factors μ1,…,μk (all of the signs will become +1), and therefore for all σ∈Σk, (μ1,…,μk) and (μσ(1),…,μσ(k)) give the same summand. Choosing one element from each equivalent class, we obtain an element γk(x) such that xk=k!γk(x).

We will omit checking that the properties are satisfied. □

We now need to make sure that this divided power structure behaves well with respect to the chain differential.

Proposition A.1.0.6. Let R∈scRing be a simplicial commutative ring. Then

  • If x is even, then dγk(x)=γk−1(x)⋅dx;
  • The maps γk preserve boundaries;
  • The γk give a well-defined divided power structure on H∗(R).

Proof. Suppose that x is a boundary. Then x=dy for x with diy=0 for all i>0. Define

γk′(y)≔∑(μ1,…,μk)Σk-representativessign⁡(μ1,…,μk)sμ1′(y)⋯sμk′(y).

Here, for maps μi:[kn]→[n], we set μi′:[1+kn]→[1+n] to be the maps given by sticking a 1 in front. Then d0γk′(y)=γk(x) and diγk′(y)=0 for all i>0, and therefore dγk′(y)=γk(x). □

A.2 Cotangent complexes and obstruction theory

A.2.1 Definition of the cotangent complex

Recall that we defined

LΩ−/k1:Ani(k−alg)→𝒟(ℤ)≥0

as the nonabelian derived functor of

Ω1:k−alg→Ab.

Lemma A.2.1.1. The following constructions agree:

1.
The functor
LΩ−/k1:Ani(k−alg)→𝒟(ℤ)≥0

evaluated on R;

2.
The functor
L(A↦R⊗AΩA/k1):Ani(k−alg/R)→𝒟(R)≥0

evaluated on R.

Proof. If we begin with the second construction, we obtain

colimi∈Δop⁡R⊗AiΩAi/k1≃colimi∈Δop⁡(colimj∈Δop⁡Aj)⊗Ai𝕃ΩAi/k1≃colimi∈Δop⁡(colimj∈Δi/op⁡Aj)⊗Ai𝕃ΩAi/k1≃colimi→j∈(Δop)Δ1⁡Aj⊗Ai𝕃ΩAi/k1≃colimi∈Δop⁡ΩAi/k1≃LΩR/k1.

with Ai polynomial rings. Here, we have used the fact that identity morphisms are cofinal in the arrow category. □

The second functor has better categorical properties than the first. Namely, it commutes with coproducts. By definition, this implies that it preserves all colimits.

Example A.2.1.2. If R=k[x1,…,xn]/(f1,…,fm) is defined by a regular sequence, then the diagram is a pushout in Ani(k−alg/R). The functor L(R⊗∙Ω∙/k1) takes this to where the top arrow is the Jacobian matrix of f1,…,fm. This is also a pushout in 𝒟(R)≥0, and therefore LΩR/k1 has as H0 and H1 the cokernel and kernel of the Jacobian matrix.

Definition A.2.1.3. We will call ΩR/k1 the cotangent complex of R relative to k and denote it by LR/k.

A.2.2 Applications to obstruction theory of rings

Let S be a ring and M be an S-module. We can form a split square-zero extension on the S-module S⊕M where

  • If m1,m2∈M, we have m1m2=0;
  • Elements of s multiply as usual;
  • If s∈S and m∈M, then sm is given by the usual action of s on M.

We would like to understand when there is a lift in the diagram These lifts correspond to φ-linear derivations R→M, which are simply R-module maps

ΩR/k1→φ∗M.

Proposition A.2.2.1. There exists a functor

𝒟(S)≥0→Ani(k−alg)/S

which sends a projective module P to the square-zero extension S⊕P. We have equivalences of mapping spaces

Map𝒟(R)≥0(LR/k,φ∗M)≃Fiber⁡(MapAni(k−alg)(R,S⊕M)↓MapAni(k−alg)(R,S)).

We would now like to apply this to study ordinary rings. Given a surjective R˜→R whose kernel I satisfies I2=0, we will call this a (not necessarily split) square-zero extension. One example of a non-split square-zero extension is

ℤ/p2→ℤ/p,

which does not even split as a morphism of abelian groups. Note that the condition that I2=0 implies that the R˜-action on I factors through R.

It turns out that LR/R˜ has H0=0 and

H1=R⊗R˜I=I.

There is a tautological morphism

LR/R˜→I[1]

of R-modules which induces an isomorphism on H1. This corresponds to a map

δ:R→R⊕I[1]

of animated R˜-algebras.

Proposition A.2.2.2. R˜ is the pullback of the diagram in the category of animated R˜-algebras.

We see that (not necessarily split) square-zero extensions R˜→R along I correspond to maps

LR/k→I[1].

Maps S→R˜ lifting a given S→R correspond to diagrams of the form which are simply lifts If we unwrap everything, we see that a lift exists if and only if the map

LS/k→I[1]

is nullhomotopic. Furthermore, lifts are in correspondence to choices of nullhomotopies. These form a torsor over π1(Map(LS/k,I[1])). We therefore see that

  • The possible square-zero extensions R˜ are classified by

    π0Map𝒟(R)(LR/k,I[1]);

  • For a given R˜ and S→R, there is an obstruction living in

    π0Map𝒟(S)(LS/k,I[1]).

  • If lifts do exist, they are parameterized by

    π1Map𝒟(S)(LS/k,I[1])≃π0Map𝒟(S)(LS/k,I).

Exercise A.2.2.3. Let S be a k-algebra. Show that the following are equivalent:

1.
For every square-zero extension R˜→R and every S→R, there is a lift (this is usually called being formally smooth).
2.
We have H1(LS/k)=0 and H0(LS/k) is a projective S-module.

We are now ready to apply this machinery.

Theorem A.2.2.4. If R1 is a perfect 𝔽p-algebra (this means that Frobenius is an automorphism), then there exist flat ℤ/pn-algebras Rn, unique up to isomorphism, with

R1≃Rn⊗ℤ/pn𝔽p.

In particular, we have

Rn−1≅Rn⊗ℤ/pnℤ/pn−1,

so we have a tower

⋯→Rn→Rn−1→⋯

whose lift

R≔limRn

is the unique flat, p-complete ℤp-algebra satisfying

R1≅R⊗ℤp𝔽p.

This theorem tells us that there is a way to escape from the positive characteristic to the mixed characteristic setting under the assumption that R1 is perfect.

We will characterize Rn as a non-split square-zero extension of Rn−1 by R1. This is because if it exists, tensoring

0→ℤ/p→ℤ/pn→ℤ/pn−1→0

with Rn gives us

0→R1→Rn→Rn−1→0.

These extensions are classified by

π0Map𝒟(Rn−1)(LRn−1/ℤ,R1[1]).

They also need to be compatible with the element of

π0Map𝒟(ℤ/pn−1)(L(ℤ/pn−1)/ℤ,ℤ/p[1])

classifying ℤ/pn→ℤ/pn−1.

Lemma A.2.2.5. Isomorphism classes of such Rn form a torsor over

π0Map𝒟(Rn−1)(LRn−1/ℤ/pn−1,Rn[1])≃π0Map𝒟(R1)(LR1/𝔽p,R1[1]).

Lemma A.2.2.6. If R1 is a perfect 𝔽p-algebra, then LR1/𝔽p≃0.

Proof. For any perfect 𝔽p-algebra A, we will consider the effect of the Frobenius φ:A→A on the contangent complex. This induces the zero morphism on ΩA/𝔽p1 (in particular for polynomial rings). Therefore, if we resolve R1 by polynomial rings, φ acts by 0 on LR1/𝔽p. However, because we assumed that R1 is perfect, it must also act by an isomorphism. The desired result follows immediately. □

Putting together the two lemmas, we see that there is a unique isomorphism class of possible Rn, which proves Theorem A.2.2.4.

Definition A.2.2.7. The R in Theorem A.2.2.4 is called the Witt vectors of R and denoted by W(R0).

Remark A.2.2.8. Usually the Witt vectors are given by an explicit construction and exist for any 𝔽p-algebra, not just perfect ones, but we believe this explanation is much more satisfying.

Example A.2.2.9. Consider the finite field 𝔽pn. The Witt vectors W(𝔽pn) is a ℤp-algebra with

W(𝔽pn)/p≃𝔽pn.

One way to construct this is to consider 𝔽pn=𝔽p[x]/f(x) and take the ring

ℤp[x]/f˜(x)

for some lift f˜ of f.

1Not in the technical sense.

2We will not discuss what this is even though it is very fundamental for working with ∞-categories.

1Because p is a morphism of spaces and not of groups, p−1G looks more algebraic than it is.
